title: Reviewer Exam Simulator
source: Almoradie A. MEMORY LAB: The Memory-First Medical Laboratory Science Reviewer. 1st ed., v2.0. 2026. Exam Simulator and Answer Key.
permission: Imported at the request of the user, who stated on 2026-10-07 that they hold the rights to the reviewer.
verification: Questions, answers and explanations are the reviewer’s own and have not been verified by this app or by a human expert. Notes link known problems to the reviewer accuracy register; a question without a note is not thereby verified.

questions.stem: A brain tissue sample from a suspected prion-disease autopsy must be decontaminated before disposal. Which agent is effective against prions?

options.text: Sodium hypochlorite, high concentration (20,000 ppm available chlorine)

questions.explanation: High-concentration sodium hypochlorite (CDC/WHO prion protocols: 1N NaOH or 20,000 ppm NaOCl soak for 1 hour, then autoclave at 121°C for 1 hour; surfaces: ≥5,000 ppm hypochlorite or 1N NaOH) inactivates prions. Bleach is not the only route — NaOH-based protocols with autoclaving are equally recognized. The trap is assuming any strong disinfectant — formalin, glutaraldehyde, or routine dry heat — works; they do not (formalin fixation preserves prion infectivity). Concentration note: a 1:10 dilution of household bleach ≈ 0.5% (≈5,000 ppm) sodium hypochlorite — undiluted household bleach is ~5.25%.

notes.note: Check prion decontamination details against current WHO/CDC guidance; see the register for specifics.

questions.stem: During a CAP inspection, the inspector pulls a 6-year-old blood bank donor record and a 3-year-old chemistry QC log, then asks which must still be on file. What is the correct response?

options.text: The donor record must be kept (10 years); the QC log may be discarded (2 years)
The QC log must be kept; the donor record may be discarded

questions.explanation: Run the "2-5-10-20" record ladder: QC/requisitions 2 years, blood bank QC 5 years, blood bank patient/donor records 10 years, cytogenetic reports 20 years.

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory launches a defect-reduction program targeting fewer than 3.4 defects per million procedures. Which methodology and originator match this target?
questions.explanation: Six Sigma (Motorola, 1986 — Bill Smith) targets fewer than 3.4 defects per million procedures; Lean (Toyota, 1980s) is about waste reduction and streamlining, not a defect rate.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist draws the lavender EDTA tube before the light blue citrate tube. The coagulation results will most likely show

options.text: No change if the tubes are mixed well
Falsely shortened PT with normal APTT

questions.explanation: Order of draw puts citrate second and EDTA fifth — EDTA carryover chelates calcium and falsely prolongs PT/APTT. Blue before lavender, always.

notes.note: The order of draw matches WHO 2010, but closed-system studies did not always find EDTA carry-over from wrong order alone.

questions.stem: When blood cultures are ordered with other tests, they are collected before any other tube. What is the primary reason?

options.text: Blood cultures require the largest volume
The needle is cleanest at first stick, so drawing cultures first minimizes skin-flora contamination
Blood cultures must clot before the serum tube is drawn

questions.explanation: Blood cultures go first because the venipuncture needle is cleanest before it passes through tube stoppers and additives — minimizing contamination with skin flora that causes false-positive cultures.

questions.stem: A glucose assay reads an absorbance of 2.8 on the spectrophotometer. The best course of action is

options.text: Dilute the sample, rerun, and multiply by the dilution factor
Switch to a silicate glass cuvette

questions.explanation: Beer's law (A = abc) holds only below A ≈ 2.0 — above that, linearity fails, so dilute the sample and multiply by the dilution factor.

questions.stem: A urine drug screen by immunoassay is positive for amphetamines. Which step confirms the result?

options.text: Report the immunoassay result as positive
Repeat the immunoassay on the same specimen
Quantitate with a second immunoassay kit

questions.explanation: Immunoassays screen because they're fast and lean toward false positives; mass spectrometry is the confirmatory test in drug toxicology.

questions.stem: A laboratory's automation RFP states maximum acceptable 90th-percentile turnaround times: general chemistry 30 minutes, immunoassay 45 minutes, CBC 20 minutes. A vendor's proposal guarantees 90th-percentile TATs of 45 minutes for general chemistry, 30 minutes for immunoassay, and 20 minutes for CBC. The lab director rejects the proposal as noncompliant. Which statement best supports the rejection?

options.text: The proposal is fully compliant; the director is mistaken
Only the chemistry guarantee is noncompliant — 45 minutes exceeds the RFP's 30-minute maximum
Only the immunoassay guarantee is noncompliant — 30 minutes exceeds the RFP's 45-minute maximum
All three guarantees exceed the RFP's stated maximum requirements

questions.explanation: Only the chemistry guarantee (45 min) exceeds the RFP's stated 30-minute maximum; immunoassay (30 min) beats its 45-minute maximum and CBC (20 min) meets its maximum. TAT targets come from the lab's own RFP, not universal goals.

questions.stem: A quantitative serum β-hCG returns 18 mIU/mL. The lab's interpretation interval is: <5 mIU/mL negative, 5–25 mIU/mL equivocal/borderline, >25 mIU/mL positive. How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Equivocal/borderline — follow up with repeat/serial testing

questions.explanation: 18 mIU/mL falls in the 5–25 mIU/mL equivocal/borderline interval (<5 negative, >25 positive); report as equivocal and follow up with repeat/serial β-hCG and clinical correlation.

questions.stem: A screening test with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity is used in a population where disease prevalence is 1 in 10,000. A positive patient's approximate chance of truly having the disease is
questions.explanation: Predictive value depends on prevalence — even a 99/99 test gives only ~1% PPV at 1-in-10,000 prevalence. The trap is confusing sensitivity/specificity (test properties) with predictive value (which needs prevalence).

questions.stem: A dehydrated elderly patient has BUN 60 mg/dL and creatinine 2.0 mg/dL. A BUN/creatinine ratio of 30:1 most suggests
questions.explanation: BUN/creatinine >20:1 points to prerenal azotemia (volume depletion raises urea reabsorption); true renal disease keeps the 10:1–20:1 ratio because both rise together.

questions.stem: A patient with Hct 25% has a reticulocyte count of 7%. The resident calls this an excellent marrow response. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Correct — 7% reticulocytes is 7× the normal production rate
Cannot be assessed without the absolute reticulocyte count
Understated — the true production rate is 14× normal
Overstated — correct for anemia severity and shift time: at Hct 25% retics linger ~2 days, so production is only ~2× normal

questions.explanation: This is the corrected-reticulocyte trap — a raw retic % means nothing without correcting for anemia severity and maturation shift time. Corrected retic index = (retic%/1%) × (patient Hct/0.45) ÷ shift time; 7% at Hct 25% with a 2-day shift = ~2× normal, not 7×.

questions.stem: A laboratory compares a new POC glucose meter against the core-lab hexokinase method using 40 patient samples spanning 40–400 mg/dL. Which regression approach is appropriate for estimating the bias between the two methods?

options.text: Ordinary least squares regression of the meter on the core-lab method
Deming regression, because both methods have measurement error
Multiple linear regression with hematocrit as a covariate

questions.explanation: Ordinary regression assumes x is error-free; Deming regression accounts for error in both methods — demand slope ≈ 1 and intercept ≈ 0 before accepting the replacement.

questions.stem: After a reagent lot change, QC values shift but patient-sample comparison (Deming regression) shows agreement. The correct QC action is

options.text: Adjust the QC target only — do not change the SD
Recalculate both the target and SD from the new lot's data

questions.explanation: Noncommutable QC materials can shift independently of patient samples, so adjust the target value only. The trap is recalculating the SD too — changing the SD after a matrix shift hides real low-bias errors and manufactures false confidence.

questions.stem: A laboratory rejects runs whenever the 1_2s rule is violated. Over a month, 10% of runs are rejected and repeated, but repeat results rarely differ clinically. What is the best next step?

options.text: Tighten control limits to catch more error
Switch to a less precise method
Run three levels of control instead of two
Stop using 1_2s as a rejection rule — it is a warning rule with ~10% false-rejection rate; use 1_3s/2_2s/R_4s multirules for rejection

questions.explanation: 1_3s rejects the run; 1_2s is only a warning — using 1_2s as a rejection rule produces ~10% false alerts.

questions.stem: After an erroneous patient-identity merge, the LIS manager needs to handle the bad records. The correct procedure is to

options.text: Inactivate them with a status flag
Delete the erroneous rows from the tables

questions.explanation: Data are never deleted — only inactivated with a status flag, so auditing, look-back, and rollback (e.g., after a bad patient merge) are preserved.

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory performs outpatient testing on a patient 2 days before an inpatient admission. Under Medicare's 72-hour rule, these tests

options.text: Require an Advance Beneficiary Notice from the patient
Can be billed separately as outpatient claims
Must be bundled into the inpatient DRG claim

questions.explanation: Testing within 72 hours before inpatient admission is not reimbursed separately — it's folded into the hospital stay (the rule doesn't cover independent nonhospital laboratories).

questions.stem: An investigator plans a retrospective study using deidentified, already-collected specimens. The correct IRB pathway is

options.text: Expedited review by a single reviewer
Exempt — the IRB, not the investigator, decides exemption

questions.explanation: Retrospective deidentified work qualifies as exempt with no annual review, but the IRB — never the investigator — determines exemption.

questions.stem: A non-oliguric patient on diuretic therapy has a FENa of 0.6%. The correct interpretation is

options.text: FENa cannot be interpreted — diuretics and a non-oliguric state invalidate it
FENa is always below 1% in renal failure

questions.explanation: The <1% prerenal / >1% ATN cutoffs are valid only in oliguria — normal subjects also run <1%, and diuretics or non-oliguric states invalidate the distinction.

notes.note: A 2025 consensus treats FENa 1–2% as indeterminate and > 2% as intrinsic (e.g. ATN); diuretics raise FENa even in prerenal states.

questions.stem: A patient with a thyroid nodule has serum calcitonin of 250 pg/mL. Which diagnosis is most suspected?
questions.explanation: Calcitonin >100 pg/mL raises suspicion for medullary thyroid carcinoma; it is secreted by thyroid C (parafollicular) cells.

questions.stem: A hypoglycemic patient has insulin of 25 μU/mL and C-peptide of 0.2 ng/mL. The pattern indicates
questions.explanation: High insulin + low C-peptide = injected insulin; insulinoma gives high insulin + high C-peptide (plus proinsulin ≥5.0 pmol/L) — check C-peptide before calling it insulinoma.

questions.stem: Which result meets the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus?

options.text: Fasting glucose 110 mg/dL on one draw
Fasting glucose 130 mg/dL on two separate draws

questions.explanation: Diabetes = fasting ≥126 mg/dL (twice), 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL, or HbA1c ≥6.5%; 100–125 and 5.7–6.4% are prediabetes.

questions.stem: A patient has total cholesterol 240 mg/dL, HDL-C 50 mg/dL, and triglycerides 450 mg/dL. The best approach to LDL-C is

options.text: Use a direct (homogeneous) LDL assay — Friedewald is unacceptable at TG >400 mg/dL
Use Friedewald but divide TG by 4 instead of 5
Repeat the lipid panel in the nonfasting state

questions.explanation: Friedewald (LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5) is unacceptable when TG exceeds 400 mg/dL; a direct LDL assay stays valid even at TG 600.

notes.note: Direct LDL-C assays are method-dependent and can be biased in high-TG samples; HEART UK/ACB does not recommend them in hypertriglyceridaemia (non-HDL-C, Sampson–NIH or apoB instead).

questions.stem: A patient with TTP has received daily therapeutic plasma exchange for 5 days. Platelet counts are 165 × 10⁹/L today and 180 × 10⁹/L yesterday, LDH is normalizing, and there are no new neurologic symptoms. What is the best next step?

options.text: Continue daily TPE for two more weeks to consolidate remission
Stop TPE — the treatment endpoint is met
Switch the replacement fluid to 5% albumin and continue daily
Reduce TPE to once weekly indefinitely

questions.explanation: TPE for TTP is given daily until platelets exceed 150 × 10⁹/L on two consecutive days (with improving LDH and no new symptoms); continuing past the endpoint adds risk without benefit.

questions.stem: A patient's urine dipstick is positive for blood but microscopy shows no RBCs. Haptoglobin is normal and CK is markedly elevated. This pattern indicates
questions.explanation: Dipstick-positive blood with no RBCs means hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria — low haptoglobin points to hemolysis, while normal haptoglobin with high CK = myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis).

questions.stem: A Lineweaver-Burk plot shows decreased Vmax and decreased apparent KM for an inhibitor. Which inhibition pattern does this describe?

options.text: Simple noncompetitive inhibition, which lowers Vmax with unchanged KM
Competitive inhibition, which raises KM with unchanged Vmax
Uncompetitive inhibition, which binds only the enzyme-substrate complex
Irreversible inhibition, which permanently destroys the active site

questions.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, so both Vmax and apparent KM fall. Competitive raises KM alone, and simple noncompetitive lowers Vmax alone.

questions.stem: A patient's blood was drawn in an EDTA tube "for convenience," and the ALP comes back unmeasurably low. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The patient has a zinc deficiency suppressing ALP synthesis
EDTA chelated the zinc cofactor of ALP, artifactually lowering the activity
The EDTA activated the ALP enzyme, causing substrate depletion
The specimen was hemolyzed, and free hemoglobin absorbed at 410 nm

questions.explanation: This is the chelator trap — EDTA strips zinc (ALP's cofactor), making ALP unmeasurably low. EDTA is almost never acceptable for enzyme assays; use serum or heparinized plasma.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic heavy alcohol use has AST 280 IU/L, ALT 80 IU/L, and elevated GGT. What does the AST/ALT ratio most strongly suggest?

options.text: Alcohol-induced liver disease with a DeRitis ratio of 3–4:1

questions.explanation: An AST/ALT ratio of 3–4:1 screams alcohol-induced liver disease — mitochondrial AST release plus B6 deficiency suppressing ALT synthesis.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with Kayser-Fleischer rings and parkinsonian symptoms has a normal serum ceruloplasmin. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Wilson disease is excluded by the normal ceruloplasmin
The patient has Menkes syndrome instead
Wilson disease is still possible; ceruloplasmin is normal in up to 15% of cases
The rings are from primary biliary cirrhosis, not Wilson disease

questions.explanation: This is the ceruloplasmin trap — it is an acute-phase reactant and is normal in up to 15% of Wilson patients (35% with hepatic disease). Trust the trio: urinary copper >100 μg/24 h, hepatic copper >250 μg/g, and the rings.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a serum amylase of 900 IU/L for three months but feels well, with normal lipase, normal urine amylase, and a low amylase:creatinine clearance ratio. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Pancreatic pseudocyst leaking amylase into serum
Macroamylasemia — benign amylase–immunoglobulin complexes too large for glomerular filtration

questions.explanation: This is the macroamylasemia trap — persistently high amylase with normal lipase and low clearance is a benign clearance defect, not pancreatitis. Do not order a pancreas CT.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with melena and suspected upper GI bleeding. Which fecal occult blood test is appropriate to detect the bleeding?

options.text: Immunochemical FOB, because it detects heme, which survives intestinal transit
Immunochemical FOB (iFOB), because it is more sensitive overall
Either test, since both detect blood from any GI source equally
Guaiac FOBT, because it detects heme and works for upper GI bleeding

questions.explanation: iFOB detects intact human globin, which is digested in the small intestine — it is insensitive to upper GI bleeding. Guaiac detects heme/pseudoperoxidase and works for upper bleeds.

questions.stem: A patient's phenytoin dose is increased from 300 to 400 mg/day, and the serum level triples, with nystagmus and ataxia. What explains this?

options.text: Phenytoin metabolism is saturable and nonlinear — small dose increases past saturation cause disproportionate level jumps
The patient became noncompliant and the levels are erratic
Carbamazepine-like autoinduction reduced the phenytoin half-life
Albumin binding increased, raising the free phenytoin fraction

questions.explanation: Phenytoin has saturable (nonlinear) metabolism, so a modest dose bump past saturation triples the level. Expect nystagmus → ataxia → diplopia → coma with toxicity.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has acral enlargement, and screening IGF-1 is high. Which finding on oral glucose tolerance testing confirms acromegaly?

options.text: GH rising above 3 μg/L during the test
GH failing to suppress below 1 ng/mL during the test
Glucose failing to suppress during the test

questions.explanation: Acromegaly is diagnosed by failure of GH to suppress below 1 ng/mL during an OGTT. Random GH is uninterpretable because GH pulses normally (peaks of 20–40 ng/mL are normal).

notes.note: The 2024 Acromegaly Consensus confirms acromegaly with IGF-I > 1.3 × ULN plus clinical signs; the OGTT is reserved for equivocal results (Giustina 2024).

questions.stem: A patient with Cushing-like features has a low ACTH of 5 pg/mL on workup. Where is the source of the cortisol excess?

options.text: The adrenal gland — this is ACTH-independent (adrenal tumor making cortisol itself)
The hypothalamus, via excess CRH secretion
The pituitary gland — this is Cushing disease

questions.explanation: This is the ACTH trap — ACTH <10 pg/mL means ACTH-INDEPENDENT, so the adrenal is making cortisol on its own. High ACTH is when you hunt the pituitary or an ectopic source.

questions.stem: A 30-week pregnant patient has a positive fetal fibronectin test. She asks if she will deliver soon. What should she be told?

options.text: A positive fFN at 30 weeks is invalid and must be repeated after 35 weeks
A positive fFN means delivery within 7 days is essentially certain
A positive fFN is much less predictive of delivery than a negative fFN is predictive of not delivering within 7 days
The test is only valid with ruptured membranes, so it cannot be interpreted

questions.explanation: This is the fFN trap — its power is the negative predictive value (99.5% will not deliver within 7 days). A positive test poorly predicts actual delivery, and it is only valid at 24–35 weeks with intact membranes.

questions.stem: A woman with a positive pregnancy test has an hCG of 2500 mIU/mL, but transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine gestational sac. What does this suggest?

options.text: A normal early pregnancy — the sac may simply not be visible yet
Ectopic or otherwise abnormal pregnancy, since hCG is above the discriminatory zone
A heterophilic antibody causing a false-positive hCG

questions.explanation: The discriminatory zone is 1500–2000 mIU/mL — at or above it, a sac should generally be visible. Higher hCG with no sac means ectopic or abnormal pregnancy should be suspected and evaluated.

notes.note: The discriminatory zone varies by centre (some use 3,500 mIU/mL) and should not by itself diagnose ectopic pregnancy; repeat hCG and ultrasound.

questions.stem: A patient has megaloblastic anemia, paresthesias, and posterior column signs. The physician plans to treat with folate alone. Which test confirms the actual deficiency that must be treated?

options.text: Serum homocysteine, which rises only in folate deficiency
Methylmalonate, which rises in B12 deficiency but not in folate deficiency
RBC folate, which reflects tissue folate stores
Serum folate, which is more reliable than RBC folate

questions.explanation: Only B12 deficiency causes irreversible demyelination of the posterior columns, and folate alone lets the neuro damage progress irreversibly. Methylmalonate rises in B12 deficiency, not folate deficiency — check B12 before treating.

questions.stem: A patient's sodium is 128 mmol/L on a routine chemistry panel run by indirect ISE, and triglycerides are 2000 mg/dL. The patient is asymptomatic. What should be done next?

options.text: Treat for hyponatremia with fluid restriction
Repeat sodium after ultracentrifugation of the sample
Repeat sodium by direct (undiluted) ISE before treating
Assume pseudohypernatremia and rehydrate the patient

questions.explanation: Severe hypertriglyceridemia causes pseudohyponatremia because indirect ISE dilutes a non-aqueous sample. Confirm with direct (undiluted) ISE before touching the patient's sodium.

questions.stem: A patient in DKA has only a weakly positive urine ketone strip despite severe metabolic acidosis. What is the best next test?

options.text: A repeat urine ketone strip on a fresh specimen

questions.explanation: The nitroprusside strip detects acetoacetate and acetone but misses β-hydroxybutyrate, which is ~78% of the ketoacids in DKA. A weak or negative strip never rules out ketoacidosis — order serum β-hydroxybutyrate.

questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient undergoes paracentesis. Serum albumin is 3.0 g/dL and ascitic albumin is 1.6 g/dL. What does this indicate?

options.text: An exudate from spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
A chylous effusion from lymphatic obstruction
Portal hypertension as the cause of the ascites

questions.explanation: SAAG = serum albumin minus ascitic albumin = 1.4 g/dL, which is ≥1.1 g/dL — 98% accurate for portal hypertension, typically cirrhosis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with an acutely swollen, hot knee. Synovial fluid shows WBC 120,000/μL with 95% PMNs and low glucose. What is the diagnosis and required next step?

options.text: Septic arthritis — Gram stain, culture, and urgent drainage

questions.explanation: Septic arthritis = synovial WBC 50,000–200,000/μL with >90% PMNs and low glucose. It is an orthopedic emergency — Gram stain and culture immediately, and drain the joint.

questions.stem: A CBC flags MCHC 38.9 g/dL. The smear shows no lipemia, no hemolysis, and no red-cell agglutination. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Iron deficiency — MCHC falls in iron deficiency
Hereditary spherocytosis — the classic anemia that truly raises MCHC
Thalassemia trait — MCHC rises with microcytosis
Cold agglutinins — they always raise MCHC

questions.explanation: A genuinely elevated MCHC (38.9 g/dL with lipemia, hemolysis, and agglutination excluded) is the classic flag of spherocytosis.

notes.note: Spherocytosis is the classic true cause of a high MCHC, but not the only one: xerocytosis also raises it, and cold agglutinins or interference raise it spuriously. A high MCHC detects only a minority of spherocytosis cases.

questions.stem: An apheresis collection of hematopoietic progenitor cells is completed at 2 p.m. Which same-day assay and cutoff determine collection adequacy?

options.text: ALDH flow assay — adequate if the collection contains "bright" cells (investigational; no validated cutoff)
Colony-forming unit (CFU) assay — adequate if >1 × 10⁵ CFUs/kg
Total nucleated cell count — adequate if >3 × 10⁶ cells/kg
CD34+ enumeration by flow cytometry — adequate if ≥2.5 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg recipient weight

questions.explanation: CD34+ enumeration by flow is the accepted same-day adequacy assay (≥2.5 × 10⁶/kg minimal engraftment dose, standard engraftment threshold). The CFU assay is the gold-standard potency test but takes 10–14 days.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman has MCV 62 fL and RBC count 6.2 × 10⁶/μL. What is the most likely diagnosis, and which index supports it?

options.text: Lead poisoning — basophilic stippling on smear
Sideroblastic anemia — ring sideroblasts on marrow

questions.explanation: High RBC count with microcytosis in an asymptomatic patient = thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency. Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) <13 points to thalassemia; >13 favors iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient has WBC 80 × 10⁹/L with a marked left shift. NAP score is high and there is no basophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Chronic myeloid leukemia — the WBC and left shift confirm it
Leukemoid reaction — high NAP with no basophilia argues against CML
Chronic neutrophilic leukemia with a CSF3R mutation
Atypical CML — basophils are absent by definition

questions.explanation: This is the CML trap — a leukemoid reaction has HIGH NAP and no basophilia, while CML has LOW NAP with consistent basophilia. BCR-ABL1 testing settles it.

questions.stem: A flow cytometry technologist analyzing a marrow sample for suspected acute leukemia first displays CD45 versus side scatter, then examines blast populations for CD34, HLA-DR, and lineage markers. A colleague suggests starting with CD19 versus forward scatter instead. What is the best response?

options.text: Agree — CD19 is the better blast gate
Skip gating and analyze all events together
Keep CD45 vs side scatter — it is the standard starting gate that separates blasts from maturing myeloid and lymphoid populations; forward scatter measures size and side scatter measures granularity
Gate on CD3 first to exclude T cells

questions.explanation: CD45 vs side scatter is the standard starting gate for identifying white-cell populations; forward scatter is proportional to cell size and side scatter to internal complexity/granularity.

questions.stem: A patient develops jaundice and a falling hemoglobin 7 days after transfusion, with a newly positive antibody. The physician asks for a DAT and an IAT. What does each test detect?

options.text: DAT detects IgG/complement coating the patient's own RBCs in vivo; IAT detects serum alloantibodies against reagent/donor cells after 37°C incubation and washing
DAT detects serum alloantibodies; IAT detects complement on the patient's cells
Both tests detect the same thing and are interchangeable for crossmatching
DAT is the antibody screen; IAT is used only for cold agglutinin workups

questions.explanation: The DAT detects in vivo coating of the patient's own red cells (AIHA, HDFN, hemolytic transfusion reactions); the IAT detects serum alloantibodies against reagent/donor cells and is the basis of the antibody screen and full crossmatch.

questions.stem: A leukemia patient needs irradiated blood products to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Leukoreduction is sufficient to prevent TA-GVHD
TA-GVHD is prevented by washing the red cells
Only irradiation (≥25 Gy center, ≥15 Gy periphery) prevents TA-GVHD — leukoreduction does not
Irradiated products carry a 10-year storage life like frozen RBCs

questions.explanation: This is the TA-GVHD trap — leukoreduction does NOT prevent it; only irradiation does. TA-GVHD presents 2–50 days post-transfusion with rash, diarrhea, fever, liver dysfunction, and pancytopenia, with >90% mortality.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with crushing chest pain. His cardiac troponin I is mildly above the assay's 99th percentile on arrival, and a repeat sample 3 hours later shows a further rise. What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: Acute myocardial injury — a rise and/or fall (delta) defines acuity
Chronic stable myocardial injury from renal failure
Analytical interference; repeat with a different platform
No myocardial injury, since the first value was only mildly elevated

questions.explanation: Any troponin elevation above the 99th percentile defines myocardial injury under the Fourth Universal Definition of MI, and a rise and/or fall (delta) makes it acute. A single mild elevation without a delta cannot establish acuity — the serial change is the key.

notes.note: The Fifth Universal Definition of MI (2026) now applies: sex-specific 99th percentile URLs, and MI classified as primary, secondary or procedure-related (Mills 2026).

questions.stem: A patient has a prolonged APTT that fully corrects on 1:1 mixing with normal pooled plasma. What does this indicate?

options.text: A factor deficiency rather than an inhibitor
A factor VIII autoantibody requiring a Bethesda assay

questions.explanation: Complete correction on 1:1 mixing with normal pooled plasma indicates a factor deficiency; incomplete or no correction indicates an inhibitor. Lupus anticoagulant and factor VIII autoantibodies are inhibitors and do NOT correct on mixing. (Trap: factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT, not the APTT — the extrinsic pathway — so it cannot explain an isolated prolonged APTT. For suspected acquired hemophilia, a two-step mix — immediate plus 2 hours at 37°C — catches time-dependent FVIII autoantibodies that a single immediate mix misses.)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and fluctuating neurologic changes. ADAMTS13 activity returns at 4%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: ADAMTS13 ≤5–10% defines TTP; HUS keeps 30–100% activity. Trap: don't assume TTP from MAHA + thrombocytopenia alone — check ADAMTS13.

questions.stem: A patient with von Willebrand disease shows hyper-responsiveness to low-dose ristocetin (0.3–0.5 mg/mL) plus mild thrombocytopenia. Which treatment must be avoided?
questions.explanation: This is type 2B VWD (gain-of-function GPIb binding) — DDAVP releases even more hyper-adhesive vWF and worsens thrombocytopenia. Trap: treating type 2B like type 1.

questions.stem: A patient's APTT is markedly prolonged in vitro, yet she has recurrent venous thrombi. The inhibitor acts immediately with no incubation needed. Which antibody is responsible?

options.text: Anti-FVIII autoantibody to the light chain

questions.explanation: Lupus anticoagulant prolongs phospholipid-dependent tests in vitro but is prothrombotic in vivo — and unlike factor VIII inhibitors it needs no incubation. The name is a misnomer: most patients don't have SLE.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with an unprovoked DVT asks which thrombophilia tests to order. Per ACMG and ACOG guidance, which test should NOT be part of a routine adult VTE workup?
questions.explanation: MTHFR C677T is not an independent adult VTE risk factor — routine testing is not recommended. Trap: ordering it just because "homocysteine" sounds thrombophilic.

questions.stem: On day 7 of heparin therapy, a patient's platelets fall >50% and a new DVT appears; the 4T score is high. What is the first action?

options.text: Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant
Reduce the heparin dose and recheck platelets in 3 days

questions.explanation: This is HIT — stop ALL heparin (anti-PF4/heparin antibodies cross-react with LMWH, so LMWH is contraindicated) and switch to argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux. Trap: "a different heparin" doesn't help.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with atrial fibrillation starts warfarin. What is his target INR range?
questions.explanation: INR 2–3 (target 2.5) for atrial fibrillation and VTE; 2.5–3.5 is reserved for mechanical mitral valves and older/caged-ball aortic valves.

questions.stem: A patient with myasthenia gravis has autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptor on the muscle cell surface. Which hypersensitivity type is this?
questions.explanation: Type II = antibody directly against cell surfaces (via complement/ADCC); type III = soluble immune complexes deposited in small vessels. Trap: calling a cell-surface antibody attack "immune complex disease."

questions.stem: A competitive immunoassay for digoxin reports a near-zero signal on a patient sample, confirmed on repeat. What does the near-zero signal indicate, and what is the best next step?

options.text: Very high digoxin — signal is inversely proportional in competitive assays; dilute and rerun to quantitate on the curve
Assay failure — zero signal means no antibody bound
Switch to a sandwich assay for digoxin

questions.explanation: Competitive = signal inversely proportional to analyte; sandwich = directly proportional. Trap: "high signal means high analyte" is only true for sandwich assays.

questions.stem: A β-hCG result is unexpectedly low in a patient with a clinically obvious molar pregnancy. What should the laboratory do first?

options.text: Switch to a sandwich assay format

questions.explanation: Hook/prozone effect — very high analyte overwhelms limited antibody in one-step assays, giving a falsely low result; diluting and retesting unmasks it. Trap: trusting a negative when suspicion is sky-high.

questions.stem: A child with recurrent bacterial infections has an NBT test showing ~10% reduction both before and after stimulation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Normal neutrophils jump from ~10% NBT reduction at rest to 80% when stimulated; failure to jump means a defective oxidative burst — CGD.

questions.stem: Oligoclonal-band testing shows identical bands in both CSF and serum. What does this pattern mean?

options.text: Intrathecal IgG synthesis supporting multiple sclerosis
Systemic immune reaction with passive transfer into CSF — not intrathecal synthesis

questions.explanation: Identical bands in both fluids is Type 4 = systemic reaction, not intrathecal synthesis; intrathecal synthesis needs CSF-only bands (Type 2) or extra CSF bands (Type 3). Trap: reading "bands in CSF" as proof of intrathecal production.

questions.stem: A patient's CH50 is approximately 0 but the AH50 is normal. Which complement components are most likely missing?

options.text: C1q, C1r, C1s, C2, or C4

questions.explanation: CH50 tests the classical pathway only; a normal AH50 localizes the defect to early classical components. If both were zero, think C3 or C5–C9 instead.

questions.stem: An HIV patient failing therapy is being considered for maraviroc. What must be determined before starting it, and why?

options.text: Nothing — maraviroc works against all HIV strains
CD4 count — maraviroc requires CD4 above 500/μL
HLA-B*57:01 status — required for all entry inhibitors
Viral tropism — maraviroc blocks CCR5, so it works only against CCR5-tropic (R5) virus, not CXCR4-tropic (X4) virus

questions.explanation: Maraviroc blocks CCR5, the predominant HIV coreceptor; plerixafor blocks CXCR4 for stem-cell mobilization — the receptor number decides the job.

questions.stem: A positive direct CDC crossmatch with current recipient serum is reported before a planned renal transplant. What does this mean?

options.text: Repeat the crossmatch with historical serum only
Transplant is acceptable if the PRA is below 20%

questions.explanation: A positive direct CDC crossmatch with current serum predicts hyperacute rejection — an absolute contraindication to renal transplantation.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected celiac disease is negative for both HLA-DQ2.5 and HLA-DQ8. What does this mean?

options.text: Celiac disease is essentially ruled out
The patient carries a protective allele
The patient has dermatitis herpetiformis instead

questions.explanation: Absence of DQ2/DQ8 has a negative predictive value >99% for celiac disease (90–95% of patients carry DQ2.5). It's a rule-out test, not a rule-in.

questions.stem: A boy presents with immunodeficiency, eczema, and thrombocytopenia with abnormally small platelets. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: The Wiskott-Aldrich triad — immunodeficiency + thrombocytopenia with small platelets + eczema (WASP defect; IgA high, IgM low). Only WAS has small platelets.

questions.stem: A woman with SLE begins effective treatment. Which antibody should fall as her C3 and C4 recover?
questions.explanation: Anti-dsDNA tracks SLE disease activity (rises in flares, falls with treatment) alongside falling complement; anti-Sm is highly specific for SLE but doesn't fluctuate. Trap: Sm and dsDNA are not interchangeable markers.

questions.stem: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is suspected. How must the specimen be handled before analysis?

options.text: Collect, transport, coagulate, and centrifuge at 37°C; chill to 4°C only for the later analytic incubation
Draw into a pre-chilled tube and transport on ice
Collect at room temperature, then refrigerate immediately
Freeze at −20°C within 30 minutes of collection

questions.explanation: Cryoglobulin testing is 90% preanalytics — chilling early precipitates cryoglobulins out of the serum, producing a false negative. The 4°C incubation (3–7 days) comes only after the 37°C steps.

questions.stem: What is the first-line screening test for celiac disease, and what must the patient do before testing?

options.text: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase; stay on a normal gluten diet for 1–3 months

questions.explanation: IgA anti-tTG (94% sensitive, 97% specific) is the first-line screen; antibodies fade on gluten withdrawal, so a normal gluten-containing diet for 1–3 months is required. Trap: testing on a gluten-free diet gives a false negative.

questions.stem: A patient develops anaphylaxis during surgery. Within what window should serum β-tryptase be drawn?

options.text: 30 minutes to 4 hours post-reaction (elevated up to 24 hours)

questions.explanation: Mature β-tryptase is detectable 30 min–4 h and stays elevated up to 24 h; histamine clears in minutes and is rarely useful. Trap: drawing days later and trusting a negative.

questions.stem: An S. aureus isolate is oxacillin-resistant on cefoxitin screening. What resistance mechanism is most likely, and what does it affect?
questions.explanation: mecA encodes the altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a, making the isolate resistant to all β-lactams (except anti-MRSA cephalosporins like ceftaroline).

questions.stem: A staphylococcal isolate shows a susceptible clindamycin zone but a flattened "D" shape toward the erythromycin disk. How should clindamycin be reported?
questions.explanation: A flattened D-zone means inducible clindamycin resistance — report R even though the zone looks susceptible. Trap: reporting the S-looking zone.

questions.stem: A health-care worker received BCG vaccination as a child abroad. Which test for latent TB infection will NOT be falsely positive because of BCG?
questions.explanation: IGRA antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10, TB7.7) are absent from BCG, so BCG doesn't cause false positives; the TST cross-reacts with BCG. Trap: blaming BCG for a positive IGRA.

questions.stem: CSF from an HIV-positive patient with meningitis is India ink–negative. Which test should the laboratory trust next?
questions.explanation: India ink sensitivity is <50% — a negative means nothing; the cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen is >90% sensitive. Trap: trusting the ink, and note that β-D-glucan misses Cryptococcus.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has a urinary tract infection; urine culture grows coagulase-negative staphylococci that are novobiocin-resistant. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: S. saprophyticus is the novobiocin-resistant CoNS causing UTI in young women ("Sapro = Stays resistant"); S. epidermidis is novobiocin-sensitive. Trap: the exam loves reversing this pair.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a diffuse maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, mucous patches, and generalized lymphadenopathy. His treponemal antibody test is positive but the RPR is nonreactive. What is the next best step?

options.text: Rule out syphilis based on the negative RPR
Order a VDRL titer from a different lab for comparison
Diagnose tertiary syphilis and begin benzathine penicillin
Repeat the RPR on a diluted specimen

questions.explanation: This is the prozone phenomenon — sky-high antibody titers in secondary syphilis cause a falsely negative nontreponemal test, fixed by diluting the specimen. (Trap: "Negative RPR rules out secondary syphilis" — dilute and retest.)

questions.stem: An HIV-positive patient has a newly reactive RPR at a titer of 1:64 and a CD4 count of 290/μL. Which statement about this patient's neurosyphilis risk is correct?

options.text: No increased neurosyphilis risk until the titer reaches 1:128
The treponemal test will serorevert within a year
High risk of neurosyphilis, about 11× baseline in HIV-positive patients
Benzathine penicillin is contraindicated; IV penicillin is mandatory

questions.explanation: RPR ≥1:32 and, in HIV-positive patients, CD4 ≤350/μL are the classic risk factors for CSF abnormalities/neurosyphilis — this patient has both. These factors raise suspicion and support CSF evaluation; they do not by themselves diagnose neurosyphilis (CSF-VDRL is the specific test) or automatically mandate IV therapy.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with mucopurulent cervicitis. Her clinician asks for the best test to diagnose Chlamydia trachomatis infection at genital, rectal, or oropharyngeal sites. Which is correct?

options.text: Direct fluorescent antibody for all genital specimens

questions.explanation: NAAT is the diagnostic method of choice for C. trachomatis at all sites — cell culture is now reserved for suspected sexual assault and test of cure.

questions.stem: A man with nongonococcal urethritis has a urethral swab positive for Mycoplasma hominis. Which organism–drug pairing is correct?

options.text: M. hominis — clindamycin or a newer quinolone

questions.explanation: M. hominis is macrolide-resistant, so azithromycin fails; Ureaplasma is clindamycin-resistant. The pairing trap gets you only if you flip them. (Trap: "Treat M. hominis with azithromycin.")

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with fever, headache, and a rash that began on his wrists and ankles on day 4 of illness and is spreading centrally. RMSF is suspected, but acute serology is negative. What is the next best step?

options.text: Order a Weil-Felix test to confirm the diagnosis
Wait for convalescent serology before treating

questions.explanation: Serology is retrospective — fewer than 20% of rickettsial patients are seropositive at presentation — so doxycycline must be started empirically in all rickettsioses, even in young children. (Trap: "Wait for serology before treating RMSF.")

questions.stem: A patient with chronic Q fever endocarditis undergoes serologic testing. Which result fits chronic disease?
questions.explanation: Acute Q fever produces anti-phase II antibodies; chronic disease (endocarditis) shows high anti-phase I IgG — the chronic-disease cutoff is ≥1:800 (PPV of Q fever endocarditis 37% at 1:800, rising to 75% at 1:6400). (Trap: "Diagnosing chronic Q fever from anti-phase II titers" — getting the phases backwards is the classic trap.)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a reactive anti-HCV screening test and normal liver enzymes. Which result confirms active HCV infection?
questions.explanation: Anti-HCV only shows exposure, not active infection — you must follow with HCV RNA to confirm active disease, and SVR (undetectable RNA 12 weeks post-treatment) defines cure. (Trap: "Positive anti-HCV = active hepatitis C.")

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has fever, exudative pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. EBV serology shows VCA IgM positive and EBNA-1 IgG negative. What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: EBV-naive patient with another cause of symptoms

questions.explanation: VCA IgM positivity with absent EBNA-1 IgG marks current/recent infection; past infection is VCA IgG positive plus EBNA-1 IgG positive with VCA IgM negative. Note VCA IgG alone without EBNA-1 means uncertain timing, not past infection.

questions.stem: A laboratory reports "no parasites seen" on a thin film from a febrile traveler, but the thick film from the same draw shows ring forms. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Ring forms lyse on thin films
Giemsa stain only works on thick films
The thin film examines far less blood per field — low parasitemia is missed on thin film but detected on thick film (15–30× more blood per field)

questions.explanation: The thick film holds 15–30× more blood per field, so it detects; the thin film gives the intact RBC monolayer needed for species identification and quantitation.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has intense nocturnal perianal itching. Her pediatrician orders stool O&P ×3, which is negative. What is the best next diagnostic step?

options.text: Repeat stool O&P on three more specimens
Perianal cellophane tape collection first thing in the morning
Blood smear at 10 pm–2 am for microfilariae

questions.explanation: Routine stool detects only 5–10% of Enterobius infections — the correct specimen is perianal tape/cellophane paddle collected in the morning before bathing. (Trap: "Order stool for suspected pinworm.")

questions.stem: A sputum Gram stain shows 15 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field with mixed bacteria. What is the correct laboratory action?

options.text: Culture it and report the predominant organism
Repeat the Gram stain on a second slide
Reject the specimen as saliva — poor quality

questions.explanation: More than 10 squamous epithelial cells/LPF means the specimen is saliva, not sputum — reject it. An acceptable sputum has <25 epithelial cells AND >25 neutrophils/LPF. (Trap: "Pick the pathogen from a salivary Gram stain.")

notes.note: These two cut-offs conflict: a sputum with 11–24 squamous cells would be both acceptable and rejected. One published rule accepts < 10 squamous cells with > 25 leukocytes per LPF; each laboratory sets its own criteria.

questions.stem: A patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia has a negative Legionella urinary antigen. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Repeat the urinary antigen in 48 hours to confirm
The result only detects L. pneumophila serotype 1 — other serotypes and species are not excluded
A negative antigen means the pneumonia is viral

questions.explanation: The urinary antigen detects only L. pneumophila serotype 1; a negative result cannot exclude other serotypes or species. (Trap: "Negative Legionella antigen rules out Legionella.")

questions.stem: A molecular lab bills its novel 40-gene NGS panel under the closest Tier 1 single-analyte code instead of an unlisted code. A payer audit recoups the payment. What was the billing error?

options.text: Forcing the test into a Tier 1 code that doesn't fit — the correct code was 81479 (unlisted molecular pathology)
Unbundling — it should have been billed as individual Tier 2 codes
No error — nearest-code billing is accepted practice
The lab should have used G0452-26 for the technical component

questions.explanation: The unlisted molecular pathology code 81479 covers tests with no Tier 1 or Tier 2 code — don't squeeze the test into a code that doesn't fit. (Trap: "Bill a novel test under the nearest Tier 1 code." Bonus fact: FDA clearance is not required for billing, but non-cleared tests need a report disclaimer.)

questions.stem: A sequencing run produces light emission proportional to nucleotide incorporation with no fragment ladder, using PPi → ATP → luciferase chemistry. Which method is running?
questions.explanation: Sanger sequencing is chain termination — ddNTPs lacking 3′-OH randomly stop extension, creating sized fragments separated by capillary electrophoresis. Luciferase light is pyrosequencing; Bst polymerase is LAMP.

questions.stem: Two real-time PCR samples have Ct values of 24 and 30, with identical reaction efficiency. Which sample started with more template?

options.text: Ct values cannot be compared across samples

questions.explanation: Ct is inversely related to the log of starting target — lower Ct means MORE template, because the threshold is reached earlier when you start with more. (Trap: "A Ct of 30 means more template than a Ct of 24" — exactly reversed.)

questions.stem: A patient's hybrid capture test for HPV is positive. What can the laboratory report from this result?

options.text: Presence and viral load of HPV — but not the specific type
Whether the infection will progress to cervical cancer
Absolute HPV copy number per cell
The specific HPV genotype, e.g., 16 vs. 18

questions.explanation: Hybrid capture measures viral presence and load, but it does NOT type the strain — strain identification requires PCR with strain-specific primers. (Trap: "Hybrid capture types the HPV strain.")

questions.stem: A newborn girl has lymphedema of the hands and feet and a webbed neck; karyotype is pending. Which single-chromosome result would be compatible with survival to birth?
questions.explanation: 45,X (Turner syndrome) is the only monosomy that survives to birth — over 95% of 45,X conceptions are lost. 45,Y is never viable, and 47,XXY is a trisomy, not a monosomy. (Trap: "45,Y is a viable monosomy.")

questions.stem: A man develops Huntington disease at age 55. His son develops it at 32, and his grandson in the teens. Which genetic concept best explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: Anticipation — earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations as the repeat expands — is the single most testable concept here (fragile X, Huntington, myotonic dystrophy). Paternal transmission gives the largest Huntington expansions.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with one APOE E4 allele and normal cognition asks what the result means. Which counseling is most accurate?

options.text: No increased Alzheimer risk at all
A 12- to 15-fold risk of Alzheimer disease
2- to 5-fold higher risk — E4 is a risk factor, not a diagnosis
Alzheimer disease is essentially certain by age 75

questions.explanation: One APOE E4 copy confers 2- to 5-fold AD risk; two copies confer 12- to 15-fold risk versus noncarriers, with over 50% of E4 homozygotes developing AD by age 85.

questions.stem: Blood for forensic DNA identity testing arrives in a green-top heparin tube. What is the correct action?

options.text: Accept it — heparin is a recommended anticoagulant
Freeze it at −20°C to preserve DNA
Reject or recollect — heparin is not recommended for DNA testing
Accept it and note the tube type on the report

questions.explanation: EDTA (purple top) and CPD (yellow top) are acceptable; heparin (green top) is NOT recommended because it inhibits PCR, and no-anticoagulant tubes are also unacceptable. (Trap: "Heparin green top is acceptable for DNA collection.")

questions.stem: A patient is about to start abacavir. The laboratory reports HLA-B*57:01 positive. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Start abacavir with close monitoring for 6 weeks
Do not use abacavir — a positive screen is a hard stop
The screen is unreliable because its negative predictive value is only 50%

questions.explanation: Abacavir hypersensitivity occurs in 5–8% of patients within the first 6 weeks, and HLA-B*57:01 screening has a 100% negative predictive value — so a negative is trustworthy but a positive means do not use the drug. FDA recommends screening all patients before abacavir.

questions.stem: A urologist asks about NMP22 for bladder cancer follow-up. Which statement is correct?

options.text: NMP22 is measured in serum with a 10 U/mL cutoff
NMP22 is a urine ELISA with a 10 U/mL cutoff for follow-up
NMP22 identifies the tissue of origin of the malignancy
NMP22 has lower specificity than CEA and AFP

questions.explanation: NMP22 is a urine ELISA (exfoliated malignant urothelial cells lyse in urine — "22 in the loo"), FDA-approved for bladder cancer screening and post-treatment follow-up at a 10 U/mL cutoff (5.0 U/mL for recurrence monitoring). (Trap: "NMP22 is a serum test.")

questions.stem: BCR-ABL1 transcript analysis shows the p210 isoform. Which diagnosis does this indicate?
questions.explanation: p210 (M-BCR) = CML; p190 (m-BCR) = Ph-positive ALL; p230 (μ-BCR) = rare neutrophilic CML. (Trap: "p210 means Ph-positive ALL" — the isoforms flip the diagnosis.)

questions.stem: A breast tumor ISH shows HER2:CEP17 ratio 2.4 with average HER2 copy number 3.2/cell in 25 nuclei. Per ASCO/CAP 2018, how is this classified?

options.text: ISH positive — ratio ≥2.0 is sufficient for trastuzumab eligibility
ISH positive — copy number above 3.0/cell overrides the ratio
ISH negative — ratio ≥2.0 with <4.0 copies/cell requires comment and workup, not a positive call
Unscorable — fewer than 30 nuclei were examined

questions.explanation: ASCO/CAP 2018: ratio ≥2.0 AND ≥4.0 HER2 copies/cell = ISH positive; ratio ≥2.0 with <4.0 copies = NOT positive (comment/workup); ratio <2.0 with ≥6.0 copies = positive. Scored in ≥20 nuclei.

questions.stem: A 60-gene class-prediction model built from 80 patients performs perfectly on its derivation set but fails on independent samples. What is the central pitfall, and what is required?

options.text: Population stratification — re-run the model within a single ancestry cohort
Overfitting — require training/test-set splitting and independent validation
High stringency — lower the salt concentration
Batch effects across array runs — re-normalize the raw expression data

questions.explanation: Overfitting is the chapter's highest-yield concept: models built from thousands of genes across only 20–200 patients shine on their derivation set and fail on independent samples, so training/test splits and independent validation are mandatory.

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory has just passed a CAP inspection with no deficiencies. The laboratory director asks whether the lab must also undergo a separate federal CLIA inspection this cycle. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Yes, because CLIA inspections are mandatory for all hospital laboratories regardless of accreditation
No, because CAP holds deemed status and its inspection substitutes for the federal CLIA inspection
Yes, but only because the laboratory performs high-complexity testing
No, because waived laboratories are exempt from all inspection requirements

questions.explanation: CAP holds deemed status, so its inspection substitutes for the federal CLIA inspection.

notes.note: CMS lists Washington (full) and New York (partial) as CLIA-exempt states; D.C. is not listed.

questions.stem: An inspector asks for the retention schedule covering cytogenetic images and blood bank donor records. Which pair is correct?
questions.explanation: Cytogenetic reports and images are retained 20 years, the longest on the 2-5-10-20 retention ladder.

questions.stem: A new laboratory suite is being designed. Which of the following specifications is NOT consistent with accepted lab design standards?

options.text: A single exit is acceptable for any room over 100 square feet if an eyewash is present
Eyewash stations within 100 feet of work areas
Temperature maintained between 68 and 76 degrees Fahrenheit

questions.explanation: Rooms over 100 sq ft require two exits; the temperature, humidity, and eyewash specs are all correct.

notes.note: OSHA requires eyewash facilities “within the work area”; guidance adds reach within about 10 seconds. The 100-ft figure comes from a 1992 OSHA letter.

questions.stem: Quarterly review shows 90th-percentile TATs of chemistry 28 min, immunoassay 55 min, CBC 19 min, coagulation 29 min. Which test family is missing its RFP goal and should get workflow attention first?
questions.explanation: The 90th-percentile RFP goals are chemistry 30 min, immunoassay 45 min, CBC 20 min, coagulation 30 min.

questions.stem: After mapping its workflow and eliminating bottlenecks, a lab's chemistry TAT still misses the 90th-percentile goal during the morning inpatient peak. What is the best next step?

options.text: Reengineer the workflow again from scratch
Evaluate targeted automation or added analyzer capacity aimed at the peak bottleneck
Relax the TAT goal to match current performance

questions.explanation: Technology alone never improves performance; workflow must be mapped and reengineered before buying instruments.

questions.stem: Utilization review finds frequent duplicate vitamin D orders within 30 days and, separately, missed troponin orders in chest-pain patients. Which pair of actions best reflects utilization management?

options.text: Cancel all repeat vitamin D orders and add standing troponin orders for every admission
Block vitamin D reorders within 90 days via the LIS and build a chest-pain order set that prompts troponin
Restrict vitamin D to inpatients and page physicians about troponin
Batch vitamin D testing weekly and audit troponin turnaround times

questions.explanation: Utilization management reviews necessity first; the least expensive test is the test not done, but blanket restriction harms care.

questions.stem: A phlebotomist draws a blood culture, then a serum tube, and then the light blue citrate tube for a coagulation workup. The PT and APTT come back unexpectedly prolonged. What is the most likely cause, and the best next step?

options.text: Fluoride from the gray tube inhibited clotting factors; discard the result and redraw in a red-top tube
EDTA carryover from the lavender tube chelated the calcium; repeat the collection using a green-top tube
Tissue thromboplastin carryover from the venipuncture contaminated the citrate tube because serum tubes were drawn before the citrate tube; recollect the coagulation specimen in proper draw order
Prolonged tourniquet time caused hemolysis; release the results with a hemolysis comment

questions.explanation: Serum tubes drawn before the citrate tube contaminate it with tissue thromboplastin; recollect coag specimens with the blue tube second.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine collection for fractionated metanephrines arrives at the laboratory. Which preservative should have been in the collection container?

options.text: 6N hydrochloric acid, 10 mL, to bring the pH below 3.0
No preservative; refrigeration alone is sufficient

questions.explanation: Metanephrines, catecholamines, VMA, and oxalate are preserved with 10 mL of 6N HCl to pH below 3.0.

questions.stem: A lumbar puncture is performed and the first tube is visibly blood-tinged from a traumatic tap. The physician needs an accurate CSF cell count. Which tube should the laboratory use for the count?

options.text: Tube 1, because it is drawn first and is the freshest
Tube 2, because it goes to microbiology anyway
Tube 3, because it has the least bloody-tap contamination
Any tube, because the blood will be evenly distributed

questions.explanation: Tube 3 goes to hematology and has the least bloody-tap contamination after a traumatic tap.

questions.stem: Before an arterial blood gas draw, the technologist performs a modified Allen test: both radial and ulnar arteries are occluded, the patient opens the fist, and the ulnar artery is released — but the palm does not regain color. What is the best next step?

options.text: Proceed with the radial puncture since the radial artery is the preferred site
Release the radial artery instead and reassess
Do not perform the radial puncture; select an alternate arterial site
Apply firm pressure for 10 minutes and attempt the draw anyway

questions.explanation: No ulnar reperfusion means inadequate collateral circulation; do not puncture the radial artery — choose another site.

questions.stem: A spectrophotometer reports an absorbance of 2.0 for a patient sample. What percent transmittance does this correspond to?
questions.explanation: A = -log T, so absorbance 2.0 equals 1 percent transmittance, the practical ceiling for Beer's law linearity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a principle of molecular luminescence instrumentation?

options.text: Chemiluminescence requires an excitation light source just like fluorescence does
Fluorometers measure emission at a right angle to the excitation beam
Phosphorescence has a shorter excited-state lifetime than fluorescence
Luminometers require a monochromator to select the emission wavelength

questions.explanation: Fluorometers read emission at a right angle to excitation; chemiluminescence needs no excitation source.

questions.stem: On an aperture-impedance cell counter, a cell passing through the aperture generates a voltage pulse proportional to its volume. After red cell lysis, particles larger than 35 fL are counted. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Platelets generate larger voltage pulses than red blood cells
The voltage pulse is inversely proportional to cell size
Impedance counters distinguish cells by forward light scatter
The post-lysis particles counted are white blood cells

questions.explanation: By the Coulter principle, pulse height tracks volume; post-lysis particles above 35 fL are white blood cells.

questions.stem: In a time-of-flight mass analyzer, three ions with mass-to-charge ratios of 200, 450, and 900 are accelerated with the same kinetic energy. Which ion reaches the detector first?
questions.explanation: In TOF, all ions get equal kinetic energy, so the lowest m/z ion flies fastest and arrives first.

questions.stem: A toxicology lab reports exact ng/mL drug concentrations from a GC-MS method run without an internal standard. The reviewing pathologist flags the report. What is the most defensible criticism?

options.text: GC-MS cannot detect drugs of abuse
Without an internal standard the method is qualitative — the reported concentrations are unreliable
GC-MS requires derivatization of every analyte
An immunoassay screen must precede every GC-MS result

questions.explanation: Quantitative mass spectrometry (GC-MS or LC-MS/MS) requires an internal standard of known concentration in every sample to correct for losses and anchor the calibration curve.

questions.stem: A thermally labile drug metabolite decomposes in the GC inlet. The lab derivatizes it to improve volatility and thermal stability. Which platform is now appropriate, and why?

options.text: LC-MS — derivatization is only for immunoassays
GC-MS — the analyte is now volatile and thermally stable enough to survive the inlet
MALDI-TOF — derivatization enables intact protein analysis
Direct infusion MS — derivatization removes matrix effects

questions.explanation: GC-MS needs volatile, thermally stable analytes; nonvolatile, thermally labile molecules belong on LC-MS.

questions.stem: A laboratory wants normal chemistry results to be released automatically when they meet preset criteria, with load balancing and reflex-test routing handled in software rather than by technologists. Which component provides these functions?

options.text: The laboratory information system billing module

questions.explanation: Middleware performs autoverification, load balancing, and reflex/repeat routing between analyzers and the LIS.

questions.stem: A laboratory director wants the freedom to use third-party reagents on a new chemistry analyzer to reduce costs. Which type of reagent system must the analyzer have?
questions.explanation: Open reagent systems accept third-party reagents; closed systems lock the lab to the manufacturer.

questions.stem: A microbiology laboratory wants to reduce the time to identify pure bacterial colonies from days to hours. Which technology best accomplishes this, and what performance should be expected?

options.text: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry with approximately 90 percent species and 98 percent genus specificity
16S rRNA sequencing with 50 percent species accuracy
Automated biochemical panels with overnight incubation

questions.explanation: MALDI-TOF identifies pure colonies in hours with about 90 percent species and 98 percent genus specificity.

questions.stem: A hospital proposes running ICU glucometers under a Certificate of Waiver with nursing staff and no QC documentation. The lab director objects. What is the strongest regulatory basis for the objection?

options.text: Most glucometers' FDA clearance (and waived status) covers only lay-user self-monitoring — their labeled intended use does not extend to critically ill patients, so ICU use under a Certificate of Waiver exceeds the waiver's scope and requires the test system's own complexity requirements (QC, personnel, competency)
Bedside testing is prohibited in ICUs
The FDA banned inpatient glucometer use in 2014

questions.explanation: CLIA classification follows the test system's own FDA clearance/intended use, not the location; most glucometers are waived only for lay self-monitoring, so ICU use under a Waiver exceeds its scope — unlike systems such as Nova StatStrip whose waiver explicitly covers critically ill hospitalized patients.

questions.stem: A remote clinic wants to deploy urine dipstick testing at the point of care. What is the minimum method validation the laboratory should require before patient testing begins?

options.text: No validation is needed because dipsticks are waived devices
Testing of 10 to 20 specimens with both normal and abnormal results
A full CLSI method comparison with 100 patient samples against the central lab
Six months of parallel testing before independent reporting

questions.explanation: Simple manual POCT such as dipsticks requires validation on 10-20 specimens with normal and abnormal results.

questions.stem: A new screening test for a serious disease has 98 percent sensitivity and 90 percent specificity. A patient with no symptoms tests negative. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: The disease is confirmed absent, because specificity determines negative results
The disease is effectively ruled out, because a highly sensitive test that is negative rules disease out
The result is uninterpretable without knowing the disease prevalence
The patient should be retested because screening tests are always repeated

questions.explanation: SnNOut: a highly sensitive test that is negative rules disease out.

questions.stem: A laboratory establishes a new reference interval by testing 40 healthy volunteers and reports the central 95 percent as the interval. Which statement about this approach is correct?

options.text: It is acceptable because 40 subjects is sufficient for any partition
It is acceptable only if the data are Gaussian
It is acceptable if the interval is verified annually thereafter
It is not acceptable; establishing a reference interval requires at least 120 nondiseased subjects per partition

questions.explanation: CLSI EP28-A3c requires at least 120 nondiseased subjects per partition to establish a reference interval.

questions.stem: An analyte has an index of individuality of 0.45. A patient's result rises from 140 to 155, still inside the population reference interval of 135-170. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The index of individuality only applies to critical values
The result is normal because it falls within the reference interval
The reference interval should be narrowed for this patient
The change is likely clinically significant because an index below 0.6 means the patient's own serial results are more informative than the population interval

questions.explanation: An index of individuality below 0.6 means the patient's own serial results outweigh the population reference interval.

questions.stem: A patient's basic metabolic panel repeatedly shows an anion gap of 2 mEq/L. The clinician calls it "a nice low normal gap." What is the most appropriate next step in interpretation?

options.text: Evaluate for a monoclonal paraprotein, because a persistently low gap suggests possible multiple myeloma
Repeat the electrolytes, because this must be a calculation error
Reassure the patient, because low gaps have no clinical significance
Agree, because a low anion gap rules out metabolic acidosis

questions.explanation: A persistently low anion gap of 1-3 mEq/L suggests a monoclonal paraprotein and possible multiple myeloma.

questions.stem: A patient presents with serum sodium 122 mEq/L, serum osmolality 262 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium 55 mEq/L. Which pattern best fits these findings?

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
Diuretic-induced hyponatremia with low urine sodium

questions.explanation: Hyponatremia with serum osmolality below 280, urine osmolality above 300, and urine sodium above 40 fits SIADH.

questions.stem: A patient's total calcium is 8.4 mg/dL (reference 8.5-10.5) with albumin 2.0 g/dL. Using the book's corrected-calcium formula, what is the corrected calcium and the best interpretation?

options.text: 8.4 mg/dL — true hypocalcemia; begin calcium replacement
Cannot be corrected; ionized calcium by ISE is the only valid measurement

questions.explanation: Corrected Ca = 8.4 + 0.8 x (4.4 - 2.0) = 10.3 mg/dL, which is normal; the 4.0 reference albumin is the outdated Payne version.

questions.stem: A 2×2 table has expected cell counts of 3 and 4, and the chi-square p-value is 0.04. What is the best next step?

options.text: Combine rows to raise the expected counts
Reanalyze with Fisher's exact test, which is required when expected counts are below 5
Raise alpha to 0.10 to confirm significance

questions.explanation: Chi-square requires expected counts of at least 5 per cell; smaller expected counts require Fisher's exact test.

questions.stem: An investigator measures hemoglobin A1c in the same 50 diabetic patients before and after a new education program. Which test best evaluates whether the program changed A1c?
questions.explanation: Before/after measurements on the same subjects call for the more powerful paired t-test.

questions.stem: In a proficiency testing event, a laboratory reports glucose 112 mg/dL. The peer group mean is 100 mg/dL with a standard deviation of 4 mg/dL, and the result is within the acceptance limits. What should the laboratory do?

options.text: File the result with no further action since it passed
Recalibrate the instrument immediately before reporting patient results
Investigate the result for bias or drift, because an SDI of 3.0 exceeds the approximately 2.5 threshold for concern
Switch to a different peer group with a wider standard deviation

questions.explanation: SDI = 3.0 exceeds the approximately 2.5 threshold, so investigate for bias or drift even though the result passed.

questions.stem: A glucose method has a total allowable error of 10 percent, a bias of 2 percent, and an imprecision (SD) of 4 percent. What is the sigma metric, and what does it imply for QC design?

options.text: Sigma 3.0 — routine QC rules are adequate
Sigma 2.0 — the method needs stringent QC with more rules and controls
Sigma 4.5 — QC frequency can be relaxed
Sigma 6.0 — the method is essentially error-free

questions.explanation: Sigma = (10 - 2) / 4 = 2.0, a low sigma that demands stringent QC with more rules and controls.

questions.stem: Morning QC fails on a chemistry analyzer. The technologist repeats the QC and it fails again. What is the best next step before recalibrating?

options.text: Run a fresh vial of QC material
Release patient results with a comment about the QC failure
Repeat patient samples back to the last acceptable QC and report them

questions.explanation: After repeat QC failure, run a fresh QC vial before investigating the instrument or recalibrating.

questions.stem: A lab's PT glucose runs 8% above its peer-group mean, but a patient-sample comparison against the reference method shows 0.5% bias. The supervisor recalibrates, shifting all patient results 8%. What error occurred?

options.text: Appropriate correction of a calibration bias
The PT failure proves the patient results were wrong
Recalibrating to a noncommutable PT material — the method was accurate on patient samples, and the recalibration introduced an 8% patient bias

questions.explanation: PT materials are usually noncommutable, so between-method PT disagreement without patient-sample disagreement does not prove inaccuracy.

questions.stem: A laboratory is implementing bar-code labels for a new automation line. According to CLSI Auto-14, what is required for the 2D barcode placement on the specimen label?

options.text: The barcode printed once in the center of the label
A 1D Code 128 barcode with no redundancy
The barcode printed a minimum of three times at different vertical positions on the label
Handwritten accession numbers as backup instead of barcodes

questions.explanation: CLSI Auto-14 requires the 2D barcode printed at least three times at different vertical positions on the label.

questions.stem: A technologist runs a report while another edits the same patient record; the report shows the old result for one analyte and the new result for another from the same edit session. Which ACID property has been violated?
questions.explanation: Isolation makes concurrent transactions behave as if executed sequentially.

questions.stem: A bioinformatician wants to inspect raw per-base quality scores of a sequencing run before alignment. Which file should be opened?
questions.explanation: The NGS pipeline runs FASTQ (raw fragments) to BAM (aligned) to VCF (variants).

questions.stem: A physician orders a vitamin D screening test for an asymptomatic patient, and the laboratory suspects Medicare may deny the claim for lack of medical necessity. What must the laboratory do before performing the test?

options.text: Provide the patient with a written Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) stating Medicare may not cover the test
Perform the test and write off the charge if denied
Change the diagnosis code to one that supports medical necessity
Bill the test as part of a bundled panel to ensure payment

questions.explanation: An Advance Beneficiary Notice must be given in writing before service when Medicare may deny for lack of medical necessity.

questions.stem: A proposed analyzer purchase has a payback period of 4 years, a net present value of negative $10,465 at a 10 percent discount rate, and an internal rate of return of 8 percent. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Approve, because the project pays back within 4 years
Reject, because the payback exceeds 3 years and the IRR is below the cost of capital
Approve, because the IRR is positive
Reject, because NPV is the only criterion that matters

questions.explanation: Negative NPV, 8 percent IRR below the 10 percent cost of capital, and 4-year payback beyond the 3-year target mean rejection.

questions.stem: Investigators want to study a new resuscitation protocol in emergency department patients with severe trauma, where obtaining informed consent before treatment is infeasible. Which regulatory provision could allow this research?

options.text: A waiver of documentation, because verbal consent is sufficient
Exception from informed consent (EFIC), with advance community notification and consent obtained later from the subject or a representative
Exempt review, because emergency research is always minimal risk
Expedited review, because trauma studies qualify for single-member approval

questions.explanation: EFIC permits emergency research without prior consent when the community is notified in advance and consent is obtained later.

questions.stem: An investigator plans two studies: (1) a retrospective chart review of deidentified anemia cases, and (2) prospective blood collection with written consent comparing two approved anemia therapies at minimal risk. Which review pathway fits each?
questions.explanation: Prospective minimal-risk research with consent obtainable qualifies for expedited review by a single IRB member.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man in diabetic ketoacidosis has serum sodium 128 mEq/L and glucose 700 mg/dL. What is his corrected sodium, and how should the low sodium be managed?

options.text: 138 mEq/L - no specific sodium therapy; treat the hyperglycemia
128 mEq/L - the sodium is truly low and needs no correction

questions.explanation: Corrected Na = 128 + 1.6 x 6 = ~138 (normal); hyperglycemia dilutes sodium via water shift, so treat the glucose, not the sodium.

questions.stem: Na 140 mEq/L, glucose 90 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL. Calculated osmolality = 290 mOsm/kg; measured osmolality = 322 mOsm/kg. The comatose patient has calcium oxalate crystals in the urine. Most likely ingestion?
questions.explanation: Osmolal gap of 32 flags a toxic alcohol; calcium oxalate crystals identify ethylene glycol (methanol causes blindness instead).

questions.stem: An oliguric patient (urine output 200 mL/24 h) with acute kidney injury has FENa 3.2% and a BUN-to-creatinine ratio of 12:1. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: In oliguria, FENa >1% means ATN (tubules cannot reabsorb Na); the BUN/Cr ratio of 12:1 also argues against prerenal disease.

notes.note: A 2025 consensus treats FENa 1–2% as indeterminate and > 2% as intrinsic (e.g. ATN); diuretics raise FENa even in prerenal states.

questions.stem: Na 140, Cl 110, HCO3 21 (anion gap = 9), albumin 1.8 g/dL. Lactate is 4.5 mmol/L and pH is 7.28. Best interpretation?

options.text: The normal anion gap excludes lactic acidosis
Albumin-corrected anion gap is elevated; the high lactate confirms lactic acidosis despite the deceptively "normal" calculated gap
The primary disorder is a respiratory alkalosis
This is hyperchloremic normal-gap acidosis from diarrhea

questions.explanation: Hypoalbuminemia lowers the anion gap (~2.5 mEq/L per 1 g/dL albumin below normal), masking the lactate-driven high gap; the lactate confirms lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: K+ 6.2 mEq/L drawn with a prolonged tourniquet and fist clenching; platelets 850,000/uL; ECG normal; patient asymptomatic. Best next step?

options.text: Repeat potassium on a properly collected, non-hemolyzed sample before treating

questions.explanation: Prolonged tourniquet, fist-clenching collection, and marked thrombocytosis suggest pseudohyperkalemia from collection interference; redraw on a properly collected sample before treating (the HIT-FLED checklist: increased tourniquet time, fist clenching, thrombocytosis). A normal ECG does NOT rule out true hyperkalemia (KDIGO).

questions.stem: Two hyponatremic patients both show serum osmolality 250 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Patient A is clinically euvolemic; Patient B is hypovolemic with orthostatic hypotension. Which diagnoses best fit?

options.text: A: SIADH; B: cerebral salt wasting

questions.explanation: Euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and urine Na >30 mmol/L is SIADH; the hypovolemic patient with the same pattern has cerebral salt wasting — volume status distinguishes the two.

questions.stem: Four hours after cardiopulmonary bypass, a patient's creatinine is unchanged from baseline but oliguria is developing. Which biomarker is most likely already elevated?
questions.explanation: Urinary NGAL rises 2-6 hours post-insult, preceding creatinine by 1-3 days; the NephroCheck cutoff is 0.3.
