questions.stem: A 45-year-old undergoes thyroidectomy for medullary thyroid carcinoma after a calcitonin of 320 pg/mL. Which genetic workup is indicated for the patient and first-degree relatives?

options.text: BRCA1/2 sequencing for hereditary breast-ovarian cancer risk
Germline RET proto-oncogene testing — medullary thyroid carcinoma occurs in MEN 2, and kindred screening guides prophylactic thyroidectomy

questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma occurs in MEN 2 (germline activating RET mutations); test the patient and first-degree relatives, since the RET genotype guides prophylactic thyroidectomy timing.

questions.stem: Calcium 13.2 mg/dL, PTH 8 pg/mL (low), PTH-rP markedly elevated, urinary cAMP high. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH but elevated PTH-rP (which shares the PTH receptor) is humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy.

questions.stem: Child with short stature, round face, and shortened 4th metacarpals: calcium 7.0 mg/dL, phosphate high, PTH 180 pg/mL (high), subnormal urinary cAMP response to PTH infusion. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypocalcemia despite high PTH is PTH resistance, and the blunted urinary cAMP response confirms pseudohypoparathyroidism (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy).

questions.stem: Elderly man with skull enlargement and hearing loss: ALP 850 IU/L, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, phosphate 3.5 mg/dL. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Markedly elevated ALP with normal calcium and phosphate is Paget disease; hypercalcemia would point to hyperparathyroidism or malignancy.

questions.stem: Adult with bone pain and muscle weakness: ALP elevated, calcium 8.4 mg/dL, phosphate 2.2 mg/dL, 25(OH)D 11 ng/mL, DEXA T-score -1.8. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Low vitamin D with low Ca/phosphate and high ALP is defective mineralization (osteomalacia); osteoporosis has normal mineralization and T-score -2.5 or lower.

questions.stem: Dialysis patient for 8 years: calcium 11.0 mg/dL, phosphate 5.8 mg/dL, PTH 900 pg/mL despite phosphate binders and cinacalcet. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia with unsuppressible PTH after years of dialysis despite binders/cinacalcet is tertiary hyperparathyroidism (autonomous parathyroids).

questions.stem: A patient has elevated PTH and low-normal calcium. 1,25(OH)2D is high-normal but 25(OH)D is 12 ng/mL. Which result defines vitamin D status?

options.text: 1,25(OH)2D - the active hormone is always the best marker
25(OH)D - it is the storage form and the status marker; PTH drives 1,25(OH)2D up even in deficiency

questions.explanation: 25(OH)D (half-life 2-3 weeks) is the status marker; PTH drives 1,25(OH)2D (half-life ~5 h) up even in deficiency, a classic trap.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic adult has HbA1c 6.1% on two occasions. Interpretation?
questions.explanation: Prediabetes is A1c 5.7-6.4%; diabetes requires 6.5% or higher.

questions.stem: At 26 weeks gestation, a 75-g OGTT shows: fasting 95, 1-hour 172, 2-hour 148 mg/dL. Interpretation?

options.text: Normal; all values are below diagnostic cutoffs
Gestational diabetes - the fasting value of 95 meets the one-step criterion, and any single exceeded value diagnoses GDM

questions.explanation: One-step IADPSG: fasting 92, 1-h 180, 2-h 153 mg/dL; ANY one exceeded = GDM, and the fasting 95 qualifies.

questions.stem: Supervised fast: glucose 48 mg/dL, insulin 9 uU/mL, C-peptide 1.8 ng/mL, proinsulin 14 pmol/L, sulfonylurea screen negative. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glucose 55 or less with insulin 3+, C-peptide 0.6+, and proinsulin 5.0+ is endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma); injected insulin would show low C-peptide.

questions.stem: A DKA patient is improving on insulin (pH 7.34, glucose 180 mg/dL), but the urine ketone strip remains strongly positive. Best explanation and monitoring approach?

options.text: Nitroprusside strips detect acetoacetate, which transiently rises as beta-hydroxybutyrate is metabolized during recovery; monitor resolution with serial beta-hydroxybutyrate
Insulin therapy is failing; double the dose
Urine strips measure beta-hydroxybutyrate directly and are the best monitor
The patient has a urinary tract infection causing false positives

questions.explanation: Nitroprusside strips detect acetoacetate, which transiently rises as beta-hydroxybutyrate is metabolized during recovery; follow serial beta-hydroxybutyrate for true resolution.

questions.stem: HbA1c is 6.8% but the home glucose log averages 200 mg/dL over 3 months. History includes a GI bleed with transfusion 6 weeks ago. Best interpretation?

options.text: The meter is inaccurate; trust the A1c
The patient has excellent control; reduce medications
Red cell turnover from bleeding and transfusion invalidates the A1c; use glucose criteria or fructosamine instead

questions.explanation: Bleeding/transfusion shortens RBC lifespan and falsely lowers A1c (6.8% predicts mean glucose ~148, not 200); use glucose criteria or fructosamine.

questions.stem: Lactate 6.2 mmol/L, pH 7.30, high anion gap, patient on metformin, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, no hypoxia. Type of lactic acidosis?

options.text: Type B - metformin-associated, non-hypoxic lactic acidosis
Not lactic acidosis; lactate must exceed 10 mmol/L

questions.explanation: Lactate >5.0 mmol/L with acidemia (pH <7.35) and a high gap defines lactic acidosis; without hypotension/hypoxia, metformin implicates type B.

questions.stem: A 10-day-old has jaundice, vomiting, oil-drop cataracts, E. coli sepsis, and reducing substances in the urine. Best immediate action?

options.text: Observe and repeat the newborn screen in 1 month
Start a high-lactose diet to confirm intolerance
Treat only the sepsis; the cataracts are unrelated
Begin a galactose-free diet immediately, before GALT results return

questions.explanation: Oil-drop cataracts + jaundice + E. coli sepsis + urinary reducing substances is classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency); start a galactose-free diet immediately, before confirmation.

questions.stem: Total cholesterol 240, HDL-C 50, triglycerides 180 mg/dL. What is the calculated LDL-C?
questions.explanation: Friedewald LDL-C = 240 - 50 - 180/5 = 154 mg/dL; valid since triglycerides are below 400 mg/dL.

questions.stem: Palmar xanthomas, tuberoeruptive xanthomas, equal elevations of cholesterol and triglycerides, and a broad-beta band on lipoprotein electrophoresis. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Palmar xanthomas are pathognomonic for type 3 dysbetalipoproteinemia (apoE2/E2), confirmed by the broad-beta (beta-VLDL) band.

questions.stem: A child with chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, acanthocytosis, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, total cholesterol 38 and triglycerides 22 mg/dL. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TC and TG below 50 mg/dL with fat malabsorption, acanthocytes, ataxia, and retinitis pigmentosa is abetalipoproteinemia (MTTP defect).

questions.stem: A statin-treated patient has LDL-C 68 mg/dL but suffers a recurrent MI; apoB is 120 mg/dL (high) and triglycerides are 220 mg/dL. Best explanation of the residual risk?

options.text: LDL-C is the only valid risk marker; the events must be non-atherosclerotic
HDL-C is the therapeutic target now
ApoB reflects atherogenic particle number (one apoB per particle) and better captures risk than LDL-C when the two are discordant
Statins lower Lp(a), so residual risk should be zero

questions.explanation: One apoB-100 per VLDL/LDL particle means apoB approximates particle number, a better CHD predictor than LDL-C when the two disagree.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old with no risk factors has LDL-C 196 mg/dL and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 4%. Best management?

options.text: High-intensity statin without a risk calculation

questions.explanation: LDL 190+ gets a high-intensity statin with no risk calculation; suspect familial hypercholesterolemia.

questions.stem: A man has: waist 106 cm, triglycerides 185 mg/dL, HDL-C 36 mg/dL, BP 138/88 mmHg, fasting glucose 108 mg/dL. How many metabolic syndrome criteria does he meet?
questions.explanation: All five criteria are met (waist, TG, HDL, BP, FPG); any 3 of 5 defines metabolic syndrome.

questions.stem: A lipid panel drawn 3 weeks after an acute MI shows surprisingly low LDL-C. Best action?

options.text: Start a statin based on these values
Reassure the patient; low lipids mean low risk
Intensify the statin to reach the new low target
Repeat the panel at least 8 weeks after the acute event

questions.explanation: Acute illness depresses lipids; wait at least 8 weeks after trauma/infection (3-4 months postpartum) before measuring lipoproteins.

questions.stem: Chest pain at rest with transient ST depression; serial high-sensitivity troponins are all below the 99th percentile. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: ACS with ischemic ECG changes but no troponin elevation is unstable angina, still managed as ACS in the high-sensitivity era.

questions.stem: Which statement about STEMI management is inconsistent with guidelines?

options.text: A negative early troponin excludes STEMI
Reperfusion should not be delayed for biomarker results
The ECG is the diagnostic standard for STEMI
Troponin can be falsely negative within the first hour

questions.explanation: STEMI is an ECG diagnosis; troponin can be falsely negative early, so never delay reperfusion for labs.

questions.stem: A dialysis patient with no chest pain has troponin I 48 ng/L (99th percentile 30 ng/L) on three draws over 24 hours with <10% variation and a normal ECG. Interpretation?

options.text: Chronic myocardial injury - a flat stable elevation (as in renal failure) is not acute MI

questions.explanation: Acute MI requires a rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile; a flat stable elevation (as in renal failure) is chronic myocardial injury.

questions.stem: A heart failure patient started on sacubitril/valsartan feels better, but BNP rises from 220 to 480 pg/mL. Best monitoring approach?

options.text: Stop sacubitril; it is causing heart failure
Follow NT-proBNP instead - neprilysin inhibition blocks BNP breakdown, falsely raising it
Recheck BNP in 2 weeks; a persistently rising BNP on sacubitril/valsartan indicates treatment failure

questions.explanation: Sacubitril blocks neprilysin, which degrades BNP but not NT-proBNP, so NT-proBNP is the only honest marker on this drug.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with low pretest probability for PE has a D-dimer of 640 ug/L FEU. Best interpretation?

options.text: Indeterminate; repeat the D-dimer in 24 hours
Negative by the age-adjusted cutoff (age x 10 = 780 ug/L) - PE is ruled out

questions.explanation: The age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff is age x 10 ug/L after 50 (780 here); 640 is negative, and a negative D-dimer rules out PE only with low pretest probability.

questions.stem: An hs-CRP of 12.4 mg/L is drawn for CHD risk stratification in an asymptomatic adult. Best action?

options.text: Classify as highest CHD risk and start a statin
Average it with a second draw next week
Discard it for risk stratification - evaluate for infection or inflammation and repeat later

questions.explanation: hs-CRP above 10 mg/L is discarded for cardiac risk stratification; evaluate for infection/inflammation and repeat later.

questions.stem: A chest pain patient with high clinical suspicion for ACS has an unexpectedly negative troponin; she takes high-dose biotin for hair loss. Best explanation?

options.text: Switch to CK-MB, which biotin does not affect
Switch to high-sensitivity troponin, which biotin does not affect
High-dose biotin saturates the avidin capture step, causing falsely low troponin - hold biotin and repeat the test
The negative result is reliable; discharge her

questions.explanation: High-dose biotin saturates the avidin capture step, causing falsely low troponin in sandwich assays (FDA 2017); hold biotin and retest.

notes.note: FDA updated its 2017 biotin warning in 2019; biotin makes sandwich assays falsely low and competitive assays falsely high.

questions.stem: Nephrotic syndrome SPEP shows low albumin and a markedly increased alpha-2 fraction. Which protein accounts for the alpha-2 rise, and why?

options.text: Alpha-2-macroglobulin (725 kDa) - retained by the damaged glomerulus, rising up to 10-fold to preserve oncotic pressure

questions.explanation: In nephrotic syndrome the damaged glomerulus retains giant alpha-2-macroglobulin (725 kDa), which rises up to 10-fold to preserve oncotic pressure.

questions.stem: A narrow band between beta and gamma appears on protein electrophoresis of a plasma sample, but the serum sample shows no band. Explanation?

options.text: True monoclonal gammopathy; begin a myeloma workup
Fibrinogen artifact - fibrinogen appears in plasma but not serum and can mimic an M-spike; run SPEP on serum

questions.explanation: Fibrinogen in plasma (absent in serum) mimics an M-spike between beta and gamma; SPEP must be run on serum.

questions.stem: After head trauma, clear rhinorrhea is tested: immunofixation of nasal fluid with antitransferrin shows two bands, while patient serum shows one. Interpretation?

options.text: CSF leak - the second band is CSF-specific beta-2-transferrin (asialotransferrin)

questions.explanation: Beta-2-transferrin (asialotransferrin) is CSF-specific, so two bands confirm a CSF leak; always run patient serum alongside to exclude allelic variants.

questions.stem: Which marker best reflects chronic heavy alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin marks chronic heavy alcohol use, while a single ethanol level only reflects recent intake; expect false negatives in women, nonsmokers, and high BMI.

questions.stem: Which laboratory marker is best for monitoring response to antibiotic therapy in bacterial infection?

options.text: CRP - the fastest-rising and fastest-normalizing acute-phase reactant

questions.explanation: CRP rises up to 1000-fold and normalizes fastest, making it ideal for tracking infection response; albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant that falls slowly.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient has a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 85 mg/g on repeat testing. Interpretation?

options.text: Moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria) - abnormal; intensify nephropathy screening and management

questions.explanation: ACR ≥30 mg/g is abnormal; 30-300 mg/g is moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria) per ADA/KDIGO. Same window, three quantities: concentration 30-300 mg/L, excretion rate 30-300 mg/day, ACR 30-300 mg/g; ACR adjusts for urine concentration.

questions.stem: Which is the best early indicator of nutritional status and refeeding response?

options.text: Prealbumin (transthyretin) - half-life ~2 days versus ~20 days for albumin

questions.explanation: Prealbumin's ~2-day half-life makes it the early nutritional canary, versus ~20 days for albumin.

questions.stem: An enzyme has a KM of 2 mmol/L. At what substrate concentration does the reaction proceed at half its maximal velocity?
questions.explanation: KM is the substrate concentration giving Vmax/2 — when [S] = KM (2 mmol/L here), velocity is half-maximal. (Competitive raises KM alone, simple noncompetitive lowers Vmax alone, uncompetitive lowers both.)

questions.stem: A hemolyzed specimen shows CK 2,400 IU/L in an asymptomatic patient with normal troponin and ECG. Most likely explanation?

options.text: Falsely elevated CK from red-cell adenylate kinase in the hemolyzed sample - recollect without hemolysis

questions.explanation: Red-cell adenylate kinase (2 ADP to ATP + AMP) feeds the coupled CK assay, so hemolysis plus high CK in a well patient means interference - recollect.

questions.stem: Preoperative pseudocholinesterase testing shows a dibucaine number of 22%. What is the implication?

options.text: Homozygous atypical variant - avoid succinylcholine (prolonged apnea); use an alternative neuromuscular blocker

questions.explanation: Dibucaine number 10-30% is the homozygous atypical variant; these patients get prolonged apnea from succinylcholine or mivacurium.

questions.stem: A result of 16.7 nkat/L is equivalent to how many IU/L?
questions.explanation: 1 IU (1 umol/min) equals 16.7 nanokatal, so 16.7 nkat/L is exactly 1 IU/L.

questions.stem: An endpoint amylase result is "normal" in a patient with classic severe pancreatitis pain and a lipase of 1,200 IU/L. Best next step?

options.text: Redilute and remeasure - very high enzyme activity depletes substrate before the endpoint read, falsely lowering the result
Rule out pancreatitis; the amylase is normal
Repeat the assay on a hemolyzed sample

questions.explanation: In endpoint assays, substrate depletion flattens the curve before the read, falsely lowering very high results; redilute and remeasure.

questions.stem: Which alkaline phosphatase isoenzyme has the longest circulating half-life?

options.text: Placental - about 7 days, versus minutes for intestinal, ~1 day for bone, and ~3 days for liver

questions.explanation: ALP isoenzyme half-lives lengthen intestine (minutes) to bone (~1 day) to liver (~3 days) to placenta (~7 days).

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours after chest pain onset, LD1 exceeds LD2 (flipped ratio). What is the historical significance?

options.text: It supports myocardial infarction - an LD1/LD2 ratio >1 at 36-72 hours classically confirmed MI before troponins

questions.explanation: The flipped LD1/LD2 ratio at 36-72 hours classically confirmed MI in the pre-troponin era; small enzymes (CK, AST) leak earlier than large ones (LD).

questions.stem: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, IgM anti-HBc positive. Interpretation?

options.text: Acute hepatitis B infection in the core window - the only stage lacking both HBsAg and anti-HBs

questions.explanation: The core window (HBsAg gone, anti-HBs not yet present) is the only stage with neither marker; IgM anti-HBc is the sole test.

questions.stem: Bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL, >80% unconjugated, with normal CBC, LD, and haptoglobin; it rises with fasting and illness. Most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Gilbert syndrome - reduced UGT1A1 activity (~30%), benign, worsens with fasting

questions.explanation: Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (2-3, seldom >5 mg/dL) without hemolysis, worsening with fasting, is Gilbert syndrome (UGT1A1 ~30% activity).

questions.stem: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total 4.0, direct 3.2 mg/dL) with otherwise normal LFTs; liver biopsy shows dark pigmentation. Diagnosis?

options.text: Dubin-Johnson syndrome - defective canalicular MRP2 excretion with lipofuscin pigmentation

questions.explanation: Conjugated bilirubin 2-5 mg/dL with a dark pigmented liver is Dubin-Johnson (MRP2 defect); Rotor syndrome is unpigmented.

questions.stem: In acute liver failure, INR is 3.2 but albumin is 4.0 g/dL (normal). Best explanation?

options.text: The INR elevation is a laboratory artifact; trust the normal albumin
Early vitamin K deficiency unrelated to liver function
Factor VII's 4-6 hour half-life makes PT/INR prolong within hours of synthetic failure, while albumin's ~20-day half-life keeps it normal until late

questions.explanation: Factor VII's 4-6 hour half-life prolongs PT/INR within hours of synthetic failure, while albumin's ~20-day half-life keeps it normal until late.

questions.stem: Which patient is most likely to develop chronic hepatitis B after acute infection?

options.text: A 30-year-old with acute symptomatic HBV (1-2% chronicity)
A neonate infected at birth - about 80% develop chronic infection, versus 1-2% in adolescents and adults

questions.explanation: Age at infection decides HBV outcome: ~80% chronicity in neonates versus 1-2% in adolescents/adults.

notes.note: CDC (2025): about 90% of infected infants, 30% of children infected at 1–5 years and about 5% of adults develop chronic hepatitis B.

questions.stem: ALP 320 IU/L with GGT 28 IU/L (normal), 5'-nucleotidase normal, and normal calcium and phosphate. What is the source of the ALP?

options.text: Bone - GGT and 5'-nucleotidase do not rise in bone disease, confirming a non-hepatic source

questions.explanation: GGT and 5'-nucleotidase confirm hepatic origin of ALP; when both are normal, the ALP comes from bone (or placenta).

questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient under surveillance has AFP 450 ng/mL and a new 3-cm liver lesion on ultrasound. Interpretation?

options.text: Normal surveillance result; continue routine screening
Highly probable hepatocellular carcinoma - AFP >400 ng/mL

questions.explanation: AFP >400 ng/mL (units ng/mL, not ng/dL) is highly probable HCC; the cirrhosis screening cutoff is 20 ng/mL.

questions.stem: On day 6 of epigastric pain radiating to the back, amylase is now normal but lipase is 5x ULN. Diagnosis?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis - lipase stays elevated 8-14 days while amylase normalizes in 48-72 hours, making lipase the better late marker
Pancreatitis excluded; amylase is the definitive test

questions.explanation: Lipase lingers 8-14 days while amylase normalizes in 48-72 hours, making lipase the better late marker; diagnosis needs clinical features plus >3x ULN.

questions.stem: Acute pancreatitis presents with AST 320 and ALT 410 IU/L (>3x ULN). Most likely etiology?

options.text: Gallstones - transaminases >3x ULN indicate a biliary cause in about 95% of cases

questions.explanation: AST/ALT >3x ULN during pancreatitis indicates a gallstone cause in ~95% of cases.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a Ranson criterion assessed at presentation (admission) for pancreatitis severity?

options.text: Calcium <8 mg/dL - this is a 48-hour criterion, not an admission one

questions.explanation: Admission Ranson criteria are age, WBC, glucose, LD >350, and AST >250; calcium <8 mg/dL is a 48-hour criterion.

questions.stem: Profuse watery diarrhea persisting during fasting, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, stool volume 4 L/day, fecal osmotic gap 30 mOsm/kg. Most likely diagnosis?

options.text: VIPoma (WDHA syndrome) - secretory diarrhea with a low osmotic gap (<50 mOsm/kg)

questions.explanation: WDHA (watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria) with fasting-persistent secretory diarrhea (gap <50) is VIPoma; octreotide controls symptoms in >90%.

questions.stem: Fasting gastrin 850 ng/L, gastric pH 1.8, recurrent duodenal ulcers; secretin stimulation raises gastrin by 350 ng/L within 15 minutes. Diagnosis?

options.text: Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) - a paradoxical gastrin rise >200 ng/L after secretin is diagnostic

questions.explanation: A paradoxical gastrin rise >200 ng/L within 15 minutes of secretin is diagnostic of gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison).

questions.stem: Flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm with markedly elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA. Which syndrome is confirmed, and what must be avoided before collection?

options.text: Carcinoid syndrome; avoid tryptophan/serotonin-rich foods and interfering drugs

questions.explanation: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is >90% sensitive/specific for carcinoid syndrome, but tryptophan/serotonin-rich foods and interfering drugs must be avoided before collection.

questions.stem: An infant with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, and recurrent respiratory infections has sweat chloride 78 mmol/L on two occasions. Diagnosis?

options.text: Cystic fibrosis - sweat chloride >60 mmol/L twice is diagnostic

questions.explanation: Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L on two occasions diagnoses cystic fibrosis; newborn screening starts with immunoreactive trypsinogen.

questions.stem: A workplace urine drug screen is positive for opiates by EMIT; the donor denies use and takes only prescribed fluoroquinolones. Best confirmatory step?

options.text: Confirm by GC-MS - one immunoassay can never confirm another; an independent method is required
Confirm with an EMIT from a different manufacturer

questions.explanation: One immunoassay can never confirm another (FPIA cannot confirm EMIT); confirmation requires an independent method (GC-MS or LC-MS/MS) with chain of custody.

questions.stem: A bipolar patient has a lithium level of 3.8 mEq/L drawn 12 hours post-dose, with confusion, coarse tremor, and oliguria. Best management?

options.text: Whole-bowel irrigation with PEG as definitive therapy
Hemodialysis - levels >3.5 mEq/L are potentially lethal and an indication for dialysis

questions.explanation: Lithium >3.5 mEq/L (read 12 h post-dose) is potentially lethal and an indication for dialysis; lithium is not protein bound and is dialyzable.

questions.stem: After moonshine ingestion: blurred vision, severe anion-gap metabolic acidosis, osmolal gap 28. What is the toxic metabolite and best treatment?

options.text: Formic acid (from formaldehyde) - fomepizole preferred, or ethanol plus dialysis

questions.explanation: Methanol becomes formaldehyde then formic acid, causing blindness and severe anion-gap acidosis; block alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole (preferred) or ethanol plus dialysis.

questions.stem: After an ingestion there is marked hyperosmolality with acetonemia and acetonuria, but normal pH and a normal anion gap. Most likely ingestion?

options.text: Isopropanol - metabolized to acetone, producing an osmolar gap without acidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis — begin an insulin infusion

questions.explanation: Isopropanol is metabolized to acetone, producing an osmolar gap without metabolic acidosis, unlike methanol and ethylene glycol.

questions.stem: A 70-kg adult ingested 16 g of acetaminophen 4 hours ago. What is the toxic dose threshold and appropriate treatment?

options.text: 229 mg/kg exceeds the 140 mg/kg toxic threshold - give N-acetylcysteine; ~5% of the dose converts to toxic NAPQI
N-acetylcysteine only after liver failure develops

questions.explanation: 16 g in a 70-kg adult is ~229 mg/kg, exceeding the 140 mg/kg toxic threshold; NAC detoxifies the ~5% converted to NAPQI, with peak injury at 2-4 days.

questions.stem: An overdose patient has an amitriptyline level of 850 ng/mL with QRS widening. Interpretation?

options.text: Toxic - above 500 ng/mL (therapeutic 100-250 ng/mL; lethal >1000 ng/mL); manage as severe TCA poisoning

questions.explanation: TCA tiers are therapeutic 100-250, toxic >500, and lethal >1000 ng/mL; at 850 ng/mL with QRS widening this is severe toxic-range poisoning.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with developmental delay, abdominal pain, and basophilic stippling has a whole blood lead of 32 ug/dL. Best action?

options.text: Start oral iron to reduce lead absorption
Consider chelation therapy - levels >25 ug/dL in children prompt chelation consideration

questions.explanation: Lead is measured in whole blood; 10+ ug/dL is excessive absorption and >25 ug/dL prompts chelation consideration in children.

questions.stem: Episodic headache, palpitations, sweating, and paroxysmal hypertension. Most sensitive screening test?

options.text: Clonidine suppression test as the first step
Plasma free metanephrines - intracellular metabolites and the most sensitive pheochromocytoma screen

questions.explanation: Plasma free metanephrines are continuously produced intracellular metabolites and the most sensitive pheochromocytoma screen, beating parent catecholamines.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with hypertension and hypokalemia has low plasma renin activity and low aldosterone. He consumes large amounts of black licorice daily. Most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess - glycyrrhizic acid inhibits 11-beta-HSD2, letting cortisol activate the mineralocorticoid receptor

questions.explanation: Hypertension with hypokalemia plus low renin and low aldosterone is Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess; the licorice history identifies 11-beta-HSD2 deficiency, letting cortisol moonlight as a mineralocorticoid.

questions.stem: Hypertension and hypokalemia with aldosterone 28 ng/dL and plasma renin activity 0.5 ng/mL/h. Interpretation?

options.text: Primary hyperaldosteronism - PAC/PRA ratio of 56 (>50 is virtually diagnostic) with elevated PAC; confirm with saline infusion

questions.explanation: PAC/PRA of 56 with elevated PAC is virtually diagnostic of primary hyperaldosteronism (>30 suggestive, >50 diagnostic); confirm with saline infusion.

questions.stem: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia, salt wasting, and markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Most likely enzyme defect?

options.text: 21-hydroxylase - the most common CAH cause; confirm with cosyntropin stimulation (post-ACTH 17-OHP >2000 ng/dL)

questions.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the #1 cause of CAH; screen with 17-OHP and confirm with cosyntropin (post-ACTH 17-OHP >2000 ng/dL).

questions.stem: Polyuria and polydipsia; water deprivation gives urine osmolality 280 mOsm/kg, rising to 460 after desmopressin (>10% increase). Diagnosis?

options.text: Central diabetes insipidus - the kidney concentrates after exogenous ADH

questions.explanation: A >10% rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin means the kidneys respond to ADH (central DI); nephrogenic DI rises <10%.

questions.stem: A 4-cm pituitary macroadenoma with bitemporal hemianopia; prolactin is reported as 22 ng/mL (normal). Best next step?

options.text: Accept the result; the adenoma is nonfunctioning
Repeat prolactin on sample dilution - giant prolactinomas cause a high-dose hook effect with falsely low results
Begin a dopamine agonist based on size alone

questions.explanation: Giant prolactinomas cause a high-dose hook effect with falsely low results on one-site assays; repeat on dilution to reveal the true value.

questions.stem: TSH 0.04 uIU/mL (low), FT4 normal, total T3 markedly elevated. Diagnosis?

options.text: T3 toxicosis - high T3 with normal T4 and suppressed TSH

questions.explanation: Suppressed TSH with normal FT4 and high T3 is T3 toxicosis; low TSH with high FT4/T3 is primary hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: At 34 weeks gestation: BP 150/105, platelets 78,000/uL, AST 210 IU/L, schistocytes on smear, RUQ pain. Diagnosis?

options.text: HELLP syndrome - hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets

questions.explanation: Hemolysis + elevated LFTs + low platelets at 34 weeks is HELLP syndrome, a preeclampsia complication.

questions.stem: hCG rises from 1,200 to 1,560 mIU/mL in 48 hours (30% rise) with vaginal bleeding. Interpretation?

options.text: Abnormal pregnancy - a rise of <53% in 2 days is abnormal with 99% sensitivity

questions.explanation: A 48-hour hCG rise under 53% is abnormal with 99% sensitivity; a normal intrauterine pregnancy roughly doubles.

notes.note: Newer data put the minimal 48-h hCG rise for a viable intrauterine pregnancy at about 35%; the older 53% threshold misclassifies some viable pregnancies.

questions.stem: First-trimester bleeding with progesterone 3.2 ng/mL. Interpretation?

options.text: Abnormal pregnancy - progesterone <5 ng/mL is 100% specific for abnormal pregnancy

questions.explanation: Progesterone <5 ng/mL is 100% specific for abnormal pregnancy; >20 ng/mL usually means normal intrauterine pregnancy.

questions.stem: In an RhD-alloimmunized pregnancy at 28 weeks, MCA peak systolic velocity is 1.7 MoM. Best next step?

options.text: Proceed to fetal blood sampling and intrauterine transfusion workup - MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM detects fetal anemia
Perform amniocentesis for the Liley curve

questions.explanation: MCA peak systolic velocity >1.5 MoM detects fetal anemia and triggers fetal blood sampling, replacing the Liley/Queenan delta-OD450 curves.

questions.stem: Semen analysis: volume 3.0 mL, concentration 8 million/mL, motility 45%, morphology 6% normal forms. Which parameter is abnormal?

options.text: Concentration - the WHO 2010 lower reference limit is 15 million/mL, so 8 million is oligospermia

questions.explanation: WHO 2010: concentration 15-50 million/mL, so 8 million/mL is oligospermia; volume, motility, and morphology here are all normal.

notes.note: WHO semen-analysis reference values changed in the 6th edition (2021); check which edition the question assumes.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old has 6 months of secondary amenorrhea. What is the first test in the workup?

options.text: Serum or urine hCG - pregnancy must be ruled out first, always

questions.explanation: The amenorrhea workup always starts with hCG to rule out pregnancy, then prolactin/TSH, progestin challenge, FSH/LH, and androgens.

questions.stem: At 16 weeks gestation, maternal serum AFP is markedly elevated. Best next step?

options.text: Detailed ultrasound for open neural tube defects - only open defects leak AFP; MSAFP detects ~95% of anencephaly and 65-80% of open NTDs
Repeat MSAFP in the third trimester

questions.explanation: Only open neural tube defects leak AFP; elevated MSAFP (peak 12-14 weeks) prompts detailed ultrasound, detecting ~95% of anencephaly and 65-80% of open NTDs.

questions.stem: Megaloblastic anemia with paresthesias; both methylmalonate and homocysteine are elevated. Which deficiency is this, and why not treat with folate alone?

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency - folate corrects the anemia but not the irreversible posterior-column demyelination; methylmalonate is B12-specific

questions.explanation: Both B12 and folate cause megaloblastic anemia, but only B12 causes irreversible posterior-column demyelination; methylmalonate rises only in B12 deficiency.

questions.stem: A teenager with tremor and Kayser-Fleischer rings has ceruloplasmin 14 mg/dL and 24-hour urinary copper 190 ug. Diagnosis?

options.text: Wilson disease - urinary copper >100 ug/24 h with low ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL) confirms defective biliary copper excretion

questions.explanation: Urinary copper >100 ug/24 h with ceruloplasmin <20 mg/dL confirms Wilson disease (ATP7B defect in biliary copper excretion).

questions.stem: A corn-staple diet with photosensitive dermatitis (Casal necklace), chronic diarrhea, and progressive dementia. Which deficiency?

options.text: Niacin (vitamin B3) - pellagra's 4 D's: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death

questions.explanation: Photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia on a corn-staple diet is pellagra from niacin (B3) deficiency - the 4 D's.

questions.stem: A physician orders 1,25(OH)2D to evaluate a patient for nutritional vitamin D deficiency; the result is normal but PTH is elevated. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The PTH result is spurious and should be ignored
The patient has normal vitamin D status
Wrong test ordered — 1,25(OH)2D is driven up by PTH even in deficiency; 25(OH)D is the nutritional status marker

questions.explanation: Vitamin D status is measured by 25(OH)D: deficient <20 ng/mL, target ~30; 1,25(OH)2D is driven by PTH and misleads.

questions.stem: A long-term denture-adhesive user develops anemia, neutropenia, and gait ataxia with low copper studies. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Excess zinc blocks intestinal copper absorption, causing copper-deficiency anemia, neutropenia, and myeloneuropathy

questions.explanation: Excess zinc blocks intestinal copper absorption, causing copper-deficiency anemia, neutropenia, and myeloneuropathy (also why zinc treats Wilson disease).

questions.stem: A chronic alcoholic with confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia is about to receive IV dextrose. Most urgent treatment?

options.text: Thiamine before or with glucose - Wernicke encephalopathy; glucose metabolism consumes thiamine and precipitates irreversible injury

questions.explanation: Confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia is Wernicke encephalopathy; give thiamine before/with glucose because glucose metabolism consumes thiamine.

questions.stem: Endemic dilated cardiomyopathy with skeletal myopathy occurs in a selenium-poor region of China. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Selenium deficiency causes Keshan disease, an endemic cardiomyopathy with skeletal myopathy; toxicity shows garlic breath and hair/nail loss.

questions.stem: A DKA patient has creatinine 2.3 mg/dL by the Jaffe method but 1.2 mg/dL by an enzymatic assay. Explanation?

options.text: Acetoacetate and acetone falsely elevate the nonspecific Jaffe reaction; bilirubin would falsely lower it - trust the enzymatic result
True acute kidney injury; the enzymatic assay is wrong

questions.explanation: The Jaffe reaction cross-reacts with ketones (acetoacetate, acetone), glucose, ascorbate, and cephalosporins, faking renal failure in DKA; bilirubin falsely lowers it.

questions.stem: Which statement about coupled-enzyme assays monitored at 340 nm is INCONSISTENT with chapter principles?
questions.explanation: NAD(P)H absorbs at 340 nm while NAD(P) does not, so ammonia, urea/BUN, ALT, and AST are tracked as a 340 nm decrease.

questions.stem: Polycythemia (Hct 62%): POCT glucose reads 68 mg/dL but simultaneous laboratory plasma glucose is 108 mg/dL. Explanation?

options.text: High hematocrit falsely lowers strip glucose - red cells occlude the strip; anemia falsely raises it

questions.explanation: High hematocrit occludes POCT strips (falsely low glucose) while anemia lets extra plasma through (falsely high): thick blood lies low, thin lies high.

questions.stem: A grossly hemolyzed sample arrives for an ammonia level. The physician asks whether the result can be reported with a hemolysis comment. What is the best response?

options.text: Report it with a hemolysis comment; the bias is predictable
Cancel — erythrocyte ammonia is ~3× plasma, so hemolysis precludes accurate ammonia measurement; recollect
Correct the result using the hemolysis index
Freeze the sample and run it tomorrow

questions.explanation: Red-cell ammonia is ~3x plasma, so hemolysis precludes ammonia testing (and invalidates LD and phosphate).

questions.stem: Which statement about the Jendrassik-Grof bilirubin assay is INCONSISTENT with chapter principles?

options.text: Both total and direct fractions use diazotized sulfanilic acid read at 600 nm
The total measurement adds a caffeine-benzoate accelerator to dissociate albumin-bound unconjugated bilirubin
Indirect bilirubin is calculated as total minus direct
The direct fraction requires the accelerator because conjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound

questions.explanation: Caffeine-benzoate dissociates albumin-bound unconjugated bilirubin for the total measurement; the direct assay omits it, and both are read at 600 nm.

questions.stem: Isolated GGT 5x ULN with normal ALT, AST, ALP, and bilirubin in a patient taking carbamazepine. Most likely explanation?

options.text: Drug-induced GGT elevation - carbamazepine induces GGT without liver injury; alcohol, phenytoin, and phenobarbital do the same

questions.explanation: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, and alcohol induce GGT up to 5x without liver injury; isolated GGT elevation needs no liver imaging.

questions.stem: Regarding calcium measurement by ion-selective electrode, which statement is correct?

options.text: Heparinized plasma is unacceptable for ISE calcium
Acidified serum measures total calcium; unacidified serum measures ionized calcium
Citrated plasma gives the most accurate ionized calcium

questions.explanation: Acidified serum measures total calcium (protein-bound released) while unacidified serum measures ionized calcium; citrate chelates calcium and interferes with Arsenazo III.

questions.stem: Which glycemic marker DECREASES as glycemic control worsens?

options.text: 1,5-Anhydroglucitol - it falls when glucose is high, reflecting 1-2 weeks of glycemia

questions.explanation: 1,5-anhydroglucitol is excreted when glucose exceeds the renal threshold, so it falls with hyperglycemia - the reverse of every other glycemic marker.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has pruritus and cholestatic LFTs (markedly elevated ALP); AMA/anti-M2 is positive with polyclonal IgM elevation. Most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Primary biliary cholangitis - AMA/anti-M2 is ~100% specific, classic in 5th-decade women

questions.explanation: AMA/anti-M2 is ~100% specific for primary biliary cholangitis, classic in 5th-decade women; PSC instead shows p-ANCA in young men with ulcerative colitis.

questions.stem: A construction worker is brought in after a crush injury to his leg. His urine is dark red and the reagent strip is strongly positive for heme, but microscopy of the sediment shows no intact RBCs, and the heme pad color change is uniform rather than speckled. What is the most likely explanation, and what is the best next laboratory test?

options.text: Hemoglobinuria; check plasma free Hb and haptoglobin
Lower urinary tract hematuria; examine the urine for blood clots
Porphyrinuria from an acute porphyria attack; protect the urine from light
Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis; check serum creatine kinase

questions.explanation: A uniform (non-speckled) heme pad with no RBCs on microscopy means free pigment in solution; in a crush-injury patient, elevated serum CK confirms myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: A woman with dysuria has a urine pH of 8.5, protein strip 1+, leukocyte esterase positive, and many bacteria on microscopy. A sulfosalicylic acid (SSA) precipitation test on the same specimen is negative. What best explains the protein result?

options.text: Orthostatic proteinuria that resolves when the patient lies down
Early glomerular proteinuria that only SSA can detect
Bence Jones proteinuria missed by the strip but caught by SSA
False-positive protein strip caused by highly alkaline urine (pH >8); the negative SSA confirms no true proteinuria

questions.explanation: Urine pH above 8 falsely turns the protein strip positive; the pH-independent SSA test is negative, proving there is no true proteinuria.

questions.stem: An elderly man with dysuria and frequency voids a specimen 30 minutes after his last void. The strip shows leukocyte esterase positive but nitrite negative; culture later grows Escherichia coli. Which best explains the negative nitrite?

options.text: The strip was read after the prescribed read time
High-dose vitamin C intake caused a false-negative nitrite
E. coli is a non-nitrate-reducing organism

questions.explanation: Nitrite formation requires nitrate-reducing bacteria to incubate in the bladder for at least 4 hours; a specimen voided 30 minutes after the last void is a classic false negative.

questions.stem: A teenager develops cola-colored urine two weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis. Urinalysis shows protein 2+, RBC casts, and dysmorphic RBCs on phase-contrast microscopy. Which additional finding would be INCONSISTENT with the likely diagnosis?

options.text: Visible blood clots in the voided urine

questions.explanation: RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs prove glomerular bleeding (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis); blood clots form in the lower tract and are inconsistent with a glomerular source.

notes.note: RBC casts are usually glomerular, but they also occur in some acute interstitial nephritis (29% in one biopsy series). Here, with dysmorphic RBCs after a strep infection, the answer stands.

questions.stem: A patient with pruritus, jaundice, and pale stools has dark urine that is bilirubin-positive on the strip with absent urobilinogen. Which diagnosis does this pattern most strongly support?

options.text: Hemolytic anemia with increased unconjugated bilirubin
Hepatocellular injury with impaired urobilinogen reuptake
Gilbert syndrome with benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia

questions.explanation: Detectable urine bilirubin is always abnormal and reflects the conjugated fraction; conjugated bilirubinuria with absent urobilinogen defines obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice.

questions.stem: A 5-day-old neonate with vomiting and jaundice has urine that is positive for reducing substances by copper-reduction testing but negative on the glucose-oxidase strip. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attribute the reducing sugar to lactose from breast milk
Work up for galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency)
Screen for phenylketonuria with a ferric chloride test
Repeat the glucose-oxidase strip after a feeding

questions.explanation: Positive copper-reduction with negative glucose-oxidase means a nonglucose reducing sugar; in a vomiting, jaundiced neonate this is galactosemia until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A patient with interstitial nephritis has a positive urine protein strip but a normal spot urine albumin. Which pattern best explains this discrepancy?

options.text: Tubular proteinuria — low-molecular-weight proteins (e.g., β2-microglobulin) that the albumin-specific assay misses
Glomerular proteinuria — the albumin result is wrong
A normal variant requiring no follow-up

questions.explanation: The dipstick detects total protein while albumin-specific assays miss tubular low-molecular-weight proteins — a positive strip with normal albumin points to tubular (not glomerular) proteinuria, as in interstitial nephritis.

questions.stem: A patient with known multiple myeloma has trace protein on the reagent strip but 3+ turbidity on sulfosalicylic acid testing. What best explains this discrepancy?

options.text: SSA gives false positives in the presence of radiocontrast dye
Bence Jones light chains are missed by the strip but precipitated by SSA
Highly alkaline urine is causing a false-positive SSA
The patient has transient functional proteinuria from fever

questions.explanation: The strip's tetrabromphenol blue misses Bence Jones light chains while SSA precipitates all proteins; trace strip with 3+ SSA is the classic myeloma pattern.

questions.stem: A young man has persistent sterile pyuria and microscopic hematuria with acidic urine; routine bacterial cultures are repeatedly negative. Which diagnosis should be considered next?
questions.explanation: Sterile pyuria with hematuria in acidic urine and negative routine cultures is the board clue for renal tuberculosis.

questions.stem: An obtunded patient has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with an elevated osmolal gap. Urinalysis shows envelope-shaped, birefringent calcium oxalate crystals. Which ingestion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Calcium oxalate crystalluria plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis plus an osmolal gap is the ethylene glycol triad.

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent urinary infections has urine pH 7.8 with coffin-lid-shaped crystals; culture grows Proteus mirabilis. Which stone type is this patient at greatest risk for?
questions.explanation: Coffin-lid struvite crystals in alkaline urine with Proteus (a urease producer) predict struvite infection stones, which grow into staghorn calculi.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic renal failure and heavy proteinuria has a fixed urine specific gravity of 1.010 on serial measurements. Which test best assesses this patient's true concentrating ability?

options.text: Repeat specific gravity by urinometer with temperature correction

questions.explanation: Protein and glucose falsely elevate specific gravity, so urine osmolality by freezing-point depression is the true measure of concentrating ability; fixed SG 1.010 is isosthenuria.

questions.stem: A markedly edematous patient with heavy proteinuria has urinary sediment showing oval fat bodies and fatty casts with Maltese-cross lipid droplets under polarized light. This finding is most consistent with:

options.text: Chronic renal failure with waxy casts

questions.explanation: Fatty casts and oval fat bodies with Maltese-cross lipid reflect the heavy lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome, not the waxy casts of chronic renal failure.

questions.stem: A patient with abdominal pain and suspected acute porphyria has a 24-hour urine collected for porphyrins. The jug sat on a sunny windowsill during the collection. What is the best action?

options.text: Recollect with the container protected from light — porphyrins degrade on light exposure
Accept the specimen — light does not affect porphyrins
Accept the specimen but freeze the aliquot before testing
Add an alkaline preservative and accept the collection

questions.explanation: Urine porphyrins are light-sensitive and degrade on exposure — the collection container must be protected from light (amber jug or foil wrap), or the result is falsely low.

questions.stem: A febrile patient with flank pain has hypotonic urine containing glitter cells (swollen granular WBCs) and WBC casts. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: WBC casts localize inflammation to the tubules/interstitium, and glitter cells in hypotonic urine are the classic pyelonephritis clue.

questions.stem: An adult with fever and nuchal rigidity has CSF showing 2,500 WBC/μL with 90% neutrophils, protein 180 mg/dL, glucose 28 mg/dL (serum glucose 110 mg/dL), and lactate 55 mg/dL. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Neutrophilic pleocytosis with glucose <40 mg/dL (CSF/serum <0.3) and lactate >35 mg/dL is the bacterial meningitis pattern; viral meningitis preserves glucose.

questions.stem: A patient with thunderclap headache undergoes lumbar puncture 10 hours after onset. Tube 1 has 50,000 RBC/μL and tube 3 has 48,000 RBC/μL, and the supernatant is xanthochromic. The correct interpretation is:

options.text: Normal variant from a difficult tap

questions.explanation: Uniform blood across tubes plus xanthochromia (6–12 hours to develop) proves subarachnoid hemorrhage; a traumatic tap clears from tube 1 to tube 3.

questions.stem: A pleural fluid analysis shows a fluid/serum protein ratio of 0.45, a fluid/serum LD ratio of 0.50, and fluid LD of 100 U/L (serum upper reference limit 200 U/L). How should this effusion be classified?

options.text: Transudate — none of Light's criteria are met
Exudate by the absolute fluid LD criterion
Exudate by the LD ratio criterion

questions.explanation: None of Light's criteria are met (protein ≥0.50, LD ratio ≥0.60, fluid LD ≥2/3 serum ULN), so this is a transudate despite the near-miss values.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has a parapneumonic pleural effusion with pH 7.15 and glucose 45 mg/dL on blood-gas analysis. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Antibiotics alone with repeat imaging in one week
Diagnostic thoracentesis repeated in one week

questions.explanation: A parapneumonic effusion with pH <7.20 or glucose <60 mg/dL is complicated and requires chest-tube drainage; it will not resolve with antibiotics alone.

questions.stem: After blunt chest trauma, a patient develops a milky pleural effusion. Fluid triglycerides are 180 mg/dL and chylomicrons are present on lipoprotein analysis. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: True chylothorax from thoracic duct disruption

questions.explanation: Triglycerides ≥110 mg/dL with chylomicrons defines true chylothorax (here from traumatic thoracic duct disruption); pseudochylous effusions have triglycerides <50 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient with ascites has an ascitic neutrophil count of 400/μL. Gram stain shows polymicrobial flora, ascitic alkaline phosphatase is 300 U/L, and glucose is low. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start empiric ceftriaxone for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Repeat paracentesis in 48 hours to confirm culture-negative neutrocytic ascites
Start anti-tuberculous therapy for peritoneal tuberculosis
Obtain urgent surgical evaluation for secondary peritonitis

questions.explanation: Polymicrobial flora with ascitic alkaline phosphatase >240 U/L and low glucose indicates secondary peritonitis needing surgery, not SBP (which is >92% monomicrobial).

questions.stem: A knee effusion examined with compensated polarized microscopy shows rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals are calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout); gout crystals are needles with strong negative birefringence.

questions.stem: During lumbar puncture on a patient with no signs of herniation or spinal block, the opening pressure is 260 mmH₂O. What is the maximum volume of CSF that should be withdrawn?
questions.explanation: With opening pressure above 200 mmH₂O, withdraw at most 2 mL; remove none if herniation or spinal block is suspected (unit is mmH₂O, not mmHg).

questions.stem: A lymphocytic pleural exudate has an adenosine deaminase (ADA) level of 55 U/L. This result most strongly supports:
questions.explanation: ADA ≥40 U/L in a lymphocytic exudate is a well-established marker for tuberculous pleuritis (sensitivity ~93%, specificity ~90% at the 40 U/L cutoff); the trap is malignancy attribution without ADA.

questions.stem: A patient with known gout presents with an acutely painful knee. Synovial fluid shows monosodium urate crystals, 60,000 WBC/μL with 92% neutrophils, and a blood-to-fluid glucose difference of 75 mg/dL. Gram stain is negative. What is the best next step?

options.text: Treat the gout flare only, since crystals explain the findings
Start empiric antibiotics for septic arthritis without further testing
Send Gram stain and culture — septic arthritis can coexist with crystal disease
No further workup; a negative Gram stain excludes infection

questions.explanation: MSU crystals never exclude infection; gout and septic arthritis can coexist, so the inflammatory fluid with low glucose still requires Gram stain and culture.

questions.stem: A lumbar puncture yields bloody CSF with 14,000 RBC/μL and 25 WBC/μL. After applying the traumatic tap correction, how should the white cell count be interpreted?

options.text: Traumatic tap; the corrected WBC count is normal

questions.explanation: Traumatic tap correction subtracts 1 WBC per 700 RBCs: 25 − (14,000/700) = 5 WBC/μL, which is normal for an adult.

questions.stem: A patient develops clear, watery rhinorrhea after head trauma. Which laboratory test best confirms that the fluid is cerebrospinal fluid?

options.text: Glucose measurement of the nasal fluid
Total protein of the nasal fluid
Chloride concentration of the nasal fluid

questions.explanation: Beta-2 transferrin is CSF-specific and confirms a CSF leak; glucose is unreliable because nasal secretions also contain glucose.

questions.stem: A patient with central obesity, hypertension, and new diabetes is being screened for Cushing syndrome. Which is the best initial screening test?
questions.explanation: Late-night salivary cortisol reflects free cortisol and loss of the midnight nadir is the most sensitive screen for Cushing syndrome.

questions.stem: A newborn's meconium is negative for ethyl glucuronide, but the mother admits to heavy drinking during the first trimester only. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The EtG result proves no alcohol exposure occurred
EtG does not detect alcohol use
The test was performed too early to detect exposure
First-trimester-only drinking falls outside the meconium detection window

questions.explanation: Meconium reflects the second and third trimesters, so first-trimester-only drinking can yield a negative EtG despite true alcohol exposure.

questions.stem: Two weeks after coronary artery bypass surgery, a patient develops a pericardial effusion. Fluid analysis shows pH 7.42 with normal glucose. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Postpericardiotomy syndrome occurs days to weeks after cardiac surgery with pericardial fluid pH in the normal range (7.35–7.45) and normal glucose; it is immune-mediated and a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.stem: A lipemic sample gives a hemoglobin of 22 g/dL by the HiCN method, but the spun hematocrit is 45% and the RBC count is normal. What is the best explanation?

options.text: True polycythemia — the hemoglobin is accurate
Turbidity from lipemia falsely raising A540 — the HiCN method reads hemoglobin at 540 nm, and any turbidity inflates the result without raising hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Drabkin's converts all hemoglobin forms except sulfhemoglobin; lipemia/high WBC falsely raise A540.

questions.stem: An automated analyzer reports a WBC count of 45 x10^9/L. The manual differential notes 25 nucleated RBCs per 100 WBCs. What is the true WBC count?
questions.explanation: True WBC = 45 x 100/(100 + 25) = 36 x10^9/L; NRBCs fool automated counters.

questions.stem: A Westergren ESR tube is inadvertently left tilted 3 degrees from vertical for the full 60 minutes. What is the expected effect on the result?

options.text: No effect; only tilts greater than 10 degrees matter
The test is invalid and cannot be interpreted

questions.explanation: A 3-degree tilt accelerates Westergren ESR up to 30%; keep the tube dead vertical.

questions.stem: A term newborn on day 1 of life has a reticulocyte count of 5.0%. The parents are alarmed. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Markedly elevated; work up for hemolytic disease of the newborn
Low for a newborn; suspect marrow failure
Normal; the newborn reference range is 2.5-6.5%
Normal only after correcting for the physiologic anemia of infancy

questions.explanation: Newborn retics are 2.5-6.5%, falling to adult 0.5-1.5% by end of week two.

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspirate stained with Perls (Prussian blue) shows 2+ blue granules in marrow macrophages. What does this indicate?

options.text: Absent storage iron, consistent with iron deficiency
Inadequate staining; the test must be repeated

questions.explanation: Perls grades marrow iron 0-5+; 2+ is normal adult storage iron.

questions.stem: A marrow aspirate from the posterior iliac crest returns a "dry tap" with no particles obtained. What is the required next step?

options.text: Repeat the aspirate at the same site immediately
Repeat the aspirate at the anterior iliac crest
Abandon the procedure; the marrow is normal

questions.explanation: A dry tap mandates a core biopsy; suspect myelofibrosis or a packed marrow.

questions.stem: A peripheral smear shows nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes (myelocytes) in a patient with no known hematologic disease. What is this finding called, and what does it most strongly suggest?

options.text: Leukoerythroblastosis; a marrow space-occupying process such as metastatic tumor or myelofibrosis

questions.explanation: Leukoerythroblastosis signals a marrow space-occupying process (tumor, myelofibrosis, MPN).

questions.stem: A CBC shows Hct 36% and RBC 4.0 x10^6/uL. Using MCV (fL) = Hct(%) x 10 / RBC(x10^6/uL), what is the MCV?
questions.explanation: MCV = 36 x 10 / 4.0 = 90 fL; the x10 numerator is the commonly dropped step.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer has an ESR of 115 mm/h. Which interpretation best fits?

options.text: Expected age-related elevation; no further action
Consistent with metastatic disease; an ESR above 100 mm/h in a cancer patient usually signals metastases

questions.explanation: ESR above 100 mm/h in a known cancer patient usually means metastases.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with microcytic anemia has coarse basophilic stippling on the smear. Which exposure history is most important to obtain?

options.text: Lead exposure such as old paint or contaminated water

questions.explanation: Coarse basophilic stippling means lead poisoning or megaloblastic anemia; in a microcytic child, check lead.

questions.stem: A smear shows red cells stacked like coins; the stacking disperses after the sample is warmed and diluted. What is this finding and its cause?

options.text: True agglutination caused by cold agglutinins
Rouleaux caused by elevated fibrinogen or globulins

questions.explanation: Rouleaux from raised fibrinogen/globulins disperses on warming/dilution; true agglutination does not.

questions.stem: A textbook states the normal red cell lifespan is about 120 days, yet the normal 51Cr red cell half-survival is only 28-38 days. What best explains the difference?

options.text: About 1% of the 51Cr elutes from hemoglobin each day, shortening the apparent half-life
Red cells truly live only 30 days and the 120-day figure is outdated

questions.explanation: 51Cr elutes ~1%/day from hemoglobin, so 28-38 day half-survival undershoots the true 120-day lifespan.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders red cell maturation in the marrow?

options.text: Reticulocyte, pronormoblast, basophilic, polychromatophilic, orthochromatic normoblast
Pronormoblast, basophilic normoblast, polychromatophilic normoblast, orthochromatic normoblast, reticulocyte
Pronormoblast, orthochromatic normoblast, basophilic normoblast, polychromatophilic normoblast, reticulocyte
Basophilic normoblast, pronormoblast, orthochromatic normoblast, polychromatophilic normoblast, reticulocyte

questions.explanation: Pronormoblast, basophilic, polychromatophilic, orthochromatic normoblast, reticulocyte.

questions.stem: A patient with hemolytic anemia has a reticulocyte count of 9% and Hct 35%. Using a reticulocyte shift (maturation) time of 1.5 days at Hct 35%, what is the corrected reticulocyte production index?
questions.explanation: (9/1) x (0.35/0.45) / 1.5 = ~4.7; correct for anemia severity AND shift time.

questions.stem: An astronaut returns from a long spaceflight and develops a mild anemia with a low reticulocyte count within days of landing. Which mechanism best explains it?

options.text: Iron deficiency from the space diet
Neocytolysis: selective destruction of young red cells after EPO withdrawal
Hemolysis from cosmic radiation damaging red cell membranes

questions.explanation: Neocytolysis: selective young-RBC loss after abrupt EPO withdrawal (postflight, descent from altitude).

questions.stem: Banked red cells stored for several weeks have depleted 2,3-DPG. Immediately after transfusion, how does this affect oxygen delivery to tissues?

options.text: Improved delivery, because the curve shifts right
Transiently reduced delivery, because low 2,3-DPG raises hemoglobin's oxygen affinity
No effect; 2,3-DPG regenerates instantly in vivo
Improved delivery, because 2,3-DPG binds the alpha chains

questions.explanation: Low 2,3-DPG raises O2 affinity (left shift), transiently impairing tissue unloading after transfusion of old blood.

questions.stem: A patient starting mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) for severe eosinophilic asthma plans travel to a Strongyloides-endemic region. What counseling is most important?

options.text: No special precautions — IL-5 blockade does not affect helminth defense
Screen for and treat Strongyloides before starting — IL-5 drives eosinophils that kill helminths via major basic protein, and blockade risks disseminated strongyloidiasis
Take prophylactic antibiotics for the trip

questions.explanation: IL-5 is the key eosinophil growth factor (with GM-CSF, IL-3).

questions.stem: Which immunophenotype correctly identifies the human hematopoietic stem cell?
questions.explanation: HSC is Lin-CD34+CD38-CD90+CD45RA-CD49f+; CD38 negativity separates stem cells from progenitors.

questions.stem: Which statement about erythropoietin action is INCONSISTENT with chapter principles?

options.text: EPO drives BFU-E and CFU-E proliferation
EPO shortens normoblast generation time and releases reticulocytes early
EPO produces normoblastic hyperplasia with normal cell ratios

questions.explanation: EPO drives BFU-E and CFU-E proliferation, shortening normoblast generation time.

questions.stem: A young woman presents with recurrent severe abdominal pain, and her urine turns dark on standing. The screening test for acute intermittent porphyria is positive with Ehrlich's aldehyde reagent. Which enzyme is defective?
questions.explanation: Acute intermittent porphyria is PBG deaminase deficiency; Ehrlich's aldehyde screens urinary porphobilinogen.

questions.stem: A marrow aspirate shows marked erythroid hyperplasia, yet the peripheral reticulocyte production index is below 2. Which concept best explains this?

options.text: Ineffective erythropoiesis: red cells are made but die before reaching the circulation

questions.explanation: Ineffective erythropoiesis: hyperplastic marrow with RPI below 2 (thalassemia, megaloblastic, MDS).

questions.stem: During B-cell development, in what order do the immunoglobulin light-chain loci rearrange, and on which chromosomes?

options.text: Heavy chain only; light chains do not rearrange

questions.explanation: Kappa (chromosome 2) rearranges before lambda (chromosome 22), after heavy-chain VDJ.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with fatigue has Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, and serum ferritin 9 ug/L. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Anemia of inflammation; ferritin is falsely low
Iron deficiency anemia; ferritin below 12 ug/L is diagnostic

questions.explanation: Ferritin below 12 ug/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient started on oral iron 4 weeks ago has had her hemoglobin rise only 0.4 g/dL. She insists she takes the pills daily. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Noncompliance or wrong diagnosis; an adequate trial raises Hb at least 2 g/dL per 3 weeks after day 5
Iron deficiency was misdiagnosed only if ferritin was normal
The dose is too low; double it immediately

questions.explanation: Hb should rise at least 2 g/dL per 3 weeks after day 5; failure means noncompliance or wrong diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old with macrocytic anemia, paresthesias, and gait instability has a serum B12 of 150 ng/L (borderline). What is the best next test?

options.text: Start folate immediately and recheck B12 later

questions.explanation: Borderline B12 (100-200 ng/L) is confirmed with MMA/homocysteine; never give folate alone with neuro signs.

questions.stem: Two patients with sickle cell disease and microcytosis (MCV 68 fL) both show HbA2 5.2% on HPLC. Patient 1 has no HbA detected; Patient 2 has 15% HbA. What is the correct pair of diagnoses?
questions.explanation: Microcytosis with HbA2 4-6% and no HbA in a sickle patient = S/beta-zero-thalassemia.

questions.stem: A young man develops episodic hemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies after primaquine therapy. A fluorescent spot test for G6PD drawn 2 days after the crisis is normal. What is the best next step?

options.text: Accept the normal result; G6PD deficiency is excluded
Repeat the test in steady state, weeks after the crisis

questions.explanation: Reticulocytes mask G6PD deficiency post-crisis; retest the X-linked defect in steady state weeks later.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and spherocytes on smear is suspected of having hereditary spherocytosis. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: Flow cytometry showing reduced eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding

questions.explanation: Reduced EMA binding on flow confirms hereditary spherocytosis; positive DAT would mean immune spherocytes.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman reports dark morning urine, has pancytopenia, and recently developed a Budd-Chiari hepatic vein thrombosis. Which test confirms the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Flow cytometry for loss of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59) with FLAER

questions.explanation: PNH is confirmed by flow loss of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55/CD59) with FLAER; Ham test is historical.

questions.stem: A patient has pancytopenia with granulocytes 0.3 x10^9/L, platelets 15 x10^9/L, reticulocytes 12 x10^9/L, and marrow cellularity below 25%. How should this be classified?
questions.explanation: Severe AA: granulocytes below 0.5, platelets below 20, retics below 20 (x10^9/L), cellularity below 25%.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old smoker has Hb 18.2 g/dL with an elevated serum EPO and no JAK2 mutation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: High EPO with no JAK2 means secondary erythrocytosis (here smoking-related hypoxia), not PV.

questions.stem: A woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has Hb 9.6 g/dL and serum ferritin 45 ug/L. What does the ferritin most likely indicate?

options.text: Likely iron deficiency that would respond to iron therapy
Adequate iron stores; the anemia is purely anemia of inflammation
A laboratory error; ferritin cannot be interpreted in inflammation

questions.explanation: In inflammation, ferritin below 50-60 ug/L still predicts a response to iron therapy.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows 38% HbS and 60% HbA in an asymptomatic adult. Which counseling statement is correct?

options.text: This is sickle cell disease; start hydroxyurea
This is sickle trait; it is benign and requires no treatment
This is sickle cell disease; the patient needs chronic transfusion
This is sickle/beta-thalassemia; HbA should be absent

questions.explanation: ~60% HbA / 40% HbS is benign sickle trait; SS disease exceeds 80% HbS.

questions.stem: A patient has confirmed hemolysis (reticulocytosis, high LD, low haptoglobin, raised indirect bilirubin) with a positive direct antiglobulin test for IgG. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hemolysis labs confirm destruction; IgG-positive DAT then defines warm AIHA.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic-phase CML has a marrow aspirate showing 14% blasts. How should the phase be classified?
questions.explanation: CML blasts 10-19% (or basophils above 20%) = accelerated phase; 20%+ = blast crisis.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old presents with bleeding, promyelocytes packed with Auer rods on smear, and DIC labs. Cytogenetics are pending. What is the most urgent treatment?
questions.explanation: APL with t(15;17) is a DIC emergency; give ATRA immediately, don't wait for genetics.

questions.stem: A marrow differential on a 500-cell count shows 25% blasts without Auer rods and normal cytogenetics. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: At least 20% blasts by morphology = AML; MDS-EB2 tops out at 10-19%.

questions.stem: A marrow shows 20% ring sideroblasts with SF3B1 mutation, multilineage dysplasia, and 3% blasts. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ring sideroblasts at or above 5% with SF3B1 (or 15% without) define MDS with ring sideroblasts.

questions.stem: For 4 months a patient has had monocytes 2.2 x10^9/L comprising 16% of WBCs, no BCR-ABL1, and 4% marrow blasts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Monocytes above 1 x10^9/L and at least 10% of WBCs for over 3 months, no BCR-ABL1, blasts below 20% = CMML.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry on a lymph node shows a CD5-positive B-cell population that is CD23-negative, FMC7-positive, with bright CD20 and cyclin D1 expression. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CD5+/CD23-/FMC7+/bright CD20/cyclin D1+ (t(11;14)) = mantle cell lymphoma, not CLL.

questions.stem: A myeloma patient develops 8% circulating plasma cells on the differential. According to current IMWG criteria, what does this represent?
questions.explanation: IMWG 2021: at least 5% circulating plasma cells = plasma cell leukemia (old 20% rule retired).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old has hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, lytic bone lesions, and an IgG kappa M-spike. What unifying diagnosis explains these findings?
questions.explanation: CRAB plus clonal M-protein = multiple myeloma; Waldenstrom makes IgM.

questions.stem: A patient with pancytopenia and massive splenomegaly has circulating lymphocytes with circumferential hairy projections that are TRAP-positive and coexpress CD103, CD25, CD11c, and CD123. What treatment offers durable remission?
questions.explanation: Hairy cell leukemia (CD103/CD25/CD11c/CD123, TRAP+, BRAF V600E) melts away with cladribine.

questions.stem: A child has persistent fever, cytopenias, splenomegaly, ferritin 14,000 ug/L, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, and marrow hemophagocytosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fever, cytopenias, hemophagocytosis, extreme hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia = HLH.

questions.stem: A smear shows numerous teardrop cells with leukoerythroblastosis; marrow is fibrotic and inaspirable ("dry tap") with JAK2 V617F detected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Teardrops + leukoerythroblastosis + fibrotic marrow + JAK2 = primary myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: Blasts in an acute leukemia workup are negative for surface lineage markers but positive for cytoplasmic CD3 with negative surface CD3. What lineage should be assigned?
questions.explanation: Cytoplasmic CD3 defines T lineage; the three commandments are cyto-MPO (myeloid), cyto-CD3/surface CD3 (T).

questions.stem: Flow cytometry reports 28% blasts, but the morphologic 500-cell differential counts only 12% blasts in a hemodiluted aspirate. Can acute leukemia be diagnosed?

options.text: Yes; either method reaching 20% is sufficient
Yes; flow cytometry is more sensitive than morphology
No; the 20% blast threshold must come from a morphologic count, and flow counts are distorted by hemodilution and RBC lysis

questions.explanation: The 20% blast threshold belongs to morphology; flow counts are distorted by hemodilution and RBC lysis.

notes.note: Blast thresholds differ between WHO-HAEM5 and ICC 2022 classifications; check which system the question assumes.

questions.stem: A bright PE-positive population appears dimly positive for PE-Cy5. Single-color controls measured PE spillover into the PE-Cy5 detector at 22%, but compensation was set at only 15% subtraction. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Undercompensation — the measured 22% spillover was only partially subtracted
True aberrant antigen expression; report it

questions.explanation: PE spillover into the PE-Cy5 detector measured 22% but only 15% was subtracted — undercompensation creates false dim positivity.

questions.stem: A CLL patient previously treated with rituximab needs measurable residual disease assessment, but no CD20-positive B cells are detectable. What is the best gating adjustment?

options.text: Conclude there is no residual disease
Use a higher antibody concentration to recover CD20
Gate B cells on CD19/CD22/CD79a instead, since rituximab erases detectable CD20

questions.explanation: Rituximab erases detectable CD20; gate B cells on CD19/CD22/CD79a instead.

questions.stem: For measurable residual disease testing at 0.1% sensitivity, with 50 events required to define the abnormal population, how many total WBC events must be acquired?
questions.explanation: 50 events / 50,000 total = 0.1% MRD sensitivity.

questions.stem: For suspected paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, flow cytometry with FLAER is ordered on granulocytes and monocytes. Why are two lineages tested, and what clone-size pattern is expected?

options.text: At least two lineages are required; WBC clones are typically larger than RBC clones
One lineage suffices; RBC clones are typically larger
Two lineages are required because FLAER only binds red cells
Lineage number does not matter; all clones are equal

questions.explanation: PNH flow needs at least two lineages; WBC clones typically exceed RBC clones.

questions.stem: A child's marrow after chemotherapy shows 15% CD10/TdT-positive blast-like cells, but flow shows orderly maturation from CD34 through CD10 to CD20 acquisition with surface immunoglobulin last. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Hematogones; benign regenerating B-cell precursors mimicking lymphoblasts

questions.explanation: Orderly CD34-to-CD20 maturation with surface Ig last = benign hematogones, not B-ALL relapse.

questions.stem: A population unexpectedly stains positive for APC in a panel using PE-Cy5. The red laser was used for excitation. What should be suspected first?

options.text: True APC expression on the blasts
Tandem dye artifact: PE-Cy5 can emit as APC under red-laser excitation
Compensation error in the PE channel

questions.explanation: PE-Cy5 can emit as APC under red-laser excitation (tandem dye artifact); APC-Cy7 can too.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry on a cytopenic patient's marrow shows isolated dim CD45 expression on blasts, with no other abnormalities. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Insufficient for an MDS flow interpretation; combined abnormalities are required
Supports MDS; dim CD45 on blasts indicates dysplastic maturation

questions.explanation: A single MDS-type flow abnormality is never enough; combined abnormalities are required.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry on a lymph node demonstrates kappa light-chain restriction in a B-cell population with an otherwise completely normal immunophenotype. What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: The result is technically invalid; normal B cells express both light chains
Diagnose B-cell lymphoma on clonality alone
Clonality alone does not equal neoplasia; correlate with morphology and clinical context

questions.explanation: Clonality alone is not neoplasia; normal B cells are kappa OR lambda restricted.

questions.stem: When setting gates for a multicolor panel, what is the purpose of fluorescence-minus-one (FMO) controls?

options.text: To define negative populations and set gates when evaluating fluorochrome combinations
To identify the blast population by CD45
To replace isotype controls in all situations

questions.explanation: FMO controls define negative populations and set gates in multicolor panels; they don't compensate.

questions.stem: A patient's prolonged APTT fully corrects on immediate 1:1 mixing with normal pooled plasma but fails to correct after 2 hours of incubation at 37C. What does this indicate?

options.text: A time-dependent factor VIII autoantibody (acquired hemophilia)

questions.explanation: Correction on immediate mix lost after 2 hours at 37C = time-dependent FVIII inhibitor (acquired hemophilia).

questions.stem: A boy with hemophilia A has a factor VIII activity of 0.5%. How is his disease classified, and what bleeding pattern is expected?

options.text: Moderate; bleeds only with major trauma
Severe; spontaneous bleeds about 2-4 times per month
Mild; bleeds 4-6 times per year with minor trauma

questions.explanation: Severe hemophilia is below 1% activity with 2-4 spontaneous bleeds/month.

questions.stem: A patient has an isolated prolonged PT with a normal APTT. Which factor deficiency should be suspected first?
questions.explanation: Isolated prolonged PT points to factor VII, which also has the shortest half-life (3-6 hours).

questions.stem: A preoperative screen shows a markedly prolonged APTT that fully corrects on mixing, but the patient has no bleeding history despite multiple prior surgeries. What is the best next step?

options.text: Reassure and proceed; consider a contact-factor deficiency such as factor XII, which prolongs APTT without bleeding
Transfuse fresh frozen plasma before surgery
Order full intrinsic factor assays urgently

questions.explanation: FXII, prekallikrein, and HMWK prolong APTT with zero bleeding risk; reassure and proceed.

questions.stem: A severe hemophilia A patient on emicizumab has a normal APTT and a one-stage factor VIII activity of 85%. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: The patient no longer has hemophilia
The dose of emicizumab is supratherapeutic
Assay artifact; emicizumab shortens APTT and falsely elevates one-stage FVIII — use a chromogenic (bovine-reagent) FVIII assay

questions.explanation: Emicizumab artifactually shortens APTT and inflates one-stage FVIII; use a chromogenic (bovine) assay.

questions.stem: In a Bethesda assay for a factor VIII inhibitor, the patient's plasma is serially diluted and incubated with normal plasma for 2 hours at 37C. Which dilutions should be used to calculate the titer?

options.text: Only dilutions giving 25-75% residual factor VIII activity
Dilutions giving less than 10% residual activity
Any dilution; the titer is read from the highest dilution

questions.explanation: Bethesda titers are read only from dilutions giving 25-75% residual FVIII; 1 BU destroys 50%.
