questions.stem: A septic patient has platelets 40 x10^9/L, strongly increased D-dimer by the local assay, PT prolonged by 4 seconds, and fibrinogen 80 mg/dL. What is the ISTH DIC score and interpretation?
questions.explanation: 2 (platelets) + 3 (D-dimer) + 1 (PT) + 1 (fibrinogen) = 7, meeting the 5+ overt-DIC threshold (local D-dimer cutoffs).

questions.stem: A neonate has delayed umbilical stump bleeding, and later develops large hematomas 24-36 hours after minor trauma. PT, APTT, and thrombin time are all normal. Which assay is indicated?
questions.explanation: FXIII deficiency has normal PT/APTT/TT (none assesses FXIII) with delayed bleeding 24-36 hours post-trauma.

questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient with INR 2.6 needs a paracentesis. The team requests fresh frozen plasma to "correct" the INR. What is the correct response?

options.text: Give FFP; the INR must be below 1.5 for any procedure
Give vitamin K instead; it works immediately
Withhold FFP; cirrhosis produces rebalanced hemostasis with normal thrombin generation, and guidelines say to ignore the preprocedural PT/INR

questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is rebalanced hemostasis (vWF 300-600% offsets thrombocytopenia); ignore preprocedural PT/INR.

questions.stem: A malnourished patient has a prolonged PT that corrects after vitamin K administration. Which proteins were deficient?

options.text: Factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C, S, Z
von Willebrand factor and factor VIII

questions.explanation: Vitamin K covers factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C, S, Z; IV onset is 2-4 hours.

questions.stem: A patient's D-dimer is markedly elevated but imaging finds no thrombus. Which statement about D-dimer is most accurate?

options.text: It proves a clot is currently present
It proves thrombin formed, fibrin was FXIIIa-cross-linked, and plasmin acted — but not that a pathologic clot persists
It is specific for pulmonary embolism

questions.explanation: D-dimer proves thrombin formed, fibrin was FXIIIa-cross-linked, and plasmin acted — not that a clot persists.

questions.stem: Platelet aggregometry shows absent aggregation to ADP, collagen, epinephrine, and arachidonic acid, but a preserved response to ristocetin with normal platelet count and morphology. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glanzmann (absent GPIIb-IIIa): no aggregation to any agonist except ristocetin; Bernard-Soulier is the mirror.

questions.stem: Platelet aggregometry shows decreased (but not absent) aggregation to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine, with a normal ristocetin response. Electron microscopy of the patient's platelets shows markedly decreased dense granules. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Dense-granule storage pool deficiency (e.g., Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome)

questions.explanation: Storage pool deficiency (dense-granule loss) gives a partial aggregation defect to multiple agonists (ADP, collagen, epinephrine) with a normal ristocetin response; Glanzmann abolishes aggregation to all agonists except ristocetin, while Bernard-Soulier abolishes the ristocetin response.

questions.stem: A bleeding workup shows vWF:RCo 28 IU/dL and vWF:Ag 55 IU/dL. What does the ratio indicate?

options.text: Type 1 von Willebrand disease (partial quantitative defect)

questions.explanation: vWF:RCo/vWF:Ag = 0.51, below 0.6 = qualitative type 2 defect.

notes.note: The 2021 ASH ISTH NHF WFH guideline suggests an activity/antigen ratio below 0.7 (not 0.6) to confirm type 2 VWD, with low certainty. A ratio of 0.51 is type 2 under either rule.

questions.stem: A boy has low factor VIII activity with normal vWF antigen and vWF activity levels, and his parents are asymptomatic. Which von Willebrand disease type best fits?
questions.explanation: Type 2N: defective FVIII binding with normal vWF levels; autosomal hemophilia mimic.

questions.stem: A patient shows hyper-response to low-dose ristocetin with mild thrombocytopenia. How can platelet-type (pseudo-) von Willebrand disease be distinguished from type 2B von Willebrand disease?

options.text: By a mixing experiment: patient platelets plus normal plasma — persistent hyper-response indicates the platelet GPIb defect of pseudo-VWD
They cannot be distinguished; treatment is identical

questions.explanation: Crossover mixing (patient platelets + normal plasma) separates platelet-type VWD (platelet GPIb defect) from type 2B VWD.

questions.stem: In acquired TTP, caplacizumab is added to plasma exchange and immunosuppression. What is its mechanism?

options.text: Anti-vWF A1-domain nanobody that blocks vWF-platelet GPIb-alpha binding

questions.explanation: Caplacizumab is an anti-vWF A1 nanobody blocking vWF-GPIb-alpha binding in acquired TTP.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic adult is found to have platelets 120 x10^9/L on routine labs with no other abnormalities. Does this meet the diagnostic threshold for immune thrombocytopenia?

options.text: Yes; any count below 150 x10^9/L qualifies
Yes, but only if the smear shows giant platelets
No; ITP requires platelets below 100 x10^9/L with no other cause
No; the threshold is below 20 x10^9/L

questions.explanation: ITP needs platelets below 100,000/uL with no other cause; 120k does not qualify.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has large, pale gray-appearing platelets on smear with a mild thrombocytopenia. Electron microscopy would most likely show which defect?

options.text: Absent alpha-granules due to NBEAL2 mutation

questions.explanation: Gray platelet syndrome (NBEAL2) lacks alpha-granules; dense-granule loss pairs with albinism (Hermansky-Pudlak).

questions.stem: Platelet aggregometry is ordered, but the sample was collected in an EDTA tube and the patient took aspirin yesterday. What is the correct action?

options.text: Run the test; EDTA and aspirin do not affect aggregometry
Run the test but ignore the arachidonic acid channel
Switch to a ristocetin-only panel, which is unaffected
Recollect in sodium citrate and reschedule after a 5-7 day aspirin washout

questions.explanation: EDTA kills aggregometry (use citrate) and aspirin needs a 5-7 day washout.

questions.stem: A blood group O patient has vWF activity 42 IU/dL with mild mucocutaneous bleeding. How should the blood group factor into interpretation?

options.text: Type O individuals run about 25% lower vWF than non-O individuals; interpret the borderline level in that context
Blood group has no effect on vWF levels
Type O raises vWF; this level is definitely abnormal
The patient must have type 3 VWD regardless of level

questions.explanation: Type O runs ~25% lower vWF; interpret borderline levels in context, don't dismiss them.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2B von Willebrand disease and thrombocytopenia is about to undergo a minor procedure. Which hemostatic agent is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: DDAVP is contraindicated in type 2B VWD; it releases hyper-adhesive vWF and worsens thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A patient with an unprovoked DVT has a positive lupus anticoagulant on a single test during the acute event. What is required before diagnosing antiphospholipid syndrome?

options.text: Nothing further; one positive LA plus thrombosis is diagnostic
Persistence of a laboratory criterion (LA, aCL, or anti-beta2GPI) on at least two occasions 12 weeks apart

questions.explanation: APS requires a lab criterion positive on at least two occasions 12 weeks apart; one acute-event positive is not a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old heterozygous for factor V Leiden is also found to have factor VIII activity of 200%. How do these two risk factors interact?

options.text: Risks multiply, not add — combined defects raise VTE risk more than either alone
They cancel out — the risks are independent
Only the factor VIII level matters

questions.explanation: Thrombotic risks multiply, not add: FVL heterozygosity (~4-5x) combined with elevated FVIII activity (200%) raises VTE risk substantially more than either defect alone; counsel contraception and risk reduction.

questions.stem: Three days after starting warfarin, a patient with known protein C deficiency develops painful necrotic skin lesions on the thighs. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Protein C deficiency protects against warfarin necrosis
Heparin contamination of the warfarin tablets
Warfarin depletes protein C before the procoagulant factors fall, tipping the microvasculature into thrombosis

questions.explanation: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis = protein C (or S) deficiency until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 20 weeks gestation has free protein S 55% of the non-pregnant reference mean. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Physiologic; free protein S falls to about 60% of non-pregnant levels from the 10th week of gestation

questions.explanation: Free protein S physiologically falls to ~60% from the 10th week of pregnancy; don't call it deficiency.

questions.stem: A thrombophilia workup includes a factor II activity assay, which returns normal. Can prothrombin G20210A be excluded?

options.text: Yes; activity assays detect all prothrombin variants
Yes, if the APC-resistance ratio is also normal
No; the variant raises prothrombin protein levels 15-30% but is invisible to activity assays — DNA genotyping is required

questions.explanation: Factor II activity assays cannot detect G20210A; only DNA genotyping can.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with an unprovoked DVT asks to be tested for MTHFR C677T because an online forum blamed it for his clot. What is the correct response?

options.text: Order it only if homocysteine is normal
Order it; it is the strongest thrombophilia
Decline routine testing; MTHFR C677T is not an independent adult VTE risk factor per ACMG/ACOG guidance
Order it; a positive result mandates lifelong warfarin

questions.explanation: MTHFR C677T is not an independent adult VTE risk factor; ACMG/ACOG advise against routine testing.

questions.stem: A patient is positive for lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG at 80 IU, and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies. What does this pattern signify?

options.text: Laboratory interference; the results cancel out
Triple positivity — the highest risk of first and recurrent thrombosis in APS
Low risk; single positivity would be worse

questions.explanation: Triple positivity (LA + aCL + anti-beta2GPI) carries the highest first and recurrent thrombosis risk.

questions.stem: A family has venous thrombosis in multiple members across generations; affected members have antithrombin activity near 50% of normal. What inheritance and penetrance pattern does this illustrate?

options.text: Autosomal dominant with high penetrance — heterozygotes at ~50% levels develop thrombosis

questions.explanation: Antithrombin deficiency is autosomal dominant with high penetrance; 50% levels still clot.

questions.stem: Two weeks after an acute DVT, a patient's factor VIII activity is 220% of normal. How should this result be used in the thrombophilia assessment?

options.text: It confirms a factor VIII-driven thrombophilia; start lifelong anticoagulation
It is diagnostic of von Willebrand disease
It is unreliable; factor VIII rises as an acute-phase reactant during and after a clot — reassess when the patient is quiet, months later, off anticoagulants

questions.explanation: FVIII is an acute-phase reactant; elevated levels near the event are unreliable — retest when quiet and off therapy.

questions.stem: An APC-resistance ratio (clotting time with APC divided by without) is 2.6 on an assay whose cutoff is 2.0. What does this indicate?

options.text: APC resistance/FVL is excluded by this assay
Factor V Leiden heterozygosity is confirmed

questions.explanation: A ratio above the assay cutoff (1.8 or 2.0) excludes APC resistance/FVL.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old presents with bleeding, a very prolonged PT and APTT, and a positive lupus anticoagulant. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency; oral vitamin K

questions.explanation: LA-hypoprothrombinemia syndrome: the bleeding exception in children, with very prolonged PT/APTT, responsive to corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A patient with an older caged-ball aortic valve on warfarin asks for her target INR. What is the correct range?
questions.explanation: Mechanical mitral (and caged-ball aortic) valves need INR 2.5-3.5, target 3.0.

questions.stem: A patient with acute HIT (high 4T score, strongly positive PF4-heparin ELISA) needs continued anticoagulation for a new proximal DVT. All heparin has been stopped. Which replacement anticoagulant is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: LMWH cross-reacts with anti-PF4/heparin antibodies in vivo and is contraindicated in HIT; argatroban, bivalirudin, and fondaparinux (no in vivo cross-reactivity) are acceptable.

questions.stem: A patient has a low 4T score (2 points) for suspected HIT. A PF4-ELISA returns weakly positive. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: HIT is confirmed; the ELISA is 100% specific
Start argatroban immediately regardless of probability
The ELISA's 98% sensitivity rules out HIT
With a low 4T score the pretest probability is only 0-3%, and the ELISA is sensitive (~98%) but less specific (~89%) — pursue a functional assay before diagnosing HIT

questions.explanation: Low 4T = 0-3% probability; the PF4-ELISA's ~89% specificity makes weak positives unreliable — confirm with a functional assay.

questions.stem: A patient on therapeutic enoxaparin has a normal APTT. The team worries the dose is subtherapeutic. What is the correct monitoring approach?

options.text: Increase the dose until the APTT is prolonged
Measure anti-factor Xa activity with a peak drawn about 4 hours post-dose; LMWH is not monitored by APTT
Stop the enoxaparin; a normal APTT proves noncompliance

questions.explanation: LMWH is monitored by anti-Xa peak ~4 hours post-dose, never by APTT.

questions.stem: A bleeding trauma patient takes dabigatran and has a prolonged thrombin time. Which test best quantifies the dabigatran level?

options.text: Dilute thrombin time or ecarin clotting time

questions.explanation: Dilute thrombin time or ecarin clotting time quantifies dabigatran within/above the on-therapy range; a normal TT only excludes clinically relevant levels.

questions.stem: A patient on apixaban needs assessment of residual anticoagulant effect before urgent surgery. The PT is normal. What is the correct test?

options.text: Repeat PT with a different thromboplastin

questions.explanation: For apixaban/rivaroxaban, only a drug-calibrated anti-Xa assay is linear and reliable.

questions.stem: A brodifacoum-poisoned patient is on prolonged high-dose oral vitamin K1. Which laboratory test best monitors therapy over the months-long course?
questions.explanation: PT/INR monitors recovery during prolonged vitamin K1 therapy for brodifacoum poisoning.

questions.stem: A life-threatening bleed on dabigatran receives idarucizumab 5 g with good initial reversal, but bleeding recurs 12 hours later with a rising dilute thrombin time. What is the best next step?

options.text: Observe; dabigatran cannot rebound after reversal
Give a second 5-g idarucizumab dose — about 23% of patients need redosing for recurrent bleeding after 12 hours

questions.explanation: Recurrent bleeding with renewed dabigatran effect warrants a second 5-g idarucizumab dose.

questions.stem: A patient on clopidogrel after stent placement has high on-treatment platelet reactivity. Genetic testing shows CYP2C19 2/2. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Ultrarapid activation causing excess bleeding risk only
CYP2C19 directly inhibits the P2Y12 receptor
Clopidogrel is a prodrug requiring CYP2C19 bioactivation; poor metabolizers generate less active drug (FDA boxed warning, March 2010)

questions.explanation: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 bioactivation; 2/3 poor metabolizers get less effect (FDA boxed warning).

questions.stem: A HIT patient is transitioned from heparin to argatroban. What are its half-life and APTT target?

options.text: Half-life 40-50 minutes; target 1.5-3.0 times the baseline APTT

questions.explanation: Argatroban: half-life 40-50 minutes, APTT target 1.5-3.0x baseline.

questions.stem: A warfarin patient's INR is supratherapeutic, but she is known to have a lupus anticoagulant. Which test best reflects her true warfarin effect?

options.text: Repeat INR with the same thromboplastin

questions.explanation: Lupus anticoagulant falsely prolongs PT with some thromboplastins; use a direct chromogenic factor X assay for warfarin monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient with warm AIHA has a panreactive antibody screen; the transfusion service must rule out underlying alloantibodies before transfusion. What is the best approach?

options.text: Transfuse without further testing — the autoantibody explains everything
Perform an autoadsorption with the patient's own cells to remove the autoantibody, then test the adsorbed serum for alloantibodies
Use only the DAT result to select blood

questions.explanation: Warm autoantibody coats all reagent cells — autoadsorption removes it so underlying alloantibodies are unmasked in the adsorbed serum. (Cold adsorption is for cold autoantibodies.)

questions.stem: An Rh-negative woman has a fetomaternal hemorrhage quantified at 60 mL of fetal whole blood. How many standard RhIG vials should she receive?
questions.explanation: One RhIG vial covers 30 mL of whole blood (15 mL packed cells); 60 mL needs 2 vials within 72 hours.

questions.stem: A daratumumab-treated patient's serum is tested against DTT-treated reagent cells to resolve IAT panreactivity. Which antibody can NO LONGER be excluded by this panel?
questions.explanation: Daratumumab (anti-CD38) causes IAT panreactivity; resolve with DTT-treated cells and give K-negative blood since DTT destroys Kell.

questions.stem: An antibody detected at the IAT phase reacts 2+ with untreated panel cells but is nonreactive with ficin-treated cells. What is the most likely specificity?
questions.explanation: Ficin/papain destroys Fya, Fyb, M, N, S, s but enhances Rh, Kidd, Lewis, P1; lost reactivity points to anti-Fya.

questions.stem: Forward typing shows group A; reverse typing agglutinates both A1 and B reagent cells, the reactions are weaker at 37°C than at room temperature, and the autocontrol is positive. The most likely explanation is:
questions.explanation: Extra reverse-type reactions that weaken on warming, with a positive autocontrol, are cold autoagglutinins; prewarm before invoking exotic ABO variants.

questions.stem: A donor unit is D-negative on direct typing but D-positive after the weak D (IAT-phase) test. How should the unit be labeled?
questions.explanation: Donor units positive by direct or weak D testing are labeled Rh-positive; recipients are typed by direct test only.

questions.stem: A transfusion candidate is found to have a partial D phenotype. Which blood should she receive?
questions.explanation: Partial D patients can make allo-anti-D, so they are managed as Rh-negative (weak D types 1/2/3 are the exception).

questions.stem: A pregnant woman's serum shows anti-D titer 32 and anti-C titer 128. What does this pattern suggest?

options.text: Two separate alloantibodies of equal concern
Laboratory error - titers cannot differ this way
The anti-C result is clinically irrelevant
Anti-G, since the anti-C titer is at least 4-fold higher than anti-D

questions.explanation: Anti-C titer at least 4-fold higher than anti-D suggests anti-G rather than true separate anti-D.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient has anti-K with a low titer of 8, yet MCA Dopplers show fetal anemia. Why can low anti-K titers still threaten the fetus?

options.text: Anti-K suppresses fetal erythropoiesis rather than just hemolyzing red cells, so titers underestimate danger
Anti-K is an IgM antibody that crosses the placenta
Anti-K titers always underestimate because of dosage

questions.explanation: Anti-Kell suppresses fetal erythropoiesis, not just hemolysis, so titers underestimate fetal danger.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative woman of childbearing potential urgently needs one RBC unit, but only Rh-positive units are available. What is the best management?

options.text: Transfuse the Rh-positive unit and give RhIG to suppress D alloimmunization
Withhold transfusion until Rh-negative blood arrives, regardless of urgency
Transfuse the Rh-positive unit without RhIG

questions.explanation: RhIG is given within 72 hours (routine at 28 weeks and postpartum); one vial covers 30 mL whole blood and it is useless once immunized.

questions.stem: Besides ABO antibodies, which alloantibody is classically associated with complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis in transfusion reactions?
questions.explanation: Kidd antibodies can fix complement and cause intravascular hemolysis; Lewis, M, and P1 are usually insignificant.

questions.stem: A healthy term newborn has a platelet count of 18,000/uL on day 1; the mother is well with a normal platelet count. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Congenital CMV with isolated neonatal thrombocytopenia
Passive transfer of maternal ITP antibodies
Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia from maternal anti-HPA-1a

questions.explanation: Isolated severe neonatal thrombocytopenia with a healthy mother is FNAIT, most often maternal anti-HPA-1a.

questions.stem: Eight days after an RBC transfusion, a multiparous woman presents with platelets below 10,000/uL and bleeding. What is the best treatment?
questions.explanation: Posttransfusion purpura (5-10 days, platelets <10,000/uL) is treated with IVIg 1-2 g/kg; transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed.

questions.stem: Which antibody specificity requires homozygous (double-dose) screening cells so it is not missed due to dosage?
questions.explanation: Anti-Jkb shows dosage and needs homozygous screening cells, like anti-Fya, -Fyb, -Jka, -M, -N, -S, -s.

questions.stem: A rosette test performed after delivery is positive. What is the required next step?

options.text: Repeat the rosette test in one week
Give one standard RhIG vial and stop
The rosette test is quantitative; no further testing is needed
Quantitate the fetomaternal hemorrhage by Kleihauer-Betke or flow cytometry to calculate additional RhIG dosing

questions.explanation: A positive rosette screen detects ~10 mL of fetal cells and triggers quantitation to dose extra RhIG.

questions.stem: A patient with hemolytic anemia has a DAT positive for C3d only, with a cold agglutinin titer of 1:32,000 at 4C. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: C3d-only DAT means complement without IgG: cold agglutinin disease (IgM anti-I), not warm AIHA (IgG +/- C3d).

questions.stem: A donor types Rh-negative by both direct and weak D testing. Could this donor's red cells immunize an Rh-negative recipient to D?

options.text: Yes - a Del phenotype, detectable only by adsorption/elution, can immunize despite typing Rh-negative
No - Rh-negative by weak D testing is always safe
Only if the recipient is pregnant
Only with whole blood, not packed cells

questions.explanation: Del phenotype is detectable only by adsorption/elution yet can immunize Rh-negative recipients.

questions.stem: A newborn's forward type shows only weak agglutination with anti-A. What best explains this?

options.text: Acquired B antigen from gut bacteria
Newborns have fewer A antigen sites per cell (250-370 x 10^3 vs 810-1,170 x 10^3 in adults), giving weaker forward reactions
Maternal anti-A coating the newborn's cells

questions.explanation: Newborns have fewer ABO antigen sites per cell, so forward typing is legitimately weaker.

questions.stem: An antibody screen is panreactive at room temperature but completely negative at the 37C IAT phase, and the patient urgently needs blood. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use the prewarm technique to remove cold autoantibody interference, then proceed
Run the screen only at room temperature and crossmatch by immediate spin
Transfuse group O red cells without further testing
Repeat the screen with enzyme-treated cells

questions.explanation: Room-temperature-only panreactivity is cold autoantibody interference; the prewarm technique clears it for 37C testing.

questions.stem: A trauma patient needs RBCs immediately; the antibody screen is negative with no history of antibodies. Which crossmatch approach is acceptable?

options.text: Full antiglobulin crossmatch is mandatory in all cases
Transfusion must wait for a full antibody panel
No compatibility testing is needed in emergencies

questions.explanation: With a negative screen and no antibody history, immediate-spin or electronic crossmatch suffices (AHTR risk ~0.0004%).

questions.stem: Before eluting antibody from DAT-positive red cells, what quality check is required?

options.text: A positive control elution in parallel
The last-wash control must be negative
Repeating the DAT with a different reagent lot

questions.explanation: The last-wash control must be negative to prove eluate antibody came off the cells, not from residual serum.

questions.stem: A DAT-positive patient's own red cells must be phenotyped to select antigen-negative units. Which treatment removes coating IgG while preserving typing antigens?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine dissociates IgG (not complement) while preserving typing antigens; DTT/ZZAP destroy Kell.

questions.stem: A group O mother delivers a group A infant with a weakly positive DAT and mild jaundice. What is the expected course?

options.text: Caused by maternal IgM anti-A crossing the placenta
Usually mild - severe ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn is rare (about 0.04%)
Identical in severity to RhD hemolytic disease

questions.explanation: Severe ABO HDFN is rare (~0.04%); it is usually mild since much ABO antibody is IgM and fetal antigens are weakly expressed.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman is genotyped as weak D type 1. How should she be managed for transfusion and RhIG?

options.text: Treat as Rh-negative and give RhIG
She may receive Rh-positive blood and does not need RhIG

questions.explanation: Weak D types 1, 2, and 3 are not at alloimmunization risk: they may receive Rh-positive blood and skip RhIG.

questions.stem: An antibody reacts weakly but is still detectable at a titer of 1:128. How should it be interpreted?

options.text: As a high-titer low-avidity (HTLA) antibody, usually clinically insignificant
As a clinically significant alloantibody requiring antigen-negative blood
As evidence of dosage requiring homozygous cells

questions.explanation: Weak-appearing antibodies reactive at >=1:64 are HTLA (e.g., Chido/Rodgers), usually clinically insignificant.

questions.stem: Which bedside practice best prevents acute hemolytic transfusion reactions?

options.text: Using one identifier plus the room number
Prelabeling tubes at the nurses' station before collection
Drawing the type and screen from an existing IV line
Labeling the sample tube at the bedside against the wristband with at least two unique identifiers

questions.explanation: Mislabeled patient/sample is the most common cause of AHTR; labels need two unique identifiers applied at the bedside.

questions.stem: In a massive hemorrhage with no time for typing, which emergency-release combination is correct?

options.text: Group A red cells with group O plasma
Group O plasma with group AB red cells
Group O red cells with AB plasma
Group AB red cells with group O plasma

questions.explanation: Emergency release: O red cells (compatible with recipient antibodies) with AB plasma (compatible with recipient red cells).

questions.stem: Two hours after plasma transfusion, a patient develops dyspnea, hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates, jugular venous distension, and a markedly elevated BNP. What is most likely?
questions.explanation: Elevated BNP with circulatory overload signs is TACO; BNP does not rise in TRALI.

notes.note: Natriuretic peptides are raised in severe TRALI and critical illness (Vlaar 2019); a low BNP argues against TACO, but a high BNP does not exclude TRALI.

questions.stem: TRALI is diagnosed 3 hours into a transfusion, with normal BNP and no cardiac history. What is the best management?

options.text: Give furosemide and continue the transfusion slowly
Stop the transfusion and provide supportive oxygen; diuretics do not help
Slow the rate and finish the unit

questions.explanation: TRALI is noncardiogenic leaky-lung edema (resolves 48-96 h) managed with oxygen only; diuresis is for TACO.

notes.note: Natriuretic peptides are raised in severe TRALI and critical illness (Vlaar 2019); a low BNP argues against TACO, but a high BNP does not exclude TRALI.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into an RBC transfusion, the patient's temperature rises 1.2C with chills. What is the best next step?

options.text: Slow the infusion and continue observing
Stop the transfusion and evaluate for hemolysis and bacterial contamination
Give diphenhydramine and restart the unit
Premedicate with acetaminophen and restart the same unit slower

questions.explanation: A fever rise >=1C means stop the transfusion, then rule out hemolysis and bacterial contamination before any restart.

notes.note: The ≥ 1 °C trigger was not found in the sources checked; WHO 2001 allows a slow restart with a new unit if the patient improves. Stopping and ruling out hemolysis and bacterial contamination is supported.

questions.stem: A patient with a platelet count of 65,000/uL needs urgent neurosurgery. Should platelets be transfused?

options.text: Yes - the threshold is 100,000/uL for CNS or retinal procedures

questions.explanation: Platelet thresholds: 10k stable, 20k low-risk procedure, 50k high-risk surgery, 100k CNS/retinal.

questions.stem: A stable critically ill patient has a hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL without active bleeding. Should RBCs be transfused?

options.text: Yes - the trigger is 8.0 g/dL for all inpatients
No - the restrictive trigger is 7.0 g/dL in critically ill patients
Only with symptoms regardless of hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Restrictive trigger is Hb <7.0 g/dL in critically ill (and non-exsanguinating UGI bleed); <8.0 only in acute coronary syndrome.

notes.note: The MINT trial (acute MI) found a restrictive 7–8 g/dL strategy may increase MI or death; a fixed restrictive trigger in acute MI is contested (Yang 2026).

questions.stem: A bleeding patient with fibrinogen 85 mg/dL also has severe volume overload. Which fibrinogen replacement is preferred, and why?

options.text: Cryoprecipitate — concentrated fibrinogen in small volume

questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen when <100 mg/dL with bleeding (~150-250 mg fibrinogen per unit).

notes.note: Current reviews place increased bleeding risk below ~200 mg/dL fibrinogen (population-dependent); AABB requires ≥ 150 mg fibrinogen per cryo unit (Rahe-Meyer 2026).

questions.stem: A stable 70-kg adult with Hb 6.8 g/dL and no active bleeding needs transfusion. What is the best practice?

options.text: No transfusion is needed at Hb 6.8 g/dL
Transfuse one unit, then recheck Hb before deciding on more

questions.explanation: One RBC unit raises Hb ~1 g/dL (Hct ~3%) in a 70-kg adult; transfuse one unit at a time in stable patients.

questions.stem: An RBC unit is irradiated on day 5 after collection. When does it expire?

options.text: No more than 28 days from irradiation

questions.explanation: Irradiated RBCs expire within 28 days of irradiation; platelet expiration is unchanged.

questions.stem: A platelet unit was accidentally stored at 1-6C overnight. What is the problem?

options.text: Cold storage is acceptable if the unit is warmed to 37C before transfusion
There is no effect on the product
Platelets must be stored at 20-24C with agitation; refrigeration impairs their function and viability

questions.explanation: Platelets are stored at 20-24C with agitation (up to 5 days, pH >=6.0); refrigeration injures them.

notes.note: Platelet storage is now 5–7 days at 20–24 °C where bacterial-risk controls are used, and licensed cold-stored platelets (FDA 2023 variance, up to 14 days at 1–6 °C) are an exception (Akaraphanth 2026).
A 2022 US licensing study used end-of-storage platelet pH ≥ 6.2 as its acceptance endpoint; the reviewer’s ≥ 6.0 is unconfirmed.

questions.stem: A stable premature infant has a platelet count of 45,000/uL without bleeding. Should platelets be transfused?

options.text: Yes - the threshold is 50,000/uL for stable premature infants
No - the 10,000/uL threshold applies to all patients
Give a full adult apheresis unit

questions.explanation: Neonatal platelet thresholds: term <30k, stable premature <50k, unstable premature <100k.

questions.stem: A unit of FFP was thawed 6 days ago and kept refrigerated. Can it still be transfused?

options.text: No - thawed plasma is good refrigerated for only 5 days
Yes, if factor VIII activity is verified

questions.explanation: Thawed plasma keeps only 5 days refrigerated with adequate factor V/VIII.

questions.stem: Which carries the highest per-unit infection risk among blood components?

options.text: Bacterial sepsis from platelets, about 1 in 75,000 culture-negative apheresis units

questions.explanation: Bacterial sepsis from platelets (~1:75,000) dwarfs current viral risks (HIV ~1:1.86M).

questions.stem: Which scenario meets the definition of massive transfusion?

options.text: Replacement of one blood volume in 24 hours, or ongoing loss of at least 150 mL/min
Any transfusion given to a trauma patient

questions.explanation: Massive transfusion: 1 blood volume/24 h or ongoing loss >=150 mL/min.

questions.stem: A granulocyte unit is ordered for a neutropenic patient with sepsis. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It can be frozen for later use
The unit must be ABO-compatible and transfused within 24 hours of collection

questions.explanation: Granulocytes contain substantial RBCs, so they must be ABO-compatible and transfused within 24 h.

questions.stem: A patient shows poor platelet increments on two occasions, with a 1-hour CCI of 4,000. What does this indicate?

options.text: Platelet refractoriness - success requires CCI above 7,500 at 1 hour (4,500 at 24 hours)
A normal result for a large patient

questions.explanation: Refractoriness is poor increments on >=2 occasions; success is CCI >7,500 at 1 h or >4,500 at 24 h.

questions.stem: During a platelet transfusion, a patient on an ACE inhibitor develops a 25 mmHg systolic drop that resolves 20 minutes after stopping. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Hypotensive reaction from bradykinin accumulation with ACE inhibition and negatively charged filters

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors plus negatively charged filters cause bradykinin-mediated hypotensive reactions (>=10 mmHg drop, resolving within 30 min).

questions.stem: Ten days after receiving non-irradiated RBCs from a first-degree relative, a patient develops fever, maculopapular rash, diarrhea, liver dysfunction, and pancytopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Only irradiation (>=25 Gy center, >=15 Gy periphery) prevents TA-GVHD; leukoreduction does not.

questions.stem: An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is suspected 15 minutes into an RBC unit. What is the first priority?

options.text: Speed up the infusion to finish before hemolysis worsens
Stop the transfusion, keep IV access open with saline, verify patient and unit identity, and notify the blood bank
Restart with a different unit immediately

questions.explanation: For suspected AHTR: stop, keep IV open with saline, verify identity, quarantine units, notify the blood bank.

questions.stem: A patient with IgA deficiency and anti-IgA needs RBC transfusion after a prior anaphylactic reaction. Which product is best?

options.text: Washed RBCs (or RBCs from an IgA-deficient donor)

questions.explanation: Washed RBCs (or IgA-deficient donors) prevent IgE anti-IgA anaphylaxis to donor plasma IgA.

questions.stem: A patient with warm AIHA (DAT IgG-positive) needs urgent transfusion; all crossmatches are incompatible due to the autoantibody. What is the best approach?

options.text: Withhold transfusion until a fully compatible unit is found
Transfuse only group O red cells
Transfuse the "least incompatible" unit — the autoantibody reacts with all cells, so delay risks death

questions.explanation: In warm AIHA no unit will be truly compatible — transfuse the least-incompatible unit when the patient needs it; the autoantibody destroys the patient's own cells too, so transfusion still nets oxygen-carrying capacity.

questions.stem: A patient has anti-E identified on antibody panel and needs RBCs. Which crossmatch is appropriate?

options.text: No crossmatch is needed with a single antibody
Antiglobulin crossmatch using E-negative units - immediate-spin is unacceptable

questions.explanation: With any clinically significant antibody, crossmatch must be antiglobulin-phase against antigen-negative units.

questions.stem: A nonbleeding patient with an INR of 1.5 needs a bedside procedure. Should plasma be transfused?

options.text: No - plasma offers no benefit to nonbleeders with INR below 1.8-2.0

questions.explanation: Plasma offers no benefit to nonbleeders with INR <1.8-2.0; dose is 15-30 mL/kg for real deficiency or bleeding.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of anti-Jka (now undetectable on the current screen) needs transfusion. Which units should be selected?

options.text: Jk(a-) units, honoring the history of a clinically significant antibody
Any units - the current screen is negative
Group O negative units regardless of Jk type
Washed units to remove the antibody

questions.explanation: A history of a clinically significant antibody (e.g., anti-Jka) must be honored even when currently undetectable.

questions.stem: A physician orders "plasmapheresis" expecting a 1.5-plasma-volume exchange with albumin replacement for myasthenia gravis. What is the terminology error?

options.text: The terms are interchangeable; no error occurred
What was ordered is therapeutic plasma exchange — plasmapheresis removes less than 15% of plasma volume with no replacement fluid
Albumin replacement is contraindicated in myasthenia gravis

questions.explanation: Plasmapheresis removes <15% of plasma volume with no replacement; TPE exchanges 1.0-1.5 volumes with replacement.

questions.stem: After exchanging one full plasma volume during TPE, approximately how much of an intravascular substance remains?
questions.explanation: TPE kinetics (Y = Y0 x e^-x): ~30% remains after one plasma volume, ~10% after two.

questions.stem: A patient with TTP needs urgent therapeutic plasma exchange. Which replacement fluid is required?

options.text: Plasma (60-70% FFP with saline remainder) — to supply ADAMTS13

questions.explanation: TTP needs plasma replacement to supply ADAMTS13 — albumin is the default for most other indications but useless here. Always draw ADAMTS13 before the first TPE.

questions.stem: Using Gilcher's rule of fives, what is the estimated blood volume of a muscular 80-kg man?
questions.explanation: Gilcher's rule: muscular male = 75 mL/kg; 80 x 75 = 6,000 mL.

questions.stem: A 50-kg donor is undergoing plateletpheresis. What is the maximum blood volume allowed outside the donor at one time?
questions.explanation: AABB donor extracorporeal circuit limit is 10.5 mL/kg; 50 x 10.5 = 525 mL.

questions.stem: During plateletpheresis, a donor reports tingling around the mouth. What is the best action?

options.text: Slow the reinfusion and give oral calcium - this is early citrate toxicity

questions.explanation: Perioral paresthesia is the first sign of citrate toxicity; slow reinfusion and give oral calcium.

questions.stem: A patient develops carpopedal spasm during large-volume leukapheresis. IV calcium gluconate gives only transient improvement, and spasms recur. Which electrolyte abnormality best explains the calcium resistance?

options.text: Hypomagnesemia — Mg2+ falls faster and recovers slower than Ca2+ during citrate anticoagulation; its symptoms mimic hypocalcemia and resist calcium

questions.explanation: Citrate chelates magnesium too — Mg2+ falls faster and recovers slower than Ca2+, and hypomagnesemia symptoms (spasm, tetany, arrhythmia) mimic hypocalcemia but resist calcium replacement.

questions.stem: A patient on a long-half-life ACE inhibitor is scheduled for TPE in 24 hours and had flushing and hypotension during a prior procedure. What is the best plan?

options.text: Postpone TPE until the ACE inhibitor has been withheld longer than the standard 24-48 hours — longer agents need extended washout
Proceed on schedule; 24 hours suffices for all ACE inhibitors

questions.explanation: Withhold ACE inhibitors 24-48 h before hemapheresis to prevent bradykinin-mediated hypotension.

questions.stem: What is the optimal G-CSF mobilization regimen for a healthy allogeneic HPC-apheresis donor?

options.text: 20 mcg/kg as a single daily dose

questions.explanation: Healthy allogeneic HPC-A donors: 10-16 mcg/kg/day split into 2 SC doses; 5-10 mcg/kg x 4-5 days is the patient/autologous regimen.

questions.stem: A healthy donor is receiving G-CSF 20 mcg/kg/day for HPC mobilization. What is the expected effect of this dose?

options.text: Greater CD34+ yield than standard dosing
No further CD34+ gain, only more toxicity
No further CD34+ gain but less toxicity

questions.explanation: Above 16 mcg/kg/day there is no further CD34+ gain, only more toxicity.

questions.stem: A non-Hodgkin lymphoma patient has failed G-CSF mobilization for autologous HPC collection. What is the next best step?

options.text: Add plerixafor, a CXCR4 inhibitor approved for NHL/multiple myeloma patients failing G-CSF
Repeat with a higher G-CSF dose alone
Use plerixafor in a healthy allogeneic donor instead

questions.explanation: Plerixafor (CXCR4 inhibitor) is approved for NHL/myeloma patients failing G-CSF, not for normal donors.

questions.stem: An apheresis HPC product contains 9 x 10^6 CD34+ cells/kg recipient weight. What is the main concern?

options.text: Engraftment failure from too few cells
No concern - this is an ideal dose
Increased risk of chronic GVHD above 8.0 x 10^6/kg

questions.explanation: CD34+ doses above 8.0 x 10^6/kg increase chronic GVHD risk; minimum engraftment dose is 2.5 x 10^6/kg.

questions.stem: What are the red cell exchange targets for a sickle cell disease patient?
questions.explanation: RCE targets Hct ~30% and HbS <30%, lowering HbS without raising viscosity.

questions.stem: Therapeutic plasma exchange for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura falls into which ASFA category?
questions.explanation: ASFA category I = first-line therapy (TPE for TTP is I/1A).

questions.stem: A Waldenström macroglobulinemia patient with hyperviscosity receives TPE and improves dramatically, but symptoms recur within weeks. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The TPE technique was inadequate; repeat with larger exchange volumes
The wrong replacement fluid was used
TPE removes IgM but does not stop its production — definitive therapy is needed to prevent rebound

questions.explanation: TPE is an adjunct, never primary therapy; without definitive treatment the substance rebounds.

questions.stem: An extracorporeal photopheresis product has a hematocrit of 12%. What should be done?

options.text: Reduce red cells - the product hematocrit must be below 7% or red cells block UVA light
Add plasma to dilute the cells

questions.explanation: ECP product Hct must be <7% or red cells block UVA activation of 8-MOP.

questions.stem: A homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia patient has LDL 550 mg/dL despite maximal drug therapy and diet. Does he meet FDA criteria for LDL apheresis?

options.text: Yes - homozygotes qualify with LDL above 500 mg/dL
No - diet must be tried for another year first

questions.explanation: FDA LDL-apheresis criteria: homozygotes LDL >500, heterozygotes >=300 after maximal therapy, >=200 with CAD.

questions.stem: Citrate anticoagulation in the apheresis circuit works by lowering ionized calcium to what target?
questions.explanation: Citrate anticoagulation targets ionized calcium 0.2-0.3 mmol/L in the circuit.

questions.stem: During blood donation, a donor becomes pale, sweaty, bradycardic, and hypotensive. What mechanism best explains this?
questions.explanation: Vasovagal is parasympathetic (bradycardia, decreased tone); hypovolemia is sympathetic (tachycardia).

questions.stem: A patient undergoing repeated large-volume plasma exchange with citrate anticoagulation develops a rising serum bicarbonate (38 mEq/L) and a falling potassium (2.8 mEq/L). What is the mechanism?

options.text: Citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate, causing metabolic alkalosis with secondary hypokalemia
Citrate chelation of calcium causing symptomatic hypocalcemia
Volume overload from the replacement fluid
Heparin contamination of the apheresis circuit

questions.explanation: Citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate, causing metabolic alkalosis (HCO₃⁻ >35 mEq/L) with secondary hypokalemia (K⁺ <3.0 mEq/L).

questions.stem: A donor with a precollection platelet count of 140,000/uL wants to undergo plateletpheresis. Is he eligible?

options.text: Only for a double platelet collection
Yes, if the postcollection count stays above 50,000/uL
No - the precollection count must be at least 150,000/uL, and postcollection must stay above 100,000/uL

questions.explanation: Plateletpheresis requires precollection >=150,000/uL and postcollection staying above 100,000/uL.

questions.stem: During apheresis, a donor loses 350 mL of red cells due to a procedural issue. What deferral applies?
questions.explanation: A single RBC loss >=300 mL defers the donor 16 weeks.

questions.stem: A granulocyte product is found to contain 5 mL of red cells. What is required?

options.text: No crossmatch is needed for granulocytes
A serologic crossmatch, required when red cell content exceeds 2 mL

questions.explanation: Granulocyte products with >2 mL RBCs require a serologic crossmatch.

questions.stem: After albumin-replacement TPE, which coagulation factors recover fastest?

options.text: Factor VIII, factor IX, and von Willebrand factor, normalizing in about 4 hours

questions.explanation: After TPE, factor VIII, IX, and vWF normalize in ~4 h; fibrinogen falls to 25% and recovers slowly.

questions.stem: Large-volume leukapheresis is defined as processing how much blood?
questions.explanation: Large-volume leukapheresis processes >5 blood volumes (>15 L).

questions.stem: Which assay is the gold-standard potency test for an HPC product?

options.text: CFU (colony-forming unit) assay, read after 10-14 days of culture

questions.explanation: The CFU assay (10-14 day culture) is the gold-standard potency test; CD34+ flow is the same-day adequacy assay.

questions.stem: A child needs a cardiac valve allograft. What ABO/HLA matching is required?

options.text: Full ABO and HLA matching like a heart transplant
Neither - valve allografts rely on nonviable connective tissue for long-term function

questions.explanation: Cardiac valve allografts need no ABO/HLA matching (nonviable connective tissue), though they induce HLA antibodies.

questions.stem: A potential corneal donor died 4 hours ago. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Enucleate within 6 hours of death, store at 4C, and transplant within 48-72 hours

questions.explanation: Corneas: enucleate within 6 h of death, store at 4C, transplant within 48-72 h; no HLA/ABO matching needed.

questions.stem: An anonymous sperm donor sample is collected today. When may it be released for use?

options.text: After a 180-day quarantine with monthly donor testing
Immediately if nucleic acid testing is negative

questions.explanation: Anonymous sperm donor samples are quarantined 180 days with monthly donor testing before release.

questions.stem: What is the standard cryopreservation protocol for HPC products?

options.text: 10% DMSO with controlled-rate freezing, stored at or below -150C

questions.explanation: Standard HPC cryopreservation: 10% DMSO, controlled-rate freeze, storage at or below -150C.

questions.stem: What G-CSF mobilization regimen is used for a multiple myeloma patient collecting autologous HPCs?

options.text: No mobilization - collect at steady state
5-10 mcg/kg for 4-5 days, giving a 5- to 10-fold HPC increase

questions.explanation: Patients/autologous donors: G-CSF 5-10 mcg/kg for 4-5 days (5-10x HPC increase); 10-16 mcg/kg/day split is the healthy-donor regimen.

questions.stem: What is the target bone marrow harvest for a 70-kg adult recipient?

options.text: 2-3 x 10^8 viable nucleated cells/kg (about 700 mL total), aspirated 3-5 mL per pull

questions.explanation: Bone marrow harvest target: 2-3 x 10^8 viable nucleated cells/kg (~700 mL for 70 kg), 3-5 mL per pull.

questions.stem: A cord blood collection yields 30 mL. What should be done with it?

options.text: Discard it - collections under 40 mL are usually discarded

questions.explanation: Cord blood collections under 40 mL are usually discarded; typical is 40-150 mL.

questions.stem: A healthy donor is choosing between PB-HPC donation (with G-CSF mobilization) and bone marrow harvest for an unrelated recipient. What should she be told about the engraftment and GVHD trade-offs?

options.text: PB-HPCs engraft fastest (neutrophils ~5 days earlier, platelets ~7 days sooner) but cause more chronic GVHD; marrow has more graft failures
Marrow engrafts faster with less GVHD
Cord blood is the fastest-engrafting option

questions.explanation: PB-HPCs engraft fastest (neutrophils ~5 days earlier, platelets ~7 days sooner than marrow) but cause more chronic GVHD.

questions.stem: A donor graft undergoes T-cell depletion before infusion. What is the expected trade-off?

options.text: Less GVHD but increased relapse from loss of the graft-versus-leukemia effect

questions.explanation: T-cell depletion reduces GVHD but increases relapse by removing the graft-versus-leukemia effect.

questions.stem: An HPC-apheresis product is major ABO-incompatible with the recipient. Which statement is true?

options.text: The recipient's red cells must be HLA-matched
HPCs do not express ABO antigens so they engraft, but mature incompatible red cells in the product require reduction or washing

questions.explanation: HPCs lack ABO antigens and engraft across ABO barriers; mature incompatible red cells in the product need reduction/washing.

notes.note: One 2024 review states that ABO antigens are present on hematopoietic stem cells, so the reason given here is uncertain. The practical point stands: ABO mismatch is not a contraindication, and incompatible red cells (major) or plasma (minor) in the product are reduced.

questions.stem: During HPC reinfusion the patient develops chills, nausea, emesis, and dyspnea. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: ABO incompatibility of the progenitor cells
DMSO/volume-related reinfusion toxicity - premedicate with antihistamines and antiemetics

questions.explanation: Reinfusion reactions (chills, nausea, dyspnea) are DMSO/volume-related; premedicate with antihistamines/antiemetics.

questions.stem: Anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy received FDA approval in 2017 for which indications?

options.text: B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

questions.explanation: Anti-CD19 CAR-T cells were FDA-approved in 2017 for B-ALL and DLBCL.

questions.stem: How is acute graft-versus-host disease graded?
questions.explanation: GVHD is graded 1 (mild) to 3-4 (severe), with major morbidity/mortality at grades 3-4.

questions.stem: Which investigational assay measures HPC potency by flow cytometry in 1-2 hours?
questions.explanation: ALDH activity is an investigational 1-2 hour flow-cytometry potency assay; CFU remains the gold standard.

questions.stem: In the ex vivo expansion study, how did double-cord transplant neutrophil engraftment compare with historical single-cord controls?

options.text: Neutrophils engrafted faster but platelet engraftment was delayed (60 vs 49 days)
No difference — median neutrophil engraftment was 24 days in both arms

questions.explanation: Double-cord with expansion: neutrophil engraftment 15 vs 24 days historically (platelets 42 vs 49 days).

questions.stem: Approximately what fraction of normal bone marrow cells are hematopoietic progenitor cells?
questions.explanation: HPCs are about 1% of normal marrow cells (1-2% of marrow leukocytes).

questions.stem: A transplant recipient develops mild graft-versus-host disease. What is the prognostic implication for the underlying malignancy?

options.text: It is associated with lower relapse due to the graft-versus-leukemia effect

questions.explanation: Mild GVHD correlates with lower neoplastic relapse via the graft-versus-leukemia effect.

questions.stem: An HPC product report shows CFU-GM 0.3×10⁵/kg. The transplant physician asks whether the dose is adequate. What is the best response?

options.text: Adequate — CFU-GM does not predict engraftment
Inadequate — the adequacy threshold is CFU-GM 0.5–2.0×10⁵/kg; this product is below it

questions.explanation: HPC engraftment doses per kg: CD34+ 2.5×10⁶, CFU-GM 0.5–2.0×10⁵, MNC 6.0–6.5×10⁸. A CFU-GM dose of 0.3×10⁵/kg falls below the adequacy threshold.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of corneal graft rejection?
questions.explanation: Corneal graft rejection (~10%) is mostly from vascularization of the graft bed, not HLA mismatch.

questions.stem: Sickle cell gene therapy aims for what threshold of corrected red cells?

options.text: At least 30% of red cells with normal beta-hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Sickle cell gene therapy target: >=30% of red cells with normal beta-hemoglobin.

questions.stem: What is the steady-state frequency of CD34+ cells in nonmobilized peripheral blood?
questions.explanation: Steady-state peripheral blood CD34+ frequency is only 0.1-0.2% of leukocytes, hence mobilization.

questions.stem: After chemotherapy-based mobilization, when does circulating HPC content peak and how long is the collection window?

options.text: Peak on day 5 with a 2-week window
Peak about 14-21 days post-therapy with only a 2-3 day collection window

questions.explanation: Chemotherapy mobilization peaks ~14-21 days post-therapy with only a 2-3 day collection window.

questions.stem: Haploidentical transplantation outcomes are improved with which strategy?

options.text: Selective T-cell depletion or posttransplant cyclophosphamide

questions.explanation: Haploidentical transplant outcomes improve with selective T-cell depletion or posttransplant cyclophosphamide.

questions.stem: During bone marrow harvest, the surgeon takes large-volume pulls from a single site to finish faster. What is the consequence?

options.text: Higher stem cell yield per pull
Hemodilution of the marrow with peripheral blood — aspirating 3–5 mL per site from multiple sites gives a richer product

questions.explanation: Larger aspirate volumes dilute marrow with peripheral blood — the standard is 3–5 mL per aspiration from multiple sites to provide at least 2–3×10⁸ nucleated cells/kg.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old develops a 14-mm indurated, erythematous lesion 48 hours after intradermal tuberculin injection. Biopsy shows perivascular macrophages and CD4+ T cells with no antibody or complement deposition. Which hypersensitivity type is this?
questions.explanation: Delayed 48-72 h induration with T-cell/macrophage infiltrate and no antibody is type IV delayed hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: Ten days after receiving horse-derived antivenom for a snakebite, a patient develops fever, arthralgia, and urticaria. Lab work shows circulating immune complexes and low C3/C4. Which hypersensitivity type best explains this illness?
questions.explanation: Serum sickness 7-10 days after foreign protein with immune complexes and complement consumption is classic type III.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry of a patient's lymphocytes shows a population of large granular lymphocytes that are CD3-negative, CD16-positive, and CD56-positive. These cells can lyse virally infected targets without prior sensitization. They are:
questions.explanation: CD3-negative, CD16/CD56-positive large granular lymphocytes are NK cells, killing without prior sensitization via missing-self.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has a markedly elevated TSH on a sandwich immunoassay but normal free T4, no symptoms, and a normal TSH last year. Repeat testing after incubation in a heterophile blocking tube gives a normal TSH. The most likely explanation is:

options.text: Hook effect from an extremely high TSH
Heterophile (human anti-mouse) antibodies bridging the capture and detection antibodies

questions.explanation: Heterophile (human anti-mouse) antibodies bridge sandwich-assay antibodies causing falsely elevated results; blocking-tube resolution confirms it.

notes.note: FDA updated its 2017 biotin warning in 2019; biotin makes sandwich assays falsely low and competitive assays falsely high.

questions.stem: In an Ouchterlony double-diffusion experiment, a technician keeps doubling the antigen concentration and watches the precipitin line first intensify, then dissolve completely. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Excess antibody solubilizes the immune precipitate
The dissolving line proves the antiserum lacks antibody
Maximal precipitation occurs at the zone of equivalence; antigen excess resolubilizes the complex
Prozone effects occur only in agglutination, not precipitation

questions.explanation: Maximal precipitation occurs at the zone of equivalence; antigen excess forms soluble complexes and dissolves the line (prozone).

questions.stem: A laboratory needs to quantify a peptide hormone expected at femtogram-per-milliliter concentrations. Which platform offers the best analytical sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Chemiluminescent EIA (~0.1 pg/mL) tops the sensitivity ladder, roughly 50-fold more sensitive than RIA (~5 pg/mL).

questions.stem: A new point-of-care immunoassay mixes sample with labeled antibody in a single tube with no wash step, giving results in 10 minutes but poor detection at low analyte concentrations. The limited sensitivity is best explained by:

options.text: Competitive formats are always less sensitive than sandwich formats
Heterogeneous assays cannot detect small-molecule analytes
The homogeneous format lacks a separation/wash step to remove background signal
The label decays too quickly to be measured

questions.explanation: Homogeneous assays lack a wash/separation step, so background label limits low-end sensitivity; heterogeneous assays are more sensitive.

questions.stem: A T cell binds peptide-MHC through its T-cell receptor but receives no CD28-B7 costimulation from the antigen-presenting cell. The most likely outcome for this T cell is:

options.text: Partial activation with reduced IL-2 production and proliferation

questions.explanation: TCR signal without CD28-B7 costimulation produces anergy/tolerance, not activation ("two to tango, one to snooze").

questions.stem: Which assay can detect a single interferon-gamma-secreting T cell among 100,000 to 1,000,000 cells and is used clinically to screen for latent tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: ELISPOT detects single cytokine-secreting T cells at 1:10^5-10^6 sensitivity and underlies interferon-gamma release assays for latent TB.

questions.stem: A physician orders lymphocyte blastogenesis and NK-cell cytotoxicity studies on a patient. Which collection tube is acceptable for these functional cellular assays?
questions.explanation: Functional cellular studies require fresh blood in preservative-free sodium heparin or ACD; lithium heparin and EDTA are forbidden.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with relapsing optic neuritis has CSF isoelectric focusing showing oligoclonal bands present in CSF but absent from paired serum, plus several additional bands shared with serum. This pattern indicates:

options.text: Intrathecal IgG synthesis (type 3), supporting multiple sclerosis
Systemic immune activation with passive transfer (type 4)

questions.explanation: Type 3 (CSF-only bands plus extra shared bands) indicates intrathecal IgG synthesis, supporting multiple sclerosis.

questions.stem: Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M-spike comprising 40% of the total protein; total protein is 8.0 g/dL. The M-spike concentration is:
questions.explanation: M-spike = 0.40 x 8.0 g/dL = 3.2 g/dL, exceeding the IgG threshold suspicious for malignancy.

questions.stem: A myeloma patient in complete remission on daratumumab maintenance develops a new faint IgG-kappa band on immunofixation. Marrow shows <5% plasma cells and the serum free light chain ratio is normal. The best interpretation is:

options.text: Therapeutic monoclonal antibody interference mimicking an M-spike

questions.explanation: Daratumumab (IgG1-kappa therapeutic antibody) forges its own M-spike on SPEP/IFE; check the medication list before calling relapse.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old has an involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio of 150, 8% bone marrow plasma cells, and no CRAB features. By current criteria this patient has:
questions.explanation: An involved:uninvolved sFLC ratio >=100 is a SLiM biomarker, but multiple myeloma additionally requires >=10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma; with 8% plasma cells and no CRAB this is MGUS.

questions.stem: A workup for recurrent infections shows CH50 ~0 U/mL and AH50 also ~0. The deficiency most likely involves:
questions.explanation: Both CH50 and AH50 ~0 implicates a component shared by both pathways: C3 or C5-C9.

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent nonpruritic angioedema has a normal C1-inhibitor protein level but markedly reduced C1-inhibitor function. This pattern defines:
questions.explanation: HAE type II = normal C1-inhibitor protein with low function; type I has both low.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old has Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, and pancytopenia. Which test confirms the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 on red cells and granulocytes

questions.explanation: Flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 confirms PNH (acquired PIGA mutation, loss of GPI-anchored regulators); DAT is negative since it is not autoimmune.

questions.stem: Which antibody isotype does NOT activate the classical complement pathway through C1?
questions.explanation: IgG4 does not bind C1; IgM and IgG1/IgG2/IgG3 do activate the classical pathway.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has recurrent bacterial skin infections, delayed umbilical cord separation, poor wound healing, and persistent neutrophilia (WBC 28,000/uL). The underlying defect is in:
questions.explanation: LAD type I = CD18 (beta-2 integrin) defect; neutrophils trapped in blood cause paradoxical neutrophilia while tissues go undefended.

questions.stem: A patient with Crohn disease needs an anti-integrin biologic but has prior JC virus exposure, making progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy a concern. The best choice is:
questions.explanation: Vedolizumab (gut-selective anti-alpha4/beta7) avoids the PML risk carried by systemic natalizumab.

questions.stem: A patient has severe asthma, atopic dermatitis, AND chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Which single biologic targets the shared pathway driving all three conditions?
questions.explanation: Dupilumab blocks IL-4R-alpha, shutting down both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling.

questions.stem: A renal transplant candidate has a panel-reactive antibody (PRA) of 80%. This means:

options.text: She has an 80% chance of finding a compatible donor
The result is invalid without a CDC crossmatch
80% of her HLA antigens are already matched
She reacts against 80% of the donor panel, so finding a compatible donor will be difficult

questions.explanation: PRA is the percent of the donor panel the patient reacts against; 80% PRA means most donors are incompatible.

questions.stem: The gene encoding beta-2 microglobulin, the invariant light chain of HLA class I molecules, is located on:
questions.explanation: Beta-2 microglobulin is encoded on chromosome 15, not in the MHC on 6p21.

questions.stem: For hematopoietic progenitor cell transplantation, a "10 of 10" match refers to high-resolution allele-level matching at:
questions.explanation: HCT "10 of 10" = high-resolution matching at HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DQB1 (five loci x two chromosomes).

questions.stem: A patient receives a bone marrow transplant from an HLA-identical sibling but develops graft-versus-host disease. The most likely explanation is:
questions.explanation: Minor histocompatibility antigens (e.g., HA-1) are encoded outside the MHC and can cause GVHD even between HLA-identical siblings.

questions.stem: Before starting allopurinol, HLA-B*58:01 testing is recommended for:

options.text: Only patients with a prior gout flare
High-risk populations (e.g., Han Chinese, Thai, Korean descent, African Americans)

questions.explanation: HLA-B*58:01 testing before allopurinol is recommended for high-risk groups (Han Chinese, Thai, Korean descent, African Americans), not universally.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with chronic low back pain tests positive for HLA-B27. The correct counseling is:

options.text: He will almost certainly develop ankylosing spondylitis
B27 supports but never diagnoses AS: ~90% of Caucasian AS patients carry it, yet only ~2% of carriers develop disease

questions.explanation: ~90% of Caucasian AS patients carry B27 but only ~2% of carriers develop AS; it is a rule-out test, not a diagnosis.

questions.stem: The most common complement protein deficiency in Caucasians is:
questions.explanation: C2 deficiency (1 in 10,000 Caucasians) is the most common complement deficiency in that population.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy has recurrent otitis media and pneumonia, absent tonsils and palpable lymph nodes, and no circulating mature B cells. The most appropriate management is:

options.text: Administer MMR and varicella vaccines on schedule
Begin IVIG replacement and withhold all live vaccines

questions.explanation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (no mature B cells, absent lymphoid tissue) is managed with IVIG; live vaccines are contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has serum IgA <7 mg/dL with normal IgG and IgM and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. If she requires transfusion, she must receive:

options.text: Standard packed red cells; no special handling is needed
IgA-deficient blood products, because anti-IgA antibodies can trigger fatal anaphylaxis

questions.explanation: Selective IgA deficiency (<7 mg/dL after age 4) can produce anti-IgA antibodies causing fatal anaphylaxis to IgA-containing products.

questions.stem: An infant being evaluated for suspected severe combined immunodeficiency is due for routine immunizations. The correct guidance is:

options.text: Withhold all vaccines from the entire household
Withhold live vaccines from the infant, but household contacts should stay current on age-appropriate vaccines including live MMR and varicella
Give the infant live vaccines on schedule to build immunity

questions.explanation: No live vaccines for the SCID infant, but household contacts should stay current including live MMR/varicella per ACIP.

questions.stem: A boy has normal-to-elevated IgM with markedly decreased IgG, IgA, and IgE plus recurrent sinopulmonary infections. The underlying defect is in:
questions.explanation: Normal-to-high IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE = class-switch failure (CD40L/CD40 pathway), i.e., hyper-IgM syndrome.

questions.stem: Which autoantibody is most specific for the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation: Anti-Sm is virtually SLE-specific (does not track activity); anti-dsDNA tracks activity and nephritis.

questions.stem: A patient treated with procainamide for 8 months develops arthralgia, pleuritis, and a positive ANA. Anti-dsDNA is negative and antihistone antibodies are positive. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Procainamide exposure with ANA limited to antihistone and absent anti-dsDNA is drug-induced lupus, not idiopathic SLE.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has symmetric small-joint polyarthritis. Which serologic test has the highest specificity for rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: Anti-CCP (2nd gen) has 95-98% specificity for RA versus ~72% for rheumatoid factor.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has pulmonary infiltrates, hematuria with red-cell casts, and rapidly rising creatinine. Per the 2017 ANCA consensus, the best initial screening test for suspected ANCA-associated vasculitis is:
questions.explanation: The 2017 ANCA consensus recommends screening suspected AAV with PR3- and MPO-ANCA antigen-specific immunoassays first, not IIF.

questions.stem: A patient taking hydralazine develops pulmonary-renal syndrome and tests positive for BOTH MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA. Dual positivity most strongly suggests:
questions.explanation: Dual MPO-ANCA plus PR3-ANCA positivity is rare except in drug-induced ANCA vasculitis (hydralazine, PTU, minocycline, levamisole-cocaine).

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has hemoptysis, glomerulonephritis, and linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence. Besides anti-GBM antibody testing, which additional test is recommended?

options.text: C-ANCA only if PR3 is positive

questions.explanation: About one-third of anti-GBM patients are also ANCA-positive, so ANCA testing is always indicated alongside anti-GBM testing.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old has tense bullae on erythematous skin with a negative Nikolsky sign. Biopsy shows a subepidermal blister, and direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Subepidermal blister with negative Nikolsky and linear IgG/C3 on DIF = bullous pemphigoid; pemphigus splits intraepidermally with positive Nikolsky.

questions.stem: A patient with primary membranous nephropathy has falling anti-PLA2R titers but persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria. The best interpretation is:

options.text: Treatment has failed and therapy must be switched
The ELISA result is spurious and should be ignored
Immunologic remission precedes renal remission; proteinuria resolves after the antibody disappears
Progression to end-stage renal disease is now certain

questions.explanation: Anti-PLA2R disappears before proteinuria resolves (immunologic before renal remission); falling titers with persistent proteinuria is expected, not treatment failure.

questions.stem: A physician orders insulin autoantibodies (IAA) on a patient who started insulin therapy 6 weeks ago. The laboratory should:

options.text: Cancel the test: after more than 14 days of insulin therapy, the assay cannot distinguish true autoantibodies from antibodies against injected insulin
Perform the test; IAA remains interpretable for up to 1 year on insulin
Dilute the sample to remove insulin interference

questions.explanation: After >14 days of insulin therapy, IAA cannot distinguish true autoantibodies from antibodies against injected insulin; the order should be canceled.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man in Tennessee develops urticaria and hypotension 4 hours after eating steak. He reports multiple recent tick bites. The most likely mechanism is:

options.text: Type IV hypersensitivity to beef protein

questions.explanation: Delayed (3-6 h) red-meat anaphylaxis after tick bites in the southeastern US is alpha-gal (IgE to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose) syndrome.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has detectable peanut-specific IgE but eats peanuts regularly without symptoms. Component testing shows reactivity to Ara h 8 but not Ara h 2. The best interpretation is:

options.text: High risk of anaphylaxis; prescribe epinephrine and strict avoidance
A peanut allergy that has been outgrown
PR10/profilin cross-reactivity; sensitization without clinical peanut allergy

questions.explanation: Ara h 8 (PR10) reactivity without Ara h 2 indicates pollen cross-reactivity with sensitization but no clinical peanut allergy.

questions.stem: A patient taking daily antihistamines needs testing for suspected allergic rhinitis. The best approach is:

options.text: Stop the antihistamine and perform skin prick testing immediately
Order serum allergen-specific IgE, which antihistamines do not affect
Perform intradermal testing while the patient remains on antihistamines

questions.explanation: Antihistamines suppress skin tests but do not affect in vitro specific-IgE testing.

questions.stem: A positive skin prick test is defined as a mean wheal diameter of:
questions.explanation: A positive skin prick test is >=3 mm mean wheal (intradermal 1+ = 5-10 mm).

questions.stem: A blood culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. The cefoxitin screen is resistant and PCR detects mecA. According to current reporting rules, how should the laboratory report β-lactam susceptibility for this isolate?

options.text: Report all β-lactams as susceptible if the MIC tests susceptible
Report all β-lactams as resistant except ceftaroline
Report all β-lactams as resistant with no exceptions
Report only oxacillin and cefoxitin as resistant

questions.explanation: mecA/mecC encodes PBP2a, so all β-lactams are reported resistant except the anti-MRSA cephalosporin ceftaroline.

questions.stem: A coagulase-negative staphylococcus from two blood culture sets is identified as Staphylococcus lugdunensis. The oxacillin MIC is 1 μg/mL. How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Use coagulase-negative staphylococcal breakpoints; report oxacillin susceptible
Use S. aureus breakpoints; report oxacillin susceptible only if the cefoxitin screen is also susceptible
Report as resistant regardless of MIC because all CoNS are methicillin-resistant
Repeat with a 24-hour incubation before any interpretation

questions.explanation: S. lugdunensis behaves clinically like S. aureus, so CLSI requires S. aureus breakpoints for its oxacillin/cefoxitin results.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old neonate develops meningitis. The mother reports a flu-like illness one week before delivery after eating unpasteurized soft cheese. CSF Gram stain shows short gram-positive rods with tumbling motility at room temperature. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Listeria shows tumbling motility at room temperature, grows at 4°C, and causes neonatal meningitis after maternal ingestion of contaminated dairy.

questions.stem: Four college students develop profuse vomiting 2 to 4 hours after eating reheated fried rice from a buffet. Which organism and toxin type best explain this outbreak?

options.text: Bacillus cereus, preformed heat-stable emetic toxin

questions.explanation: Fried rice with 1- to 6-hour onset is the emetic form of B. cereus (preformed heat-stable toxin); S. aureus shares the window but is linked to meats and dairy.

questions.stem: An oxidase-positive, gram-negative diplococcus is isolated from CSF. In CTA carbohydrate testing it produces acid from glucose and maltose but not lactose or sucrose. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: N. meningitidis ferments glucose plus maltose, while N. gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only.

questions.stem: An Enterobacter cloacae bloodstream isolate tests susceptible to ceftriaxone by MIC, but the patient has received ceftriaxone for 5 days and remains bacteremic. Which reporting approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Report ceftriaxone as susceptible and continue therapy
Treat as resistant to extended-spectrum cephalosporins except cefepime because of inducible AmpC
Report all cephalosporins as susceptible since the MIC is low
Repeat the MIC using a higher inoculum before reporting

questions.explanation: SPACE organisms carry inducible AmpC that can derepress during therapy, so treat as resistant to extended-spectrum cephalosporins except cefepime.

questions.stem: A child presents with a gray, adherent pseudomembrane over the tonsils. A swab taken from beneath the membrane grows club-shaped gram-positive rods in "Chinese-letter" arrangements on Tinsdale agar as gray-black colonies. Which test confirms toxin production?
questions.explanation: The Elek immunodiffusion test confirms diphtheria toxin production and is performed at a reference laboratory.

questions.stem: A renal transplant recipient develops a pulmonary nodule and a ring-enhancing brain lesion. Bronchial washings show beaded, branching gram-positive rods that are partially acid-fast on modified Kinyoun stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Partially acid-fast branching rods with pulmonary plus brain disease in a cellular-immune-deficient host is Nocardia, not TB.

questions.stem: A patient with poor dentition develops subacute endocarditis with low-grade fever and weight loss. Blood cultures grow small gram-negative coccobacilli that require 5 to 10 percent CO2 and fail to grow on MacConkey agar. Which group is most likely?
questions.explanation: CO2-requiring coccobacilli that fail to grow on MacConkey in subacute endocarditis from oral flora are HACEK organisms.

questions.stem: An Enterococcus faecium bloodstream isolate is resistant to vancomycin (MIC >32 μg/mL) and resistant to teicoplanin. Which resistance gene is most likely?
questions.explanation: vanA confers high-level vancomycin plus teicoplanin resistance; vanB affects vancomycin only and vanC is intrinsic low-level.

questions.stem: An Escherichia coli urine isolate is resistant to ceftriaxone and cefoxitin. Adding clavulanic acid does not restore ceftriaxone susceptibility. What is the most likely resistance mechanism?
questions.explanation: AmpC resists cefoxitin and is not inhibited by clavulanic acid, whereas ESBLs are clavulanate-inhibited and usually cefoxitin-susceptible.

questions.stem: A carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate shows high-level temocillin resistance. Molecular testing is pending. Which β-lactamase inhibitor is most likely to restore activity of a partner β-lactam against this isolate?
questions.explanation: High-level temocillin resistance is the phenotypic screening marker for OXA-48, which is inhibited by avibactam.

questions.stem: A patient with Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis has an isolate susceptible to ampicillin. The high-level gentamicin screen (500 μg/mL) is resistant. What is the therapeutic implication?

options.text: Report gentamicin as susceptible by routine MIC and add it to ampicillin for synergy
Gentamicin cannot provide synergy; do not add it for endocarditis therapy
Switch to streptomycin for synergy instead
Repeat the screen at 1000 μg/mL before deciding

questions.explanation: High-level aminoglycoside resistance abolishes the bactericidal synergy needed for enterococcal endocarditis therapy.

questions.stem: A Staphylococcus aureus blood isolate tests penicillin-susceptible by broth microdilution. Why does CLSI recommend also performing a nitrocefin test on this isolate?

options.text: Dilution methods can miss β-lactamase production in staphylococci
Nitrocefin detects the mecA gene directly
The MIC must be confirmed because the inoculum was too light

questions.explanation: Dilution methods can miss β-lactamase production in staphylococci, so CLSI pairs the MIC with nitrocefin for blood/CSF isolates.

questions.stem: A laboratory verifies a new automated AST system against broth microdilution and finds 88 percent essential agreement within one doubling dilution, with no very major errors. What is the correct conclusion?
