options.text: The system is verified because there were no very major errors
The system is verified because agreement exceeds 85 percent
The system fails verification because essential agreement must be at least 90 percent
The system passes if categorical agreement is above 90 percent

questions.explanation: CLSI M52 requires at least 90% essential agreement within one doubling dilution; 88% fails verification.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin is colonized with Streptococcus agalactiae. The isolate is erythromycin-resistant and clindamycin-susceptible by disk diffusion. What must the laboratory do before reporting clindamycin as susceptible?

options.text: Repeat disk diffusion with disks placed 12 mm apart for confirmation
Perform a nitrocefin test for β-lactamase
Perform a D-zone test to rule out inducible clindamycin resistance

questions.explanation: A D-zone test must rule out inducible clindamycin resistance before clindamycin can be reported susceptible.

questions.stem: A hospital's rapid-AST program shortens time to effective antibiotics in septic shock by 3 hours on average. Using the Kumar 2006 estimate, what absolute survival benefit does this predict?
questions.explanation: Survival in septic shock falls about 7.6% for every hour effective antibiotics are delayed (Kumar 2006).

questions.stem: A 13-mm zone of inhibition is measured around a cefepime disk for a Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate. Which statement about interpreting this result is correct?

options.text: A 13-mm zone corresponds to the same MIC for cefepime against any organism
The zone must be interpreted with species-specific breakpoints because the same zone size means different MICs for different drug-organism pairs
Zone diameter increases as the MIC increases
The MIC can be read directly from the zone ruler without breakpoint tables

questions.explanation: Zone diameter is inversely correlated with MIC, and the same millimeter reading means different things for different drug-organism pairs.

questions.stem: A health care worker who is HIV-positive and a close contact of an active TB case has a Mantoux test showing 6 mm of induration at 48 hours. How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Positive; the cutoff is 5 mm or more for HIV-infected persons and close contacts
Negative; the cutoff for all adults is 15 mm
Indeterminate; repeat the TST in one week
Positive only if an IGRA is also positive

questions.explanation: The TST cutoff is 5 mm for HIV-infected persons and close contacts, 10 mm for other risk factors, and 15 mm for everyone else.

questions.stem: A CSF specimen is submitted for AFB smear and mycobacterial culture. Which processing step is correct?

options.text: Decontaminate with NALC-2 percent NaOH before culture
Inoculate directly to culture without decontamination
Hold the specimen at 4°C for 24 hours before processing
Concentrate by centrifugation at 3,000 to 3,600 g for 15 minutes, then decontaminate

questions.explanation: Sterile-site specimens such as CSF go directly to culture; NALC-NaOH decontamination would kill the mycobacteria being sought.

questions.stem: A sputum Xpert MTB/RIF reads "MTB detected; rifampin resistance detected" in under 2 hours. Which conventional workflow step does this result compress from weeks to hours?
questions.explanation: Xpert probes the 81-base-pair rpoB fragment to detect rifampin resistance in under 2 hours.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old welder with COPD develops chronic cavitary upper-lobe pulmonary disease. Culture grows a slow-growing mycobacterium whose colonies develop yellow pigment only after exposure to light. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Pigment produced only after light exposure defines a photochromogen; M. kansasii causes cavitary disease in older men with dust exposure.

questions.stem: A fisherman develops a papulonodular lesion on his hand three weeks after cleaning a home aquarium. A skin biopsy is submitted for mycobacterial culture. What incubation condition is essential in addition to 37°C?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous specimens need a second set at 30°C because M. marinum grows optimally at 30-33°C.

questions.stem: An isolate identified as Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex is resistant to pyrazinamide but susceptible to isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. It is niacin- and nitrate-negative. Which member of the complex is most likely?
questions.explanation: M. bovis is intrinsically pyrazinamide-resistant and niacin/nitrate-negative, unlike M. tuberculosis.

questions.stem: An AIDS patient with a CD4 count of 35 cells/μL is receiving azithromycin for MAC prophylaxis and starts antiretroviral therapy. When can prophylaxis be discontinued?

options.text: When the CD4 count remains above 100/μL for at least 3 months on ART
When the CD4 count first exceeds 50/μL
After 6 months of prophylaxis regardless of CD4 count
Only after a negative mycobacterial blood culture

questions.explanation: Disseminated MAC prophylaxis stops once the CD4 count stays above 100/μL for at least 3 months on ART.

questions.stem: By the agar proportion method, 3 percent of a Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolate grows at the critical concentration of isoniazid. How should this result be reported?

options.text: Susceptible, because 97 percent of the population is inhibited
Intermediate, because resistance requires more than 10 percent growth
Resistant, because growth of more than 1 percent at the critical concentration defines resistance

questions.explanation: The agar proportion 1% rule: more than 1% growth at the critical drug concentration means the isolate is resistant.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a single well-circumscribed, anesthetic hypopigmented macule and an enlarged greater auricular nerve. Biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas with very few acid-fast bacilli. Which form of leprosy is this?

options.text: Indeterminate leprosy with erythema nodosum leprosum

questions.explanation: Few anesthetic lesions, enlarged nerves, granulomas, and scarce bacilli define tuberculoid (paucibacillary) leprosy.

questions.stem: A yeast isolate is incubated in serum at 35°C for 3 hours. Microscopy shows filamentous extensions with a distinct constriction at the junction with the mother cell. How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Not a true germ tube; the extensions are pseudohyphae
Positive germ tube; identify as Candida glabrata
Positive germ tube; identify as Candida albicans

questions.explanation: A true germ tube has parallel walls with no constriction at the mother-cell junction; constricted forms are pseudohyphae.

questions.stem: A lung biopsy shows 8–15 μm yeasts with broad-based budding and thick double-contoured walls. Which additional finding would be INCONSISTENT with Blastomyces dermatitidis?

options.text: Narrow-based budding 3–5 μm yeasts inside macrophages

questions.explanation: Large yeast with broad-based buds and a thick double-contoured wall is Blastomyces; Histoplasma is 3-5 μm with narrow-based buds.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient in ketoacidosis develops necrotic nasal turbinates. Biopsy shows broad, aseptate, ribbonlike hyphae with wide-angle branching invading blood vessels. How should the tissue be handled for culture?

options.text: Homogenize the tissue to release the organisms
Mince or tease the tissue; do not homogenize
Freeze the tissue before plating to preserve hyphae

questions.explanation: Mucormycete hyphae are fragile and aseptate, so mince or tease tissue for culture rather than homogenizing it.

questions.stem: A neutropenic leukemia patient receiving piperacillin-tazobactam has a positive serum galactomannan. Chest CT shows no nodules or halo sign. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Definite invasive aspergillosis; start antifungal therapy immediately
The result may be a false positive caused by piperacillin-tazobactam
The result rules out Pneumocystis pneumonia

questions.explanation: Piperacillin-tazobactam causes false-positive galactomannan results, a limitation the FDA requires be disclosed.

questions.stem: A candidemia isolate forms pink colonies on CHROMagar Candida and is resistant to fluconazole. Which species is most likely, and what is the therapeutic implication?

options.text: Candida albicans; switch to a higher fluconazole dose
Candida glabrata; fluconazole resistance is always acquired
Candida tropicalis; metallic blue colonies were misread
Candida krusei; it is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole

questions.explanation: Pink colonies on CHROMagar plus fluconazole resistance identify C. krusei, which is intrinsically fluconazole-resistant.

questions.stem: An AIDS patient with cryptococcal meningitis has a negative serum (1→3)-β-D-glucan. Which statement explains this result?

options.text: The assay was performed incorrectly; glucan is positive in all fungal infections
Cryptococcus species are among the few pathogenic fungi not detected by the glucan assay
A negative glucan rules out cryptococcosis
The patient must have mucormycosis instead

questions.explanation: The (1→3)-β-D-glucan assay misses Cryptococcus species and Mucorales even though it detects most other pathogenic fungi.

questions.stem: A laboratory receives a rapidly growing mold culture from a patient with valley fever. The technologist notes barrel-shaped arthroconidia. What biosafety practice is required?

options.text: BSL-2 practices; the tissue phase is not infectious
BSL-3 practices; Coccidioides mold cultures are risk group 3

questions.explanation: Coccidioides mold cultures are RG3 agents requiring BSL-3 containment with screw-capped tubes.

questions.stem: A patient has persistent candidemia with negative blood cultures after 5 days of therapy. The physician asks about the T2 Candida assay. Which statement about this test is correct?

options.text: It requires at least 10,000 CFU/mL of blood to detect Candida
It replaces the need for antifungal susceptibility testing
It detects 1 to 3 CFU/mL of whole blood with 99.4 percent specificity, far faster than blood cultures
It is FDA-cleared for mold detection from blood

questions.explanation: T2 Candida detects 1-3 CFU/mL from whole blood in about 4 hours versus more than 120 hours for blood cultures.

questions.stem: A neutropenic patient with suspected invasive aspergillosis has a positive serum galactomannan and a positive (1→3)-β-D-glucan. Which statement best compares the two assays?

options.text: Both assays are positive in mucormycosis
Galactomannan is relatively Aspergillus-specific, while β-D-glucan is a broad panfungal marker that also detects Pneumocystis
β-D-glucan is more specific for Aspergillus than galactomannan
A negative galactomannan invalidates a positive β-D-glucan

questions.explanation: β-D-glucan is positive in Pneumocystis with high negative predictive value for PCP, while it misses Cryptococcus and Mucorales.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient with primary syphilis reports a history of penicillin anaphylaxis. What is the recommended management?

options.text: Desensitize and treat with benzathine penicillin G — no proven alternative exists in pregnancy

questions.explanation: Penicillin is the only documented effective syphilis therapy in pregnancy — azithromycin fails against macrolide-resistant T. pallidum (23S rRNA mutations) and doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy. Desensitize, then treat with benzathine penicillin G.

questions.stem: A laboratory using the reverse syphilis algorithm reports a positive treponemal chemiluminescence screen with a nonreactive reflex RPR. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a second, different treponemal test such as TPPA to arbitrate the discordance
Report as a biological false positive and take no further action
Report as active syphilis and recommend treatment
Repeat the RPR using a different manufacturer's kit

questions.explanation: Discordant reverse-algorithm results are arbitrated with a second treponemal test, preferably TPPA.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive serum treponemal test, a positive CSF VDRL, and CSF pleocytosis. Which treatment is indicated?

options.text: Single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G
High-dose intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days

questions.explanation: Benzathine penicillin G does not reach treponemicidal CSF levels, so neurosyphilis requires 10-14 days of high-dose IV aqueous penicillin G.

questions.stem: A patient treated for secondary syphilis had a pretreatment RPR titer of 1:64 at Clinic A. Six months later, Clinic B reports a VDRL titer of 1:16. How should treatment response be assessed?

options.text: Response cannot be assessed; follow-up must use the same nontreponemal method
The patient has failed treatment because the titer is still reactive
The patient has been reinfected and needs retreatment
The fourfold drop from 1:64 to 1:16 confirms an adequate response

questions.explanation: RPR and VDRL titers are not interchangeable, so follow-up must use the same nontreponemal method.

questions.stem: A hiker presents with a 6-cm expanding erythematous lesion with central clearing that appeared one week after removing an Ixodes tick. Lyme serology is negative. What is the best next step?

options.text: Reassure the patient; negative serology rules out Lyme disease
Order a Lyme PCR on blood to confirm the diagnosis
Treat empirically with doxycycline; serology is only 40 to 60 percent sensitive in early disease
Wait 4 weeks and repeat the two-tier serology before treating

questions.explanation: Erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis, and standard two-tier Lyme serology is only 40-60% sensitive in early disease.

questions.stem: A patient with 6 weeks of migratory arthralgias after a treated tick bite has a positive Lyme IgM immunoblot but a negative IgG immunoblot. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Likely false-positive IgM; IgM should not be relied upon alone beyond 4 weeks of symptoms
Early Lyme disease that has not yet seroconverted
Confirmed late Lyme disease; the IgM blot is diagnostic
Reinfection with a different Borrelia strain

questions.explanation: Most patients develop IgG within 4 weeks, so an isolated IgM immunoblot late in illness is usually a false positive.

questions.stem: Six hours after receiving benzathine penicillin G for secondary syphilis, a patient develops fever, rigors, and hypotension. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Treatment failure from macrolide-resistant T. pallidum

questions.explanation: Fever, rigors, and hypotension within hours of starting antibiotics for syphilis is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, not an allergy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old camper from the western United States presents with his third episode of high fever, shaking chills, and myalgias, each lasting about 3 days and separated by a week of feeling well. The physician suspects tick-borne relapsing fever. Which laboratory approach is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Serologic testing for GlpQ antibodies during the afebrile interval
Darkfield microscopy of peripheral blood collected during a febrile episode
Weil-Felix agglutination using Proteus OX antigens
Blood culture on chocolate agar incubated for 7 days

questions.explanation: Spirochetemia peaks during febrile episodes, so relapsing-fever Borrelia are seen by darkfield or stained smear only then.

questions.stem: A reference laboratory reports a Treponema pallidum isolate with 23S rRNA gene mutations. What is the clinical implication of this finding?

options.text: Resistance to benzathine penicillin G, requiring an alternative regimen
Resistance to macrolides such as azithromycin, which should not be used for treatment
Resistance to doxycycline, eliminating the standard penicillin-allergy option
Resistance to ceftriaxone, eliminating the preferred neurosyphilis alternative

questions.explanation: T. pallidum remains uniformly penicillin-susceptible, but 23S rRNA mutations make macrolide resistance rampant, so azithromycin is not a treatment option.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man who has sex with men presents with a healed painless genital ulcer followed two weeks later by tender inguinal buboes with a "groove sign." Rectal NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. How does management of this infection differ from non-LGV chlamydial infection?

options.text: It is caused by genotypes L1-L3 and requires a 3-week course of doxycycline
It requires a single 1-g dose of azithromycin, identical to non-LGV infection
It resolves without antibiotics once the buboes drain
It is treated with benzathine penicillin G because of lymphatic invasion

questions.explanation: LGV is caused by invasive C. trachomatis genotypes L1-L3 and requires 3 weeks of doxycycline, far longer than non-LGV regimens.

questions.stem: An electron micrograph shows 0.3-μm dense extracellular chlamydial forms and larger intracellular forms. Which statement is INCORRECT?

options.text: The small dense forms are the infectious elementary bodies
The larger forms are reticulate bodies that replicate intracellularly
The infectious extracellular form measures 0.6–1.0 μm
Reticulate bodies reorganize into elementary bodies before release

questions.explanation: The elementary body is the small (0.2-0.4 μm) infectious extracellular form; it transforms one-way into the larger replicating reticulate body.

questions.stem: A college student with a 2-week dry cough and low-grade fever has a cold agglutinin titer of 1:64. Which test is the optimal confirmatory test for the suspected pathogen?

options.text: Paired cold agglutinin titers 2 weeks apart
Culture on SP4 medium for 3 weeks

questions.explanation: Cold agglutinins (≥1:32) mark severe M. pneumoniae disease but are nonspecific, so NAAT on a nasopharyngeal swab is the optimal test.

questions.stem: Ureaplasma urealyticum is isolated from the respiratory secretions of a premature neonate. Which antibiotic is expected to be ineffective against this isolate?
questions.explanation: Ureaplasma is intrinsically resistant to clindamycin, while M. hominis is the one resistant to macrolides.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has persistent urethral discharge 3 weeks after completing azithromycin for nongonococcal urethritis. NAAT confirms Mycoplasma genitalium. Macrolide resistance in this species reaches 42-51% in the United States. What is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat azithromycin 1 g as a single dose
Treat with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days alone
Treat with moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7-10 days
Treat with benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly

questions.explanation: Azithromycin failure in M. genitalium signals 23S rRNA-mediated macrolide resistance; salvage therapy is moxifloxacin 400 mg for 7-10 days.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old in a trachoma-endemic region has chronic follicular conjunctivitis with repeated Chlamydia trachomatis infections over several years. What is the feared long-term outcome if reinfection continues?

options.text: Corneal blindness within one year of the first infection
Corneal opacification and blindness from entropion and trichiasis after 10-40 years of repeated infections
Irreversible entropion and trichiasis after a single treated infection

questions.explanation: Trachoma causes blindness only after 10-40 years of repeated infections drive entropion, trichiasis, and corneal scarring.

questions.stem: An endocervical swab collected on a wooden-shafted calcium alginate swab is submitted for chlamydial cell culture and returns negative, but the patient remains symptomatic and a repeat NAAT is positive. What most likely explains the false-negative culture?

options.text: Calcium alginate and wooden shafts are toxic to chlamydiae; a Dacron swab with a plastic shaft should have been used
The specimen was transported too quickly to the laboratory
The culture was incubated at the wrong temperature
Chlamydiae cannot be grown in cell culture

questions.explanation: Calcium alginate swabs and wooden shafts are toxic to chlamydiae; use Dacron or rayon swabs with plastic or wire shafts.

questions.stem: A reference lab is validating a culture-based chlamydial species panel. Which result is INCONSISTENT with Chlamydia trachomatis?
questions.explanation: Only C. trachomatis produces glycogen-positive (iodine-staining) inclusions; C. pneumoniae and C. psittaci do not.

questions.stem: A traveler returns from rural Southeast Asia with fever, headache, and a painless necrotic eschar at the site of a mite bite. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate therapy?

options.text: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) from chigger exposure; doxycycline

questions.explanation: A necrotic eschar at a chigger (mite) bite after travel in Southeast Asia is classic scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) — treated with doxycycline like other rickettsial infections. (Trap: cutaneous anthrax also eschars, but without the chigger exposure and travel pattern.)

questions.stem: A patient with suspected human monocytic ehrlichiosis was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and has clinically worsened over 48 hours. What best explains this course?

options.text: Sulfonamides cause a Jarisch-Herxheimer-like reaction in ehrlichiosis
Ehrlichia is intrinsically resistant to all folate-pathway inhibitors
The dose of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was too low
Sulfonamides are contraindicated in rickettsial infections and can worsen the disease

questions.explanation: Sulfonamides worsen rickettsial disease, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is actively harmful in suspected ehrlichiosis.

questions.stem: A resident orders a Weil-Felix test to evaluate a patient with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever. What is the best response from the laboratory?

options.text: Perform the test; it is the gold standard for rickettsial diagnosis
Do not perform the test; it is obsolete, insensitive, and nonspecific — use IFA and treat empirically with doxycycline
The test is useful for distinguishing typhus from spotted fever groups
Perform the test only if the IFA is unavailable

questions.explanation: The Weil-Felix test is obsolete, insensitive, and nonspecific; diagnosis rests on IFA and treatment cannot wait for it.

questions.stem: A febrile patient with a recent tick bite has a peripheral blood smear showing morulae within neutrophils. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Morulae in neutrophils point to Anaplasma phagocytophilum, while Ehrlichia species target monocytes.

questions.stem: A goat farmer develops an acute febrile illness with headache and atypical pneumonia; serology later confirms acute Q fever. How did he most likely acquire the infection?

options.text: By inhaling aerosols from infected livestock, especially around parturient animals
Through the bite of an infected Ixodes tick
Through the bite of an infected human body louse

questions.explanation: C. burnetii spreads by inhalation of aerosols from infected livestock such as goats and sheep, not by tick bite.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man who lived in a refugee camp 40 years ago now presents with fever, headache, and a truncal rash resembling typhus. No lice are found and he has had no recent travel. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Primary epidemic typhus from a new louse infestation
Brill-Zinsser disease, a recrudescence of latent Rickettsia prowazekii infection

questions.explanation: Brill-Zinsser disease is recrudescence of latent R. prowazekii years after epidemic typhus and can seed new outbreaks.

questions.stem: A healthy 15-year-old presents with a small papule at a kitten scratch site and a tender, enlarged axillary lymph node of 2 weeks' duration. He is afebrile and otherwise well. What is the best management?

options.text: Start doxycycline plus rifampin for disseminated Bartonella infection
Excise the lymph node for diagnosis
Reassure and observe; typical cat scratch disease is self-limited and needs no antibiotics

questions.explanation: In immunocompetent hosts, about 80% of cat scratch disease is self-limited regional lymphadenopathy requiring no antibiotics.

questions.stem: A patient with culture-negative endocarditis has a Bartonella henselae IFA IgG titer of 1:2048. How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Nonspecific; only a fourfold rise in Coxiella titers is diagnostic
A probable false positive; Bartonella does not cause endocarditis
Indicative of acute Q fever rather than Bartonella infection
Consistent with Bartonella endocarditis; titers of 1:800 or higher carry a 95% positive predictive value

questions.explanation: Bartonella titers of 1:800 or higher carry a 95% positive predictive value for Bartonella endocarditis.

questions.stem: A college student with 3 weeks of fatigue and atypical lymphocytosis has EBV serology: VCA IgM negative, VCA IgG positive, EBNA-1 IgG positive. What does this indicate?

options.text: Past EBV infection with immunity — not the cause of current symptoms; consider CMV or toxoplasmosis

questions.explanation: VCA IgM negative with VCA IgG and EBNA-1 IgG positive marks past EBV infection with immunity; EBNA-1 IgG appears 6-12 weeks post-infection and persists for life.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with sore throat, fatigue, and cervical lymphadenopathy has a negative heterophile (Monospot) test. What is the best next step?

options.text: Rule out infectious mononucleosis; the Monospot is definitive
Order EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM); heterophile testing is not recommended in children under 12
Repeat the Monospot in 2 weeks before further testing
Order EBV DNA NAAT on whole blood to diagnose IM

questions.explanation: Heterophile testing is not recommended in children under 12, so EBV-specific serology is required; EBV DNA NAAT is not for IM diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient has positive HBsAg, negative anti-HBs, and positive IgM anti-HBc. What is the interpretation?
questions.explanation: HBsAg positivity with IgM anti-HBc marks acute HBV infection; anti-HBs is the last marker to appear in recovery. (Contrast the core window: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, IgM anti-HBc positive — the only stage lacking both.)

questions.stem: Twelve weeks after finishing direct-acting antivirals, a patient has undetectable HCV RNA, persistently reactive anti-HCV, and normal ALT. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Treatment failure; anti-HCV is still reactive
Reinfection; recheck RNA in 12 more weeks
Cure (SVR12); anti-HCV remains positive for life and does not indicate active infection

questions.explanation: HCV cure is defined as SVR: undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after completing direct-acting antiviral therapy.

questions.stem: A woman who is hepatitis B surface antigen-positive delivers a healthy term infant. What is the recommended prophylaxis for the newborn?

options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours of birth
HBIG within 12 hours; defer the hepatitis B vaccine series until 2 months of age
Hepatitis B vaccine alone within 7 days

questions.explanation: Perinatal HBV prevention requires both hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth.

questions.stem: Genotypic testing of CMV from a patient failing ganciclovir reports a UL56 mutation with wild-type UL97. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The UL56 mutation explains ganciclovir failure
Wild-type UL97 rules out all CMV drug resistance
UL56 causes foscarnet cross-resistance; switch to cidofovir
UL56 confers letermovir resistance, not ganciclovir resistance; look for UL97 mutations to explain ganciclovir failure

questions.explanation: UL97 kinase mutation is the most common first mutation conferring ganciclovir resistance in CMV.

questions.stem: A patient on antiretroviral therapy has a confirmed HIV viral load of 350 copies/mL, and the physician requests genotypic resistance testing. What is the best response?

options.text: Order a proviral DNA genotype instead, which works at any viral load
Perform genotyping immediately; any detectable viremia is sufficient
Switch the antiretroviral regimen without resistance testing
Genotyping cannot be reliably performed below 500-1000 copies/mL; assess adherence and repeat the viral load

questions.explanation: HIV genotypic resistance testing requires 500-1000 copies/mL, so at 350 copies/mL the lab should address adherence and repeat the viral load.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old presents with fever, altered mental status, and temporal lobe abnormalities on MRI. HSV encephalitis is suspected. Which test provides the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: NAAT on CSF is the most sensitive method for HSV encephalitis; culture is far less sensitive and too slow.

questions.stem: A febrile traveler needs malaria ruled out at low parasitemia and, if positive, the species identified and parasites counted. Which film workflow is correct?

options.text: Thin film for detection, then thick film for the count
Thick film to detect (15–30× more blood per field), then thin film to identify the species and quantify parasitemia
Thick film alone; it preserves RBC morphology for speciation
Thin film alone; one film suffices if Giemsa pH is 7.0–7.2

questions.explanation: Thick films concentrate 15-30 times more blood per field for detection, while thin films preserve the RBC monolayer for species ID and quantification.

questions.stem: A laboratory stains a suspected Plasmodium vivax smear with Wright stain at pH 6.5 and sees no Schüffner dots. The smear is restained with Giemsa at pH 7.1 and the dots appear. What explains this?

options.text: Schüffner dots are visible only in P. ovale, not P. vivax
Schüffner dots dissolve in Wright stain but reform in Giemsa
The first stain was performed on a thick film instead of a thin film
Giemsa at neutral pH 7.0-7.2 is required to visualize Schüffner dots and Maurer clefts; Wright stain below pH 6.8 hides them

questions.explanation: Schüffner dots and Maurer clefts require Giemsa at pH 7.0-7.2; Wright stain below pH 6.8 hides them.

questions.stem: A traveler with severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria has 12% parasitemia, and the intensive care team asks whether exchange transfusion should be performed. What is the best guidance?

options.text: Exchange transfusion is required at 10% parasitemia or higher
The CDC no longer recommends exchange transfusion for severe malaria; treat promptly with IV artesunate instead
Exchange transfusion is indicated only when parasitemia exceeds 20%
Exchange transfusion is contraindicated in all forms of malaria

questions.explanation: The CDC no longer recommends exchange transfusion for severe malaria; prompt IV artesunate is the treatment.

questions.stem: An asplenic patient develops high fever and hemolytic anemia two weeks after a tick bite in New England. A blood smear shows intraerythrocytic tetrads forming Maltese crosses. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Maltese cross tetrads are pathognomonic for Babesia, never malaria, and asplenic patients risk fatal babesiosis.

questions.stem: A trichrome-stained stool shows Entamoeba cysts with four nuclei in an asymptomatic patient who recently traveled to Mexico. What is the best next step?

options.text: Treat immediately with metronidazole; all four-nucleated cysts are pathogenic
Report as Entamoeba dispar, which is always the nonpathogenic species
Repeat the O&P examination; a single specimen is inadequate
Order a fecal antigen test to distinguish Entamoeba histolytica from the morphologically identical E. dispar before treating

questions.explanation: E. histolytica and E. dispar are morphologically identical, so a fecal antigen test must distinguish the pathogen before treatment.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man who emigrated from Southeast Asia 20 years ago is about to start high-dose corticosteroids for an autoimmune flare. He has mild eosinophilia. What is the best action?

options.text: Start empiric albendazole after the steroids take effect
Screen for Strongyloides stercoralis before immunosuppression, because hyperinfection syndrome can be fatal
No screening is needed; eosinophilia is expected with corticosteroids
Order a routine O&P examination only if diarrhea develops

questions.explanation: Immunosuppression can trigger fatal Strongyloides hyperinfection, so at-risk patients from endemic areas are screened before steroids.

questions.stem: A patient with painless hematuria after swimming in freshwater in Egypt has eggs with a terminal spine in his urine sediment. Which organism is most likely, and when should urine be collected?

options.text: Schistosoma haematobium; collect urine between 10 am and 2 pm
Schistosoma japonicum; collect the first morning void
Schistosoma intercalatum; collect urine after exercise only

questions.explanation: A terminal spine identifies S. haematobium, the urinary schistosome, whose egg excretion peaks between 10 am and 2 pm.

questions.stem: A laboratory reports "Taenia solium eggs" based on microscopic examination of a stool specimen. What is the problem with this report?

options.text: Report as Taenia solium; the radially striated embryophore distinguishes it from T. saginata
The eggs should have been reported as Hymenolepis nana
Report as Taenia saginata based on the patient's history of eating undercooked beef
Taenia species eggs (31-43 μm) cannot be distinguished as T. solium versus T. saginata; the report should read "Taenia spp."

questions.explanation: T. solium and T. saginata eggs are identical, so the report must read "Taenia spp." without proglottid or molecular confirmation.

questions.stem: A physician draws a single 10-mL blood culture set through an existing IV catheter for an adult with suspected sepsis. Which deficiencies compromise this collection?

options.text: Volume only; one set from one site is fine at 20 mL
Volume, number of sets, and site — need 20 mL per set, 2–3 sets from separate venipunctures 30–60 minutes apart
Timing only; all sets may be drawn at once from the catheter

questions.explanation: Adults need 20 mL per set with 2-3 sets from separate sites 30-60 minutes apart; two sets detect 80% and three detect 96% of bacteremias.

notes.note: Lee 2007 found one to four blood cultures detected 73%, 90%, 98% and 99.8% of bloodstream infections; 80/96% comes from a 2004 study.
CDC guidance says at least two sets within a few hours from separate sites; no fixed 30–60-minute interval was found.

questions.stem: Four CSF tubes arrive; tube 1 is visibly bloody from a traumatic tap. Which handling is correct?

options.text: Send tube 1 to Microbiology; it has the most material
Pool all four tubes to maximize recovery
Send tubes 2–4 to Microbiology; tube 1 carries skin flora from the needle track
Discard tube 1 and split tube 4 between Chemistry and Microbiology

questions.explanation: The first CSF tube carries skin flora from the needle track, so tubes 2-4 go to Microbiology.

questions.stem: A sputum Gram stain shows 8 squamous epithelial cells and 40 neutrophils per low-power field, with a predominant gram-negative rod. What should the laboratory do?

options.text: Request recollection after the patient rinses with mouthwash
Accept and process the specimen; it meets quality criteria
Report the specimen as contaminated and cancel the culture

questions.explanation: Sputum is acceptable with fewer than 25 epithelial cells and more than 25 neutrophils per LPF; only more than 10 squamous cells per LPF triggers rejection.

notes.note: These two cut-offs conflict: a sputum with 11–24 squamous cells would be both acceptable and rejected. One published rule accepts < 10 squamous cells with > 25 leukocytes per LPF; each laboratory sets its own criteria.

questions.stem: A urethral swab for Neisseria gonorrhoeae culture was inadvertently refrigerated overnight at 4°C before plating. What is the best action?

options.text: Plate it anyway; refrigeration preserves gonococci
Incubate the plate an extra 48 hours to compensate
Enrich the swab in selective broth before plating
Reject the specimen and recollect; N. gonorrhoeae must never be refrigerated and should be delivered within 2 hours

questions.explanation: Cold kills the gonococcus, so refrigerated swabs are rejected and recollected with delivery within 2 hours.

questions.stem: A clean-catch urine specimen sits at room temperature for 6 hours before reaching the laboratory. What is the best action?

options.text: Refrigerate it now and process it the next morning
Reject the specimen and request recollection; urine must be processed within 2 hours or refrigerated for no more than 24 hours
Culture it and subtract the expected overgrowth from the colony count
Accept it; colony counts are unaffected by transport time

questions.explanation: Urine held at room temperature beyond 2 hours allows bacterial multiplication that invalidates the colony count.

questions.stem: A formed stool specimen is submitted for Clostridioides difficile testing from a 5-year-old with 1 day of loose stools after starting laxatives. What is the best action?

options.text: Reject the specimen; C. difficile testing requires unformed stool from a patient with 3 or more unformed stools in 24 hours and no recent laxatives
Test it because the patient is over 2 years old
Test it and report a negative as ruling out infection
Test it; any stool is acceptable for C. difficile NAAT

questions.explanation: Formed stool is rejected for C. difficile testing, which requires 3 or more unformed stools per 24 hours without recent laxatives.

questions.stem: A surgeon submits tissue for anaerobic culture in a sterile cup with no transport medium; transport to the lab will take 4 hours. What is the best action?

options.text: Accept it; a sterile cup at room temperature is adequate for anaerobes
Refrigerate the cup to preserve anaerobes during the delay
Request recollection in anaerobic transport medium; tissue must be protected from oxygen during transport
Plate the tissue aerobically only, since anaerobes will not survive

questions.explanation: Anaerobic wound and tissue specimens are held at room temperature because refrigeration kills anaerobic organisms.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant with paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting needs pertussis testing. Which specimen and method offer the highest sensitivity?

options.text: Nasopharyngeal aspirate or Dacron/nylon nasopharyngeal swab for PCR

questions.explanation: Cotton and calcium alginate swabs are toxic to B. pertussis and inhibit PCR; Dacron or nylon swabs are required.

questions.stem: A psychiatrist orders genotyping of a patient's cytochrome P450 isoforms before starting an antidepressant, hoping to predict efficacy and avoid toxicity. This use of genetic testing is best described as:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenomics tests genetic expression of drug-metabolizing enzyme isoforms, ligands, and receptors to choose effective drug therapy and predict toxicity. (Trap: GWAS compares genomes of patients versus unaffected people to find disease associations — it does not guide drug selection.)

questions.stem: A forensic analyst explains that single-nucleotide polymorphisms are useful for parentage testing because they are abundant and stably inherited. Approximately how often does a SNP occur in the human genome?
questions.explanation: SNPs occur at ~1 per 1000 bp, giving roughly 3 million SNP differences between unrelated people — the basis for their use in parentage/forensic identification and pharmacogenomics.

questions.stem: A lung adenocarcinoma patient is evaluated for EGFR-targeted therapy, and the laboratory bills CPT 81235 (Tier 1). Which variant set does this code cover?

options.text: Exon 19 LREA, L858R, T790M, G719A/S, L861Q

questions.explanation: 81235 is the Tier 1 code for EGFR common variants — exon 19 LREA, L858R, T790M, G719A/S, L861Q. (Trap: V617F is JAK2 81270 and 20210 G>A is Factor 2 81240 — different Tier 1 single-analyte codes.)

questions.stem: A reference laboratory offers DNA sequence analysis of more than 50 exons in a single gene for a rare disorder. Which Tier 2 complexity level and code best fit this test?
questions.explanation: Tier 2 spans 9 complexity levels, from a single germline variant (level 1, 81400) up to analysis of >50 exons in one gene (level 9, 81408). (Trap: 81201 is the Tier 1 code for a different gene, APC — do not squeeze an unrelated test into it.)

questions.stem: A claim for a molecular test is denied because the payer determines the test was not medically necessary for the documented diagnosis. Which phase of the reimbursement process failed?
questions.explanation: Reimbursement has three phases — coverage (medical necessity, regulatory approval, evidence of health-outcome effect), then coding (CPT + ICD assignment), then payment. A medical-necessity denial is a coverage-phase failure. (Trap: confusing the code assignment with the medical-necessity decision.)

questions.stem: A laboratory offers a lab-developed molecular test that has not been cleared by the FDA. The billing department asks whether the test can be billed and what the report must contain. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It cannot be billed without FDA clearance
It may be billed, but the final report must carry a disclaimer that the test is not FDA-cleared
It may be billed with no special reporting requirements
It can be billed only under the unlisted code 81479

questions.explanation: FDA clearance is NOT required for billing, but a disclaimer must be added to the final report for tests not cleared by the FDA. (Trap: the unlisted code 81479 is for tests lacking any Tier 1 or Tier 2 code, not for all non-cleared tests.)

questions.stem: A pathologist microdissects tumor tissue from a slide before EGFR testing that will be billed under a Tier 1 code. The coder asks whether the microdissection is included in the Tier 1 payment. Which answer is correct?

options.text: No — cell lysis and nucleic acid extraction are also excluded
Yes — microdissection is bundled into the Tier 1 payment
No — Tier 1/2 codes include all technical components from cell lysis through detection, but not pre-extraction procedures such as microdissection
Yes — but only for Tier 2 codes

questions.explanation: Tier 1 and Tier 2 codes cover all technical components (lysis, extraction, amplification, detection) but NOT pre-extraction procedures like microdissection, which is billed separately. (Trap: assuming "all technical components" means literally everything before the report.)

questions.stem: A technologist sets up pyrosequencing but mistakenly uses dATP instead of deoxyadenosine alpha-thiotriphosphate. Why will the run produce unreliable results?

options.text: ATP sulfurylase cannot use the released PPi
Luciferase cannot distinguish dATP from ATP, creating false background light
Taq polymerase requires the thiotriphosphate analog for extension

questions.explanation: Pyrosequencing substitutes deoxyadenosine alpha-thiotriphosphate for dATP because luciferase would otherwise use dATP as a substrate and generate spurious light. The true cascade is nucleotide incorporation → PPi release → ATP sulfurylase makes ATP → luciferase emits light, with apyrase degrading unincorporated dNTPs.

questions.stem: A hybridization wash is changed from high-salt buffer at low temperature to 0.1x SSC at high temperature near the Tm with formamide. Which duplexes will remain stably hybridized?

options.text: All duplexes, including those with multiple mismatches
Mismatched duplexes are stabilized under these conditions
Essentially only near-perfect matches — high temperature, low salt, and formamide create high stringency

questions.explanation: High stringency = high temperature near Tm + low salt + formamide, which tolerates essentially no mismatches (mismatches lower the Tm). (Trap: "low salt" sounds gentler — it is actually harsher, destabilizing imperfect duplexes.)

questions.stem: A therapeutic RNA oligonucleotide pairs perfectly with its target mRNA and acts through RISC. What is the expected effect on the target mRNA?

options.text: Translational blockade with bulging of the duplex
Increased transcription of the target gene
mRNA degradation by RNA interference cleavage

questions.explanation: siRNA pairs PERFECTLY → target mRNA degradation (RNAi); miRNA binds IMPERFECTLY → bulging and translational blockade. Both are 22–26 nt, cut by Dicer, and act via RISC. (Trap: assigning miRNA's muffling job to siRNA.)

questions.stem: A researcher needs to determine the molecular weight of an RNA transcript that hybridizes to a gene probe, without digesting the starting material. Which method is appropriate?

options.text: Western blot — detects proteins, not nucleic acids
Southern blot — DNA after restriction digestion
Northern blot — denaturing electrophoresis of RNA with no restriction digestion

questions.explanation: Southern blot = DNA after restriction digestion; northern blot = RNA under denaturing conditions with no digestion — both report the molecular weight of the hybridizing species. (Trap: reaching for Southern blot when the starting material is RNA.)

questions.stem: Two brothers carry dystrophin gene deletions. The older brother's deletion shifts the reading frame and he has severe, early-onset weakness; the younger brother's deletion preserves the reading frame and his course is much milder. Which diagnosis fits the younger brother?
questions.explanation: A frameshift deletion abolishes functional dystrophin → severe Duchenne; an in-frame deletion leaves partially functional protein → milder Becker. Frame status, not deletion size alone, decides severity.

questions.stem: In chronic myeloid leukemia, a reciprocal translocation fuses c-abl with bcr, producing a hyperactive fusion protein that drives the disease. Which chromosomes participate in this Philadelphia chromosome rearrangement?
questions.explanation: t(9;22) fuses c-abl (chromosome 9) with bcr (chromosome 22) → hyperactive kinase. (Trap: t(8;14) is Burkitt lymphoma, t(14;18) is follicular lymphoma, and t(15;17) is acute promyelocytic leukemia — the exam loves swapping translocations.)

questions.stem: A child has extreme sun sensitivity and develops multiple skin cancers in early childhood. Which DNA repair defect best explains this presentation?

options.text: Nucleotide excision repair defect — xeroderma pigmentosum

questions.explanation: Nucleotide excision repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum (inability to repair bulky UV damage → extreme sun sensitivity, early skin cancers). (Trap: mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome — hereditary colorectal cancer, not sun sensitivity.)

questions.stem: During real-time PCR extension, a dual-labeled probe is cleaved and its reporter dye separates from the quencher, producing fluorescence proportional to the amount of product. Which probe chemistry is being used?

options.text: FISH probe — fluorescent hybridization without nuclease cleavage
Molecular beacon — a hairpin probe that fluoresces on hybridization
SYBR Green — a nonspecific dsDNA-binding dye
TaqMan 5-prime nuclease — Taq's 5'→3' exonuclease cleaves the nonextendable probe during extension

questions.explanation: TaqMan is the 5' nuclease (hydrolysis) chemistry: Taq's exonuclease chews the probe like Pac-Man, freeing reporter from quencher only when primer and probe bind the same template strand. (Trap: molecular beacons fluoresce by hairpin opening on hybridization — no cleavage involved.)

questions.stem: A real-time PCR probe is designed as a hairpin with an internally quenched fluorophore; when its loop sequence binds the target, the stem is forced apart and fluorescence is restored. Which probe format is this?
questions.explanation: Molecular beacons are hairpin probes — internally quenched until target binding in the loop forces the stem apart. (Trap: Scorpion probes fuse the primer and beacon on the same molecule for intramolecular kinetics; TaqMan probes are cleaved, not opened.)

questions.stem: Shortly after a laboratory switches to nested PCR, sporadic false-positive results appear across unrelated runs. What is the most likely source, and the best fix?

options.text: Heparin inhibition — recollect specimens in EDTA
Low-stringency annealing — raise the annealing temperature
Amplicon contamination from opening the tube between rounds — switch to closed-tube real-time PCR

questions.explanation: Nested PCR's major downside is contamination when first-round product is transferred to a second tube; closed-tube real-time PCR eliminates post-PCR handling. (Trap: the specificity of nested PCR comes from the second primer set annealing internal to the first product, not from "more cycles.")

questions.stem: A technologist sets up a TMA assay for HIV RNA and includes a 95°C initial denaturation step "to separate the DNA strands." What is wrong with this setup?

options.text: The temperature is too low for denaturation
TMA starts from single-stranded RNA and needs no initial denaturation; the step is unnecessary and indicates a protocol error

questions.explanation: TMA and NASBA need no initial denaturation because they start from single-stranded RNA — contaminating DNA cannot bind primers, so it cannot inflate an RNA measurement (key for retroviral and intronless transcripts), with ~10^9-fold amplification in ≤2 h via T7 RNA polymerase.

questions.stem: A laboratory needs absolute quantification of a rare mutant allele without running a standard curve. The chosen method partitions template into thousands of droplets, counts positive versus negative partitions, and applies Poisson correction for double occupancy. Which method is this?

options.text: Endpoint PCR with an external standard curve

questions.explanation: Digital PCR gives absolute quantification with NO standard curve — partition, count positives/negatives, Poisson-correct. (Trap: competitive PCR co-amplifies known and unknown templates with the same primers for reliable endpoint quantification, but it is not standard-curve-free absolute counting.)

questions.stem: A SYBR Green real-time assay amplifies product, but the technologist cannot tell whether it represents the intended amplicon or primer-dimers. What is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat the assay with a TaqMan probe
Run a melting curve — the true product and primer-dimers have different characteristic Tm values

questions.explanation: SYBR Green binds ALL dsDNA (specific plus junk), so it is not sequence-specific; specificity comes from the melting curve, where the true product shows its characteristic Tm and primer-dimers typically melt lower. (Trap: "SYBR Green is sequence-specific.")

questions.stem: An assay detects a mutant allele present at 0.1% in glioma tissue. Its specificity comes from the 3-prime end of the primer matching only the mutant allele. Which method is this?
questions.explanation: Allele-specific PCR is allele-specific because the 3' primer end matches only the target allele, reaching ~0.1% sensitivity for minor alleles in tumors (e.g., IDH1, TERT). (Trap: multiplex PCR needs similar annealing temperatures and noncomplementary primers — a different design problem.)

questions.stem: A line-probe assay for M. tuberculosis rifampin resistance interrogates the rpoB hot spot and is described as "reverse" hybridization. What makes it reverse?

options.text: It detects RNA rather than DNA
The probe is bound to the membrane first and the sample is hybridized to it — the opposite of Southern/northern blotting

questions.explanation: "Reverse" line-blot hybridization is called reverse because the PROBE is immobilized on the membrane first and the labeled sample is hybridized to it — opposite of Southern/northern blotting, where the sample is on the membrane. (Trap: nonisotopic labels replaced radioactive ones long ago.)

questions.stem: In 2013 the Supreme Court decided AMP v. Myriad Genetics. A company now seeks to patent an isolated, naturally occurring BRCA1 genomic sequence. What is the correct outcome under that ruling?

options.text: Not patent-eligible — naturally occurring DNA is not patentable even when isolated, but cDNA IS patent-eligible because it is not naturally occurring
Patentable, because isolating the sequence required human effort
Neither genomic DNA nor cDNA is patent-eligible
Patentable only if the sequence is used in a diagnostic test

questions.explanation: The Court held that isolated naturally occurring DNA is a product of nature and not patent-eligible; synthetic cDNA is patent-eligible because it does not occur naturally. (Trap: the pre-2013 "we isolated it, so we own it" argument.)

questions.stem: A microarray study reports 50 significant genes using FDR control at 5%. A reviewer asks: "How many of these 50 are expected to be false positives?" What is the best answer?

options.text: Zero — FDR guarantees no false positives at all
About 25 — half of the 50 significant genes
It cannot be estimated from the reported data

questions.explanation: FWER controls the chance that even one reported gene is wrong (the perfectionist — Bonferroni is strictest); FDR instead controls false positives as a proportion of significant genes (the pragmatist). (Trap: choosing FDR when the requirement is "not even one false gene.")

questions.stem: A microarray flags a 2.5-fold upregulated gene as a potential biomarker. Before reporting it clinically, what should the laboratory do?

options.text: Report it — array results are definitive on their own
Confirm by qRT-PCR, because genes with less than 4-fold changes cross-validate inconsistently
Repeat the assay on a nylon macroarray
Re-run quantile normalization on the data

questions.explanation: Array differential-expression findings require independent confirmation, and genes with <4-fold differences cross-validate inconsistently — confirm by qRT-PCR before calling them real. (Trap: small fold-changes feel precise; they are the least trustworthy.)

questions.stem: Two normalization methods are compared: one assumes most genes are unchanged across arrays, while the other assumes the entire intensity distribution is invariant across arrays. Which method makes the stronger assumption?

options.text: Median-intensity normalization — it assumes the entire distribution is invariant
Quantile normalization — it assumes the entire intensity distribution is invariant

questions.explanation: Median-intensity normalization assumes only that most genes are unchanged (the weaker assumption); quantile normalization assumes the ENTIRE intensity distribution is invariant across arrays — a much stronger claim. (Trap: swapping which method assumes what.)

questions.stem: A company seeks clearance for a new pharmacogenetic microarray. The FDA asks for a predicate device — the first microarray chip cleared as a diagnostic device. Which is it?
questions.explanation: The Roche AmpliChip (CYP2D6 + CYP2C19) was the first microarray chip cleared as a diagnostic device — a pharmacogenetics pioneer for drug dosing. (Trap: EGFR/KRAS guide therapy selection but were not the first cleared chip.)

questions.stem: A student assumes the probes spotted on a microarray are the labeled component of the experiment. The supervisor corrects this misconception. By convention, which component carries the label?

options.text: The sample is labeled; the arrayed features are the probes
Both the sample and the features equally

questions.explanation: On microarrays the convention is the reverse of instinct: the SAMPLE is labeled and the arrayed features serve as the probes. (Trap: assuming the spotted probes are labeled because "probes" are labeled in Southern blots.)

questions.stem: A child with dysmorphic features has a normal high-resolution karyotype, but a 1-Mb deletion is strongly suspected clinically. What is the best next test?

options.text: Repeat the karyotype with higher-resolution banding
Single-cell whole-genome sequencing of the patient
Noninvasive prenatal screening of maternal plasma
FISH or chromosomal microarray — karyotype resolves only ~3 Mb (conventional ~5 Mb), while FISH resolves ~150 kb

questions.explanation: Karyotype resolution is megabase-scale (~3 Mb high-resolution, ~5 Mb conventional), so a 1-Mb deletion is invisible to it; FISH (~150 kb) or microarray will detect it. (Trap: repeating the same insufficient test at "higher resolution.")

questions.stem: A bone marrow karyotype shows loss of chromosome 7 in a single cell; the other 19 cells examined are normal. How should the laboratory interpret this finding?

options.text: Regard it as a culture artifact — a loss requires at least 3 cells (a gain or structural rearrangement at least 2) with the same change
Confirm by FISH on interphase nuclei, then report the clone
Report a monosomy 7 clone with clonal evolution noted

questions.explanation: Score 15–20 cells per study; an abnormality requires ≥3 cells with the same loss or ≥2 with the same gain/rearrangement — single-cell findings are artifacts. (Trap: reporting a one-cell "clone" as mosaicism.)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with Turner syndrome has karyotype 45,X/46,XY. Beyond the Turner features, what is the critical clinical concern?

options.text: Gonadoblastoma risk from Y-chromosome material — gonadectomy is indicated
No added concern — Y material is clinically inert

questions.explanation: In Turner syndrome, 45,X occurs in ~50% of cases, but any Y-chromosome material (seen in ~15% with deletions/rings/Y material) confers gonadoblastoma risk and warrants gonadectomy. (Trap: dismissing Y material as harmless.)

questions.stem: A phenotypically normal woman is found to carry a balanced Robertsonian translocation. How many chromosomes does she most likely have, and why is she healthy?

options.text: 47 — the fusion created an extra chromosome
44 — both homologues fused into a single chromosome
45 — two acrocentric chromosomes fused into one, and the lost short arms carried only rRNA genes

questions.explanation: Robertsonian carriers have 45 chromosomes — two acrocentrics fused into one. The short-arm loss is harmless because those arms carry only redundant rRNA genes. (Trap: assuming a "balanced" carrier must still have 46.)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with a 15q11.2 deletion had neonatal hypotonia and now shows hyperphagia with obesity. Which syndrome is this, and what does it reveal about the deletion's parent of origin?
questions.explanation: The SAME 15q11.2 deletion causes different diseases by parent of origin (imprinting): paternal loss → Prader-Willi (hyperphagia/obesity, hypotonia); maternal loss → Angelman (ataxia, seizures, inappropriate laughter). (Trap: swapping the parent of origin.)

questions.stem: Noninvasive prenatal screening at 12 weeks is positive for trisomy 21. The patient asks whether this is a definitive diagnosis. What is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat NIPS in 4 weeks for confirmation
Proceed as if the diagnosis is confirmed — NIPS is diagnostic
Confirm with diagnostic testing on amniocytes — NIPS is screening only (98–99% accurate) and analyzes placental DNA
CVS is the only acceptable confirmatory test

questions.explanation: NIPS is screening, not diagnosis, and it assays placental DNA — confirm on amniocytes (not CVS, which is also placental and subject to placentofetal discordance) before acting. (Trap: treating a positive screen as a diagnosis.)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with developmental delay has a normal chromosomal microarray. The geneticist still suspects a chromosome abnormality. Which abnormality could explain a normal CMA?

options.text: A balanced translocation — CMA detects copy-number changes but is blind to balanced rearrangements

questions.explanation: CMA is first-tier since 2010 for developmental delay/ID/autism/congenital anomalies because it detects genome-wide copy-number changes — but it is blind to balanced rearrangements, which require karyotype or FISH. (Trap: "microarray sees everything.")

questions.stem: A 2-year-old presents with bilateral retinoblastoma; her father had unilateral retinoblastoma as a child. Which mechanism best explains the early, bilateral disease?

options.text: Anticipation from a trinucleotide repeat expansion
Genomic imprinting of the RB1 allele
Mitochondrial inheritance through the maternal line
Knudson's two-hit hypothesis — a germline RB1 first hit plus a somatic second hit inactivates both alleles

questions.explanation: Tumor suppressor genes (RB1, BRCA1/2, APC) need BOTH alleles inactivated — a germline first hit plus a somatic second hit produces early, bilateral, multifocal hereditary cancers. (Trap: anticipation belongs to trinucleotide repeat disorders, not RB1.)

questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old man carries 38 CAG repeats in the HTT gene. His counselor warns that his children face risk of juvenile-onset Huntington disease. What best explains this warning?

options.text: 38 repeats is fully penetrant, and maternal transmission expands repeats the most
Huntington anticipation occurs only through maternal transmission
38 repeats cannot expand further in transmission
36–39 repeats is the intermediate range, and paternal transmission produces the largest expansions

questions.explanation: Huntington ranges are 6–35 normal, 36–39 intermediate, 40+ expanded — and PATERNAL transmission gives the largest expansions (juvenile onset). (Trap: fragile X expands through female meiosis instead — the exam loves swapping the parent.)

questions.stem: A newborn has severe congenital myotonic dystrophy type 1 with approximately 1500 CTG repeats; the mother is mildly affected and the father is unaffected. Which statement is correct?

options.text: 1500 repeats falls within the normal range
The father must be an asymptomatic carrier
The congenital form (1000–2000 CTG repeats) is transmitted maternally only
Congenital myotonic dystrophy is paternally transmitted, like Huntington disease

questions.explanation: Normal is 5–35 CTG; the congenital form carries 1000–2000 repeats and is transmitted MATERNALLY only. (Trap: confusing this with Huntington disease, where the largest expansions are paternal.)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman homozygous for Factor V Leiden (R506Q) asks whether she will definitely develop thrombosis. What is the best counseling?

options.text: No — despite ~80-fold relative risk (vs ~7-fold heterozygous), lifetime penetrance is only ~10%

questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden (R506Q) affects 5–7% of whites; thrombosis risk is ~7× heterozygous and ~80× homozygous, but lifetime penetrance is only ~10%. (Trap: equating a large relative risk with certain disease.)

questions.stem: An Asian couple receives negative results on the 25-mutation CF carrier screening panel and asks whether they are in the clear. What is the correct counseling?

options.text: A negative panel rules out carrier status
They should be screened for MTHFR instead
Only the symptomatic partner needs further testing
Residual risk remains — the panel has under 10% sensitivity in Asians, and more than 2000 CFTR mutations are known

questions.explanation: The core CF panel's sensitivity is ~97% in Ashkenazi Jews but <10% in Asians — a negative panel leaves substantial residual risk given >2000 known CFTR mutations. (Trap: "a negative screening panel rules out carrier status.")

questions.stem: A patient has a classic maternally inherited mitochondrial phenotype, but mtDNA testing on blood is negative. What is the best next step?

options.text: Test DNA from the affected tissue — heteroplasmy means mutant and normal mtDNA proportions vary by tissue
Test the father's mtDNA for the mutation
Repeat blood testing at higher sequencing depth

questions.explanation: mtDNA (16,569 bp, circular) is strictly maternally inherited, but heteroplasmy means the mutant load differs across tissues — detecting the mutation may require biopsy of the AFFECTED tissue. (Trap: testing the father — paternal mtDNA is not transmitted.)

questions.stem: A child's exome sequencing identifies 25,000 variants but no definitive diagnosis. The parents ask whether a genetic cause is now excluded. What is the correct response?

options.text: Yes — a negative exome definitively excludes genetic disease
No — diagnostic yield is only 25–50%, and each exome carries 20,000–30,000 variants that must be filtered
The exome should be repeated immediately
Finding 25,000 variants indicates a laboratory error

questions.explanation: The exome is only ~1.5% of the genome, diagnostic yield is 25–50%, and variant filtration (including VUS interpretation) is the real detective work — a negative exome does not exclude a genetic cause. (Trap: treating exome sequencing as a rule-out test.)

questions.stem: The father of a healthy 10-year-old has Huntington disease. The parents request predictive testing of the child so they "can plan for the future." What is the appropriate guidance?

options.text: Defer testing — predictive testing of children under 18 for adult-onset disorders is discouraged: no childhood medical benefit and real psychosocial harm
Test the mother instead of the child
Test the child and disclose the result to the school
Test now — earlier knowledge is always beneficial

questions.explanation: Predictive testing of healthy children under 18 for adult-onset disorders is discouraged — there is no medical benefit in childhood but genuine psychosocial harm. (Trap: "more information is always better.")

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for intellectual disability. He has a long narrow face, large ears, flexible fingers, and macroorchidism. His maternal uncle had similar features. Repeat-expansion testing of the FMR1 gene is ordered. Which result would confirm the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is diagnosed at >200 CGG repeats on FMR1; normal is <45, gray zone 45–54. The X-linked pedigree and phenotype fit fragile X, the classic repeat-expansion cause of intellectual disability.

questions.stem: A researcher reviews statements about amyloid-beta in Alzheimer disease. Which statement is inconsistent with current understanding?

options.text: Aβ42 aggregates readily and is neurotoxic
Aβ40 is protective against Aβ42 aggregation
ACE converts Aβ40 into neurotoxic Aβ42
Presenilin mutations raise the Aβ42:Aβ40 ratio

questions.explanation: ACE converts neurotoxic Aβ42 into Aβ40, so ACE inhibition is a risk factor for cognitive impairment and AD onset — the conversion runs 42→40, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Which statement about copy-number variation in psychotic and mood disorders is FALSE?

options.text: Bipolar disorder shows a significantly increased overall CNV burden, similar to schizophrenia
Duplication 16p11.2 is the strongest individual bipolar disorder CNV
The 22q11.2 deletion is a schizophrenia CNV hot spot
Duplication 1q21.1 is observed in bipolar disorder

questions.explanation: Schizophrenia shows enriched overall CNV burden across seven hot spots, but bipolar disorder does NOT show a significantly increased overall burden — only a few strong individual hits (1q21.1 dup, 3q29 del, 16p11.2 dup).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man of East Asian ancestry develops intense facial flushing, nausea, and vomiting after a single alcoholic drink. Which variant best explains his reaction?

options.text: ALDH2 Glu→Lys at position 487, loss of function
ADH1B His→Arg at position 48, gain of function

questions.explanation: ALDH2 Glu→Lys at 487 is a loss-of-function variant that stalls ethanol metabolism at acetaldehyde, which accumulates and causes flushing, nausea, and vomiting. ADH1B His→Arg is a gain of function that speeds ethanol catabolism and is protective.

questions.stem: A depressed patient genotyped as a CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizer fails multiple SSRI trials at standard doses. What is the best explanation?

options.text: SSRIs are ineffective in ultrarapid metabolizers for pharmacodynamic reasons
Switch to a tricyclic at the standard dose
The patient simply needs higher SSRI doses indefinitely
Ultrarapid CYP2D6 clears the drug too fast — standard doses give subtherapeutic levels; consider a non-CYP2D6 substrate or dose adjustment per CPIC

questions.explanation: MDD pharmacogenetics centers on CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 — poor versus ultrarapid metabolizer status determines antidepressant response and toxicity, requiring dose adjustments.

questions.stem: A genome-wide association study of lithium response in bipolar disorder identifies a signal in the gene encoding diacylglycerol kinase η, part of the lithium-sensitive phosphatidylinositol pathway. Which gene is this?
questions.explanation: DGKH encodes diacylglycerol kinase η in the lithium-sensitive phosphatidylinositol pathway. GPR98 and ZNF804A (rs1344706) are schizophrenia GWAS hits, and APOE is the Alzheimer risk gene — all wrong pathways here.

questions.stem: A forensic analyst testifies that a 13-locus STR profile match between a suspect and a crime scene sample is powerful evidence. What random match probability is expected for 13 loci among unrelated individuals?
questions.explanation: With 13 loci the random match probability is rarer than 1 in 1 trillion; with 20 CODIS core loci it reaches rarer than 1 in 1 nonillion. About 1 in a few thousand is the discriminatory power of mtDNA, not STRs.

questions.stem: A vaginal swab from a sexual assault case contains a mixture of victim epithelial cells and assailant sperm. Which procedure best separates the male sperm DNA from the female epithelial DNA?

options.text: Differential lysis, in which dithiothreitol reduces the disulfide bridges of the sperm's protective capsule
Centrifugation alone to pellet the sperm before lysis
Proteinase K digestion, which lyses only the sperm nuclei
Washing the swab with heparin to remove PCR inhibitors

questions.explanation: Differential lysis exploits the sperm's disulfide-bonded protective capsule — DTT (dithiothreitol) reduces those bridges so sperm lyse separately from epithelial cells. Heparin inhibits PCR and is not used in extraction.

questions.stem: Burned skeletal remains are recovered, and nuclear DNA amplification fails. The missing man's sister provides a reference sample. Which marker is most appropriate for identification, and why?

options.text: Autosomal 20-locus STR, because it has the highest discriminatory power
Y-STR haplotype, because it traces the paternal line
mtDNA, because it is maternally inherited, present in hundreds to thousands of copies per cell, and survives degradation
RFLP, because it was the original DNA fingerprinting method

questions.explanation: mtDNA is a 16,569-bp circular molecule, maternally inherited with no recombination, and its high copy number survives in burned bone and shed hairs; the sister shares the maternal mtDNA lineage. Autosomal STRs fail on degraded samples, Y-STRs need a paternal relative, and RFLP requires large amounts of intact DNA.

questions.stem: A parentage test returns a paternity index of 99. Under AABB Standards (2019), what is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The result is invalid and the lab must be sanctioned
The PI is below the required 100 (99:1 odds) — additional testing is needed

questions.explanation: AABB requires PI ≥ 100 for parentage determination — "100 = 99:1." A single-locus exclusion is also insufficient evidence of nonpaternity because of mutation rates.

questions.stem: A sexual assault sample contains an overwhelming background of female epithelial DNA with a small amount of male DNA. Which marker best resolves the male contributor?
questions.explanation: Y-STRs are paternally inherited and produce a haplotype that resolves male DNA in overwhelming female backgrounds. The trade-off is that Y-STRs are less discriminating than autosomal STR profiles, since all paternal-lineage males share the haplotype.

questions.stem: Detectives upload crime-scene DNA to a public consumer genealogy database containing about 1 million SNPs and build a family tree to identify a suspect. Which method is this?
questions.explanation: Forensic genealogy (Golden State Killer, April 2018) uploads DNA to public consumer SNP databases to build family trees. Familial searching (Grim Sleeper, July 2010) instead searches the crime-lab CODIS/NDIS offender database for a perpetrator's relatives.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man receives a coronary stent and starts clopidogrel. Genotyping shows CYP2C19 2/3 (poor metabolizer). What is the best next step?

options.text: Double the clopidogrel dose to overcome reduced activation
Switch to prasugrel or ticagrelor, which do not depend on CYP2C19 activation
Continue clopidogrel and monitor platelet function
Switch to warfarin for antiplatelet therapy

questions.explanation: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19; 2/3 loss-of-function alleles reduce the active metabolite, causing less platelet inhibition and more cardiac events. The FDA boxed warning (2010) directs poor metabolizers to alternatives such as prasugrel or ticagrelor.

questions.stem: A patient with CYP2C9 3/3 and VKORC1 -1639 A/A genotypes is about to start warfarin. What dosing approach is indicated?

options.text: A lower dose, reflecting very high warfarin sensitivity
The standard 5 mg daily starting dose
A normal-sensitivity phenotype requiring no adjustment
A higher-than-average dose, because both variants accelerate clearance

questions.explanation: CYP2C9 2/3 variants slow clearance of S-warfarin (the potent enantiomer), and VKORC1 -1639A increases target sensitivity — both push toward a lower dose. The FDA label carries a genotype-based dosing table combining both genes.

questions.stem: A CYP2D6 normal metabolizer on tamoxifen starts paroxetine for hot flashes. What is the concern?

options.text: Paroxetine phenocopies poor-metabolizer status — choose an antidepressant without CYP2D6 inhibition
No interaction exists between the two drugs
Stop tamoxifen and treat the hot flashes instead

questions.explanation: CPIC recommends alternative hormonal therapy for CYP2D6 poor/intermediate metabolizers — aromatase inhibitors (plus ovarian suppression if premenopausal). Tamoxifen 40 mg/day is only a fallback if aromatase inhibitors are contraindicated, and CYP2D6 inhibitors phenocopy poor-metabolizer status.

questions.stem: Genotyping before 5-FU therapy reveals a single reduced-function DPYD allele (intermediate metabolizer). What is the correct dose adjustment?

options.text: Double the dose to overcome reduced metabolism

questions.explanation: DPD is the rate-limiting 5-FU catabolic enzyme; two nonfunction DPYD alleles make a poor metabolizer for whom a normal dose can be fatal — avoid fluoropyrimidines. One reduced-function allele (intermediate metabolizer) calls for a 25–50% dose reduction instead.

questions.stem: A patient heterozygous for TPMT *3A is about to start azathioprine. What dose adjustment is recommended?

options.text: Increase the dose to compensate for rapid clearance
Use the full standard dose; heterozygotes have normal activity
Reduce by more than 90% or avoid thiopurines entirely

questions.explanation: TPMT 2, 3A, and *3C explain >95% of low/intermediate TPMT activity. Heterozygotes need a 35–50% dose reduction; the >90% reduction (usually avoidance) applies to TPMT-deficient patients.

questions.stem: A patient with EGFR-mutant non–small cell lung cancer responds to erlotinib for 14 months, then progresses. Repeat biopsy shows the exon 20 T790M mutation. What is the best next therapy?

options.text: Continue erlotinib at the same dose

questions.explanation: T790M is the gatekeeper mutation causing about 50% of acquired resistance to first-generation EGFR TKIs (gefitinib, erlotinib), so switching between them fails. Osimertinib is the third-generation irreversible inhibitor designed for T790M-mediated resistance.

questions.stem: A metastatic colorectal cancer is KRAS/NRAS wild-type but BRAF V600E-mutant. The oncologist considers cetuximab. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Cetuximab is effective — only RAS matters
BRAF V600E is an additional resistance marker downstream of EGFR — anti-EGFR therapy is unlikely to benefit
BRAF mutation sensitizes the tumor to cetuximab

questions.explanation: Anti-EGFR antibodies (cetuximab, panitumumab) are ineffective when RAS is mutated because oncogenic ras-p21 signals downstream of EGFR. FDA labels require wild-type RAS — KRAS and NRAS, exons 2/3/4 — by an FDA-approved test, and BRAF mutation is an additional resistance marker.

questions.stem: For detecting small (<3 cm) hepatocellular carcinoma at 95% specificity, which marker and cutoff is more sensitive?

options.text: TGF-β1 at 800 pg/mL, with 68% sensitivity versus 24% for AFP
AFP, which outperforms TGF-β1 for small HCC

questions.explanation: At 95% specificity, TGF-β1 (cutoff 800 pg/mL) detects 68% of small HCCs versus only 24% for AFP (cutoff 200 pg/mL). The bigger cutoff wins here — do not assume AFP is superior.

questions.stem: A healthy blood donor's serum shows no detectable p53 protein. Which statement best explains this finding?

options.text: This is expected — wild-type p53's short half-life keeps it undetectable in normal serum
The donor has a homozygous p53 deletion
The assay must have failed due to serum interference
p53 is never detectable in serum under any circumstance

questions.explanation: Wild-type p53 turns over in about 20 minutes and is undetectable in normal serum, so detectable serum p53 represents mutant protein. Absence of serum p53 can also mean homozygous p53 deletion — no serologic test detects a deletion.

questions.stem: A serum oncoprotein assay returns a positive result in a patient with no known primary tumor. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The positive result is a normal finding, since oncoproteins circulate in healthy donors
Malignancy is confirmed, and the marker identifies the tumor's tissue of origin
Malignancy is strongly implied, but the tissue of origin is usually unidentifiable
No further diagnostic workup is needed

questions.explanation: Oncoprotein assays have 95–100% specificity — a positive strongly implies malignancy and outperforms oncofetal antigens like CEA and AFP — but the tissue of origin is usually unidentifiable. A positive means "cancer, somewhere," not "cancer of the X."

questions.stem: An asbestos-exposed patient has a serum EGFR extracellular domain level of 700 fmol/mL. What does this indicate?

options.text: An asbestos-associated malignancy such as lung carcinoma or mesothelioma, since the cutoff is ≥636 fmol/mL
Prostate cancer — 700 fmol/mL meets the diagnostic cutoff
A normal finding requiring no follow-up

questions.explanation: In asbestos-exposed patients, EGFR ECD ≥636 fmol/mL indicates asbestos-associated malignancy (lung carcinoma or mesothelioma). The prostate cancer EGFR cutoff is 67.9 ng/mL — different units and a different disease.

questions.stem: Which statement about the molecular findings in Burkitt lymphoma is FALSE?

options.text: The hallmark translocation moves c-myc from chromosome 8 to an immunoglobulin locus
The most common form is t(8;14) involving IGH
Burkitt lymphoma is driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion from t(9;22)
Variant translocations t(2;8) and t(8;22) involve the kappa and lambda light-chain loci

questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma carries the c-myc translocation from chromosome 8 to the Ig locus on chromosome 14. t(15;17) defines APL, t(14;18) defines follicular lymphoma, and t(9;22) defines CML — all wrong diseases here.
