questions.stem: A CML patient on imatinib has a single BCR-ABL1 result 0.5 log lower than the prior sample, with all previous results stable. What is the best next step?

options.text: Test for ABL1 kinase-domain mutations immediately
Continue therapy and repeat qPCR on schedule — a single 0.5-log dip is assay variation

questions.explanation: A 0.5–1 log rise in BCR-ABL1 on two consecutive samples is the trigger for ABL1 kinase-domain mutation testing — it is the rise, not a dip, that signals emerging resistance.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old adult with newly diagnosed Philadelphia-chromosome–positive ALL has BCR-ABL1 transcript analysis ordered. Which isoform is expected?
questions.explanation: p190 (minor breakpoint, m-BCR) is the isoform of Ph-positive ALL; p210 (major breakpoint, M-BCR) indicates CML, and p230 (μ-BCR) indicates rare neutrophilic CML. The isoforms flip the diagnosis, so do not default to p210.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with IgM monoclonal gammopathy, anemia, and hyperviscosity symptoms undergoes molecular testing. Which mutation most strongly supports Waldenström macroglobulinemia over IgM MGUS or myeloma?
questions.explanation: MYD88 L265P is present in >90% of Waldenström macroglobulinemia — essentially diagnostic in the right clinical context (IgM monoclonal gammopathy with hyperviscosity). BRAF V600E marks hairy cell leukemia, JAK2 V617F the myeloproliferative neoplasms, and KIT D816V systemic mastocytosis.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected essential thrombocythemia tests negative for JAK2 V617F. Which mutation should be tested next?
questions.explanation: JAK2, CALR, and MPL together account for >95% of Philadelphia-negative MPNs; CALR mutations occur in 20–30% of ET and primary myelofibrosis. BCR-ABL1 testing looks for CML, which is Philadelphia-positive by definition.

questions.stem: A CLL patient has a 17p deletion with TP53 mutation and unmutated IGHV (≤2% divergence from germline). What is the correct management implication?

options.text: Standard chemoimmunotherapy is sufficient for this favorable profile
Observation is appropriate regardless of genetics
This is high-risk disease — use BTK or BCL2 inhibitors rather than chemoimmunotherapy

questions.explanation: 17p-/TP53 and unmutated IGHV (≤2% divergence) define high-risk CLL requiring targeted agents such as BTK or BCL2 inhibitors. Mutated IGHV (>2% divergence) is the favorable finding — "mutations sound bad" is the trap, but here they are good.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with normal blood counts has next-generation sequencing showing a DNMT3A mutation at 3% variant allele frequency. How should this be classified?
questions.explanation: CHIP is defined as VAF ≥2% without cytopenias or a hematologic neoplasm, with 0.5–1% progression risk per year. The presence of cytopenias would make it CCUS instead.

questions.stem: A colorectal cancer shows microsatellite instability in 3 of 5 tested markers (MSI-H). What does this result trigger?

options.text: No further action; MSI-H has no clinical implications
Lynch syndrome workup and immunotherapy eligibility

questions.explanation: MSI-H is defined as instability in ≥2 of 5 markers and triggers both a Lynch syndrome (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM) workup and immunotherapy eligibility. It does not by itself determine anti-EGFR therapy.

questions.stem: A glioblastoma shows MGMT promoter methylation. Which therapy is this finding predictive for?
questions.explanation: MGMT promoter methylation predicts benefit from temozolomide in glioblastoma. PCV chemotherapy response is predicted by 1p/19q codeletion in oligodendroglioma — do not swap the two predictive markers.

questions.stem: An infant with marfanoid habitus and mucosal neuromas has a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma. RET testing is ordered. Which result confers the highest risk and the earliest indication for prophylactic thyroidectomy?

options.text: RET codon 634 mutation, with routine surveillance only

questions.explanation: RET codon 918 (exon 16) is found in >95% of MEN 2B and carries the highest risk, warranting the earliest prophylactic thyroidectomy. Codon 634 is the most common MEN 2A mutation — still risky, but one step below 918.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old presents with a painful diaphyseal mass of the femur. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells. Which molecular finding is expected?
questions.explanation: EWSR1-FLI1 is present in 85–90% of Ewing sarcoma. TMPRSS2-ERG defines about 50% of prostate cancers, EML4-ALK is a lung cancer target, and PML-RARA defines APL — all wrong tumors here.

questions.stem: A gastrointestinal stromal tumor harbors a cKIT exon 17 D816V mutation. What is the implication for imatinib therapy?

options.text: Imatinib will be effective, since all cKIT mutations are imatinib-sensitive
The tumor is imatinib-resistant; D816V confers resistance
ATRA is the preferred targeted agent

questions.explanation: Most cKIT mutations (75–80% of GISTs) are imatinib-sensitive, but the exon 17 D816V variant specifically confers imatinib resistance — genotype the exon, not just the gene.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with ovarian cancer is found to carry a germline BRCA1 mutation. Which class of targeted therapy is indicated?
questions.explanation: BRCA1 carriers face 50–70% breast and 30–40% ovarian cancer risk by age 70, and BRCA1/2-mutated tumors are sensitive to PARP inhibitors, which exploit defective homologous-recombination repair. EGFR-directed and BRAF-directed therapies target different pathways.

questions.stem: A researcher counts 10–14 bp tags to absolutely quantify transcripts. A colleague suggests switching to a DNA microarray for "better quantification." What is the best response?

options.text: Keep SAGE — direct tag counting gives absolute quantification
Agree — microarrays give absolute quantification too
Switch to comparative genomic hybridization instead

questions.explanation: SAGE gives absolute quantification by direct counting of 10–14 bp tags. DNA microarrays measure only relative expression by hybridization — a microarray is a photographer, SAGE is a bouncer with a clicker.

questions.stem: A laboratory wants to sequence both ends of each DNA fragment to improve alignment across repetitive regions. Which approach is used?

options.text: Single-read sequencing with longer reads only
Paired-end sequencing — reading both ends of each fragment to constrain alignment

questions.explanation: Paired-end sequencing reads both ends of each fragment — the known insert size constrains alignment and resolves repetitive regions that defeat single reads.

questions.stem: A child with an undiagnosed Mendelian disorder needs cost-effective genomic testing. Which test is best justified by the fact that about 85% of disease-causing mutations reside in the exome?
questions.explanation: Because roughly 85% of disease-causing mutations lie in the exome, WES is the cost-effective sweet spot for undiagnosed Mendelian disorders. Karyotyping misses submicroscopic variants, and single-gene Sanger is too narrow when the gene is unknown.

questions.stem: Two DLBCL patients have identical morphology; gene-expression profiling shows one is GCB-like and the other ABC-like. What 5-year survivals are expected?
questions.explanation: Gene-expression profiling splits DLBCL into germinal-center B-cell-like (72% alive at 5 years) versus activated B-cell-like (16%) — a 56-point gap. Morphology alone cannot distinguish them.

questions.stem: A laboratory wants to screen a PCR amplicon for an unknown single-base change using melting increments of 0.008–0.2°C with a dsDNA-binding dye. Which method is this?
questions.explanation: HRM melts in 0.008–0.2°C increments and is sensitive enough to detect a single base change. Karyotyping and FISH cannot resolve single-base changes, and Southern blotting is not a melting-based screen.

questions.stem: Investigators cluster tumor expression profiles with no predefined labels to discover previously unknown cancer subtypes. Which analytic approach is this?
questions.explanation: Unsupervised methods perform class discovery — clustering finds novel subtypes with no prior labels. Supervised methods perform class prediction, training on predefined classes to classify a test set.

questions.stem: A small fire starts in a laboratory wastebasket. After ensuring no one needs rescue, what is the correct sequence?

options.text: Open all doors and windows to ventilate before acting
Extinguish it first, then decide whether to pull the alarm
Activate the alarm, confine the fire, then extinguish it using PASS technique
Pour water on it regardless of the fire class

questions.explanation: RACE (Rescue-Alarm-Confine-Extinguish); extinguisher via PASS.

questions.stem: A serum sample is diluted by adding 0.5 mL of serum to 1.5 mL of diluent. The diluted sample measures 30 mg/dL. What is the true serum concentration?
questions.explanation: 0.5 mL in 2.0 mL total = 1:4 dilution; 30 × 4 = 120 mg/dL.

questions.stem: What is the normality of a 2 M H₂SO₄ solution?
questions.explanation: N = M × valence; 2 M H₂SO₄ (diprotic) = 4 N.

questions.stem: A glucose assay's calibrators run 0–500 mg/dL. A patient's sample gives an absorbance above the 500 mg/dL calibrator. What is the correct action?

options.text: Extrapolate the curve to estimate the value
Dilute the sample, re-run it, and multiply the result by the dilution factor

questions.explanation: Above the top standard: dilute, re-run, and multiply by the dilution factor; never extrapolate.

questions.stem: For the dataset 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, what is the mode, and what happens to the 95% confidence interval of the mean if the sample size is quadrupled?

options.text: Mode = 6; the CI width is halved
Mode = 5; the CI width is halved

questions.explanation: Mode = 5 (most frequent); quadrupling n halves the 95% CI width.

questions.stem: A newly hired medical laboratory scientist completes initial training and begins independent testing. How often must competency be assessed under CLIA?

options.text: Semiannually during the first year, then annually thereafter

questions.explanation: CLIA competency: initially, semiannually in year one, annually thereafter.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine collection totals 1440 mL with urine creatinine 100 mg/dL; plasma creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. What is the creatinine clearance?
questions.explanation: Clearance = (U×V)/P = (100 mg/dL × 1 mL/min) ÷ 1.0 mg/dL = 100 mL/min.

questions.stem: Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 48 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 35 mEq/L. By Henderson-Hasselbalch logic, the primary disorder is:
questions.explanation: pH = 6.1 + log(35/(0.03×48)) ≈ 7.49; the elevated HCO₃⁻ on the alkaline side of the ratio explains the alkalemia = primary metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: A patient's arterial pH falls from 7.40 to 7.10. What happened to the hydrogen ion concentration?
questions.explanation: 0.3 pH units = 2× [H⁺] (40 → 80 nmol/L); 1.0 unit would be 10×.

questions.stem: In exercising muscle, rising CO₂ and H⁺ cause hemoglobin to release more O₂. This is the:
questions.explanation: Bohr effect: CO₂/H⁺ lower O₂ affinity → tissue unloading. Haldane is the reverse (deoxyHb carries CO₂ better).

questions.stem: After ~24 hours of fasting, liver glycogen is depleted and blood glucose is maintained primarily by which pathway, occurring mainly in the liver and kidney?
questions.explanation: Early fasting burns glycogenolysis; after ~24 h gluconeogenesis (liver + kidney, from lactate/glycerol/amino acids) maintains glucose. Glycolysis and glycogenesis move the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Which sugar will NOT give a positive copper-reduction (Clinitest) test?
questions.explanation: Sucrose is non-reducing (anomeric carbons locked in the bond); glucose, fructose, and lactose reduce copper.

questions.stem: Which structural role do phospholipids play in lipoproteins?

options.text: They fill the hydrophobic core with triglycerides
They form the surface monolayer with free cholesterol and apolipoproteins

questions.explanation: Phospholipids + free cholesterol + apolipoproteins form the surface monolayer; triglycerides/cholesteryl esters fill the core.

questions.stem: Total cholesterol 265 mg/dL, HDL-C 42 mg/dL, triglycerides 520 mg/dL. Which LDL-related value can still be validly reported?

options.text: Only a direct homogeneous LDL assay

questions.explanation: Non-HDL-C = TC − HDL-C = 223 mg/dL; Friedewald dies at TG >400 but non-HDL needs no TG term.

notes.note: Direct LDL-C assays are method-dependent and can be biased in high-TG samples; HEART UK/ACB does not recommend them in hypertriglyceridaemia (non-HDL-C, Sampson–NIH or apoB instead).

questions.stem: Newborn screening shows markedly elevated phenylalanine with a high phenylalanine/tyrosine ratio. The defective enzyme and the most urgent management are:

options.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase — begin phenylalanine-restricted diet immediately
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase — restrict all protein

questions.explanation: PKU is phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; immediate phenylalanine-restricted diet prevents irreversible neuro damage.

questions.stem: Serum iron is 180 μg/dL and TIBC is 300 μg/dL. What is the transferrin saturation, and what does it suggest?

options.text: 60% — suggests iron overload; work up hemochromatosis

questions.explanation: % saturation = (180/300)×100 = 60% ≥ 45% screen → hemochromatosis workup.

questions.stem: Total protein 9.0 g/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL. What is the A/G ratio and its interpretation?

options.text: 0.5 — low, suggests globulin excess (e.g., myeloma workup)

questions.explanation: A/G = 3.0/(9.0−3.0) = 0.5, low → globulin excess; work up monoclonal gammopathy.

questions.stem: A patient with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and elevated serum ACE most likely has:
questions.explanation: Epithelioid granulomas produce ACE; elevated serum ACE supports (and monitors) sarcoidosis but is not specific.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with pica and developmental delay has elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (ZPP) and coarse basophilic stippling on the smear. Which heme-synthesis enzyme is blocked by lead?
questions.explanation: Lead blocks ferrochelatase → free erythrocyte protoporphyrin/ZPP rises. (Re-angled from draft: Q290 already tests AIP = PBG deaminase.)

questions.stem: A traveler returns with acute hepatitis: ALT 1,200 IU/L, IgM anti-HAV positive, HBsAg negative, anti-HCV negative. What counseling about chronicity is correct?

options.text: He will likely become a chronic carrier and needs long-term monitoring
He needs lifelong hepatitis B vaccination to prevent superinfection
His household contacts need no evaluation
Hepatitis A never causes chronic infection; he will recover with lifelong IgG immunity

questions.explanation: IgM anti-HAV = acute hepatitis A, which never becomes chronic; recovery gives lifelong immunity.

questions.stem: A patient on traditional thrice-daily gentamicin has a trough level of 3.5 μg/mL. The best action is:

options.text: Continue the regimen — the level is therapeutic
Hold the dose and extend the interval — the trough is too high
Increase the dose to improve killing

questions.explanation: Gentamicin trough must be <2 μg/mL on traditional dosing; 3.5 = accumulation → hold/extend to avoid nephro- and ototoxicity.

questions.stem: Which toxicities make therapeutic drug monitoring essential for aminoglycosides?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycoside TDM guards against nephrotoxicity and (often irreversible) ototoxicity.

questions.stem: A drug follows first-order elimination with a half-life of 8 hours. After stopping the drug, approximately how long until ~97% has been eliminated?
questions.explanation: 4–5 half-lives eliminate ~97% (8 h × 4–5 = 32–40 h).

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with 12 months of amenorrhea has FSH 85 mIU/mL and estradiol <10 pg/mL. The best interpretation is:
questions.explanation: Low estradiol + high FSH = primary ovarian failure; low/low would point to the hypothalamic–pituitary axis.

questions.stem: Urine sediment from a diabetic patient shows budding oval structures, some with pseudohyphae. The most likely identification is:
questions.explanation: Budding ovals with pseudohyphae = Candida; budding separates yeast from RBCs.

questions.stem: Polarized microscopy of urine sediment shows round particles with Maltese-cross patterns in a specimen collected with powdered gloves; the urine has no proteinuria. The most likely identification is:
questions.explanation: Maltese crosses + powdered-glove collection + no proteinuria = starch artifact, not fatty casts.

questions.stem: Which urine sediment finding is a normal contaminant rather than a pathologic element?
questions.explanation: Scant mucus threads are a normal finding; the other three are all pathologic.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man's 24-hour urine collection contains 800 mg of creatinine. The collection is:
questions.explanation: 70 kg × 20–25 mg/kg/d ≈ 1400–1750 mg expected; 800 mg = under-collected.

questions.stem: An automated analyzer flags "giant platelets — platelet count unreliable" with a count of 45 × 10⁹/L. The patient is not bleeding. What is the best next step?

options.text: Manual hemocytometer platelet count with smear review

questions.explanation: Giant platelets are undercounted by analyzers; confirm with a manual hemocytometer count and smear review before acting on a spurious low count.

questions.stem: Leukemic blasts stain strongly positive for nonspecific esterase, and the staining is abolished by sodium fluoride. What lineage does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Nonspecific esterase (fluoride-inhibited) = monocytic lineage; chloroacetate esterase = granulocytic.

questions.stem: Blasts containing Auer rods stain strongly positive for myeloperoxidase by cytochemistry. What is the correct lineage assignment?
questions.explanation: Cytochemical MPO positivity (Auer rods are MPO-positive) = myeloid lineage (AML); ALL is MPO-negative.

questions.stem: A Kleihauer-Betke stain of maternal blood shows scattered dark-pink cells among pale ghost cells. What explains the staining difference?

options.text: Fetal hemoglobin resists acid elution while maternal hemoglobin elutes out
Maternal hemoglobin is denatured by the alkaline buffer
Fetal cells take up the counterstain more avidly because of their higher MCV
The ghost cells are reticulocytes that failed to stain

questions.explanation: Kleihauer-Betke = acid elution: HbF resists acid (pink cells), HbA elutes (ghost cells); the pink-cell percentage sizes the bleed for RhIG dosing.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis develops a microcytic anemia. Labs: serum iron elevated, ferritin 750 μg/L, TIBC low. Marrow shows ring sideroblasts. What is the mechanism of his anemia?

options.text: Iron deficiency from chronic blood loss
Defective heme synthesis with mitochondrial iron trapping

questions.explanation: Isoniazid inhibits ALA synthase (pyridoxal-phosphate dependent) → sideroblastic anemia: microcytic anemia with high ferritin/low TIBC (iron-overload pattern, opposite of iron deficiency) and ring sideroblasts from mitochondrial iron trapping.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (creatinine 3.4 mg/dL) has Hb 9.2 g/dL, MCV 91 fL, reticulocytes 0.5%, RPI <2. What is the most likely cause of his anemia?

options.text: Erythropoietin deficiency from chronic kidney disease

questions.explanation: CKD → EPO deficiency → normocytic hypoproliferative anemia (RPI <2); microcytic iron deficiency, macrocytic B12 deficiency, and hemolysis (high retic) are excluded by the indices and retic count.

questions.stem: Two days after an acute upper GI bleed, a patient has Hb 8.4 g/dL, MCV 93 fL, reticulocytes 1.1%, RPI 0.9. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Expected early response: normocytic anemia with retic rise in 5–7 days
Marrow failure — the RPI should exceed 2

questions.explanation: Acute hemorrhage is initially normocytic (whole-blood loss) and the retic response takes 5–7 days; RPI <2 on day 2 is expected, not marrow failure.

questions.stem: A patient has MCV 107 fL with no hypersegmented neutrophils; B12 and folate are normal. She takes hydroxyurea for essential thrombocythemia. What best explains the macrocytosis?
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea causes nonmegaloblastic macrocytosis (no hypersegmented neutrophils, normal B12/folate); review medications and TSH before chasing B12.

questions.stem: A smoker on hydrochlorothiazide has Hb 17.6 g/dL, Hct 53%, JAK2 negative, EPO normal, and an elevated BUN/creatinine ratio. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: Normal EPO + negative JAK2 + volume depletion = relative erythrocytosis (plasma-volume contraction); rehydrate and recheck before working up polycythemia.

questions.stem: A microcytic adult has HPLC showing HbA2 5.6%, HbF 1.2%, remainder HbA. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HbA2 >3.5–3.8% on HPLC = β-thalassemia trait; iron deficiency lowers (not raises) HbA2.

questions.stem: A sickle solubility test is positive in an asymptomatic adult with a normal hemoglobin level. What is the required next step?

options.text: Diagnose sickle cell disease and start hydroxyurea
Repeat the solubility test in 6 months
No further testing — the screen is diagnostic
Quantitate with HPLC or electrophoresis to distinguish trait from disease

questions.explanation: Solubility screens for HbS (positive in trait AND disease); HPLC/electrophoresis quantitation is required to distinguish them.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has 10 days of fever, exudative pharyngitis, and tender posterior cervical nodes. The smear shows atypical Downey lymphocytes; Monospot is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Classic IM triad (fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical LAD) + Downey atypical lymphocytes + positive heterophile = EBV; CMV is heterophile-negative.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with fatigue and circulating blasts has marrow blasts that are TdT+, CD10+, CD19+, with t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1. What does the cytogenetic finding imply?
questions.explanation: t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1 = favorable prognosis in B-ALL (TdT+/CD10+/CD19+); do not confuse with Philadelphia-positive (BCR-ABL1) ALL.

questions.stem: An HIV-positive patient has an absolute CD4 count of 180/μL with a normal CD4%. What is the clinical significance?

options.text: Indication for immediate bone marrow biopsy
Laboratory error — the percentage matters, not the absolute count

questions.explanation: Absolute CD4 <200/μL = AIDS-defining; monitor the absolute count (not just the percentage) with consistently timed draws.

questions.stem: Which activator–inhibitor pairing in the fibrinolytic pathway is correct?

options.text: tPA — inhibited by PAI-1; plasmin — inhibited by α2-antiplasmin

questions.explanation: PAI-1 inhibits tPA/uPA; α2-antiplasmin inhibits plasmin; TAFI removes fibrin lysine residues.

questions.stem: A patient has mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal platelet count, normal PT/APTT, and normal vWF studies. What category of disorder should be considered?
questions.explanation: Normal platelets/PT/APTT/vWF with bleeding = think vascular wall disorder (scurvy, HSP, Ehlers-Danlos).

questions.stem: A patient bleeds excessively after dental extraction. PT, APTT, platelets, and vWF studies are all normal, but the euglobulin lysis time is 45 minutes and the clot lyses rapidly in the tube. What is the best treatment?
questions.explanation: Normal routine labs + rapid clot lysis = hyperfibrinolysis (α2-antiplasmin/PAI-1 deficiency); treat with tranexamic acid.

questions.stem: A patient's thrombin time is prolonged but the reptilase time is normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Prolonged TT with normal (heparin-insensitive) reptilase time = heparin effect; dysfibrinogenemia prolongs both.

questions.stem: A trauma patient's TEG shows a prolonged R time with a normal MA and normal LY30. Which component is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Prolonged TEG R time = factor deficiency → plasma; normal MA means platelet/fibrinogen strength is adequate.

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops platelets 28 × 10⁹/L. Marrow shows markedly decreased megakaryocytes with no dysplasia. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy → decreased megakaryocytes = production failure; destructive causes (ITP/TTP/HIT) show increased marrow megakaryocytes.

questions.stem: Both collagen/ADP and collagen/epinephrine closure times are prolonged on the PFA-100. The patient takes no antiplatelet drugs. What is the best next test?

options.text: von Willebrand factor activity and antigen (VWD workup)

questions.explanation: Prolonged closure times on both PFA cartridges (no drug effect) → VWD workup (vWF activity/antigen, RCo/Ag ratio).

questions.stem: A dRVVT screen is prolonged, the 1:1 mixing study still shows prolongation, and adding excess phospholipid corrects the clotting time. What does this confirm?
questions.explanation: dRVVT screen prolonged + no mixing correction + phospholipid correction = lupus anticoagulant (immediate-acting; no incubation needed).

questions.stem: Which assay approach detects a type II (dysfunctional molecule) protein C deficiency?
questions.explanation: Type II protein C deficiency (normal antigen, low function) requires a functional chromogenic activity assay; antigenic assays miss it.

questions.stem: A TEG run in a plain cup shows a markedly prolonged R time, but the heparinase cup is normal. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Correction in the heparinase TEG cup (vs plain cup) isolates a heparin effect; warfarin/factor deficiency prolong both.

questions.stem: A patient's red cells forward-type as group O, but her serum agglutinates group O reagent cells in the reverse type. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Forward O with anti-H agglutinating O cells in reverse = Bombay phenotype.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman types RhD-positive by direct test but shows a weak D discrepancy on confirmatory testing. How is her RhD status best resolved?

options.text: Repeat the direct typing with a different manufacturer's reagent
Treat her as Rh-negative and give RhIG routinely
RHD genotyping to distinguish partial D from weak D types 1, 2, or 3
Type her partner and predict the fetus by pedigree

questions.explanation: RHD genotyping resolves weak D vs partial D discrepancies.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old develops dark urine and pallor one week after a viral upper respiratory infection. DAT is positive for C3d only, and the Donath-Landsteiner test is positive. Which antibody is responsible?
questions.explanation: PCH: Donath-Landsteiner biphasic IgG anti-P in a child after viral infection.

questions.stem: A woman in her first pregnancy delivers a term infant with platelets 18,000/μL and an intracranial hemorrhage. The mother is healthy with a normal platelet count. Why is fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia still the leading diagnosis despite no prior pregnancies?

options.text: FNAIT from maternal anti-HPA-1a commonly affects the first pregnancy, unlike HDFN
First-pregnancy HDFN is more common than FNAIT
Maternal ITP always presents this way in first pregnancies
Alloimmune thrombocytopenia requires prior transfusion, which she must have forgotten

questions.explanation: FNAIT (anti-HPA-1a) strikes the first pregnancy; no prior sensitization is required.

questions.stem: After the D antigen, which red cell antigen is the most immunogenic?
questions.explanation: K (Kell) is second only to RhD in immunogenicity (relative potency 0.10 vs D's 0.70); Fya, Jka, and S rank much lower.

questions.stem: A donor types as group A forward, and the blood bank wants to determine A1 vs A2 subgroup. Which reagent settles it?
questions.explanation: Dolichos biflorus (anti-A1 lectin) distinguishes A1 from A2.

questions.stem: A D-alloimmunized pregnant woman's anti-D titer was 8 at 24 weeks and is 32 at 28 weeks, tested in parallel. What does this change signify?

options.text: A significant rise (≥2 dilutions) — intensify fetal surveillance
No change — titers fluctuate by one dilution normally
Laboratory error — titers cannot rise this fast

questions.explanation: A ≥2-dilution (4-fold) titer rise is significant in HDFN monitoring.

questions.stem: An antibody panel suggests anti-P1, but the reactivity is weak. Which confirmatory test uses soluble P1 substance to prove the specificity?
questions.explanation: Hydatid cyst fluid neutralizes anti-P1, confirming specificity.

questions.stem: A blood donor is in the early HBV window period after exposure: HBsAg is not yet detectable and anti-HBc is still negative. Which required donor screening test is most likely to detect this infectious donation?
questions.explanation: HBV NAT detects infection during the early window period before HBsAg or anti-HBc become detectable.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the ISBT 128 Donation Identification Number (DIN) on every blood unit label?

options.text: To encode the donor's blood type for emergency release
To indicate the unit's expiration date
To provide a globally unique identifier enabling traceability from donor to recipient
To certify the unit has been irradiated

questions.explanation: The DIN is a globally unique identifier for donor-to-recipient traceability.

questions.stem: An RBC unit collected in CPD (no additive solution) is 30 days old and refrigerated at 4°C. Can it be transfused?

options.text: Yes — RBCs are good for 42 days refrigerated
Yes — if the segments show no hemolysis
No — CPD-preserved RBCs expire at 21 days
No — CPD units must be frozen after 14 days

questions.explanation: CPD RBCs expire at 21 days; a 30-day unit is outdated.

questions.stem: Which preservative system permits the longest RBC storage?
questions.explanation: Additive solutions (AS-1/AS-3/AS-5) give 42-day storage, the longest.

questions.stem: A shipment of RBC units arrives from the regional blood center and the transport container's temperature logger reads 11°C. The units feel cool and look normal. What is the correct action?

options.text: Quarantine the units and do not transfuse until the excursion is evaluated
Transfuse them immediately before they warm further
Refreeze them to restore the cold chain
Accept them since they still feel cool

questions.explanation: Temperature excursion (11°C for RBCs): quarantine and evaluate; do not transfuse on appearance.

questions.stem: A neonate requires large-volume transfusion for hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. The blood bank selects RBC units less than 7 days old rather than 35-day-old units. What complication of older stored blood is being avoided?

options.text: Hyperkalemia from potassium leakage during storage

questions.explanation: Older stored RBCs accumulate extracellular K⁺; neonates getting large volumes need fresher units.

questions.stem: Washed RBCs were prepared by the open method at 8:00 AM yesterday for a patient with recurrent severe allergic transfusion reactions. Surgery is delayed and it is now 2:00 PM today (30 hours later). The unit was kept at 1–6°C. What should be done?

options.text: Transfuse it — washed RBCs keep 42 days like other RBCs
Return it to the freezer for later use
Discard it — open-method washed RBCs expire 24 hours after washing

questions.explanation: Open-method washed RBCs expire 24 hours after washing.

questions.stem: A burn patient needs plasma volume expansion but has normal coagulation studies. The team wants a product with no risk of viral transmission. Which is the best choice?
questions.explanation: Albumin: heat-treated fractionation product, no viral risk, no clotting factors — for volume expansion.

questions.stem: During pre-issue inspection, a 4-day-old apheresis platelet unit shows no swirling when gently agitated. The bag is intact and there is no discoloration. What is the correct action?

options.text: Do not issue it — quarantine and investigate per SOP
Issue it — swirling is not a required check
Warm it to 37°C to restore swirling, then issue
Issue it for a non-bleeding patient only

questions.explanation: No swirling = suspect nonviable/contaminated platelets; do not issue.

questions.stem: A leukemia patient has 1-hour CCIs of 3,200 and 2,800 after two consecutive apheresis platelet transfusions. The 24-hour counts are also poor. What is the best next step?

options.text: Increase the platelet dose to two units per transfusion
Screen for HLA antibodies and provide HLA-matched or crossmatch-compatible platelets

questions.explanation: Repeated 1-h CCI <7,500 = immune refractoriness; use HLA-matched/crossmatch-compatible platelets.

questions.stem: Six months after donating, a repeat blood donor tests positive for HCV NAT. Two RBC units from his prior donation were transfused. What must the blood bank do?

options.text: Nothing — the prior units tested negative at the time
Initiate lookback: quarantine any in-date units from that donor and notify the transfusion services that received the prior units so recipients can be informed and tested
Discard current inventory but take no action on transfused units

questions.explanation: Positive post-donation testing triggers lookback: quarantine in-date units, notify consignees about prior recipients.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with beta-thalassemia major has received monthly RBC transfusions for 10 years. Ferritin is 2,800 μg/L and cardiac MRI shows myocardial iron deposition. What is the diagnosis and required therapy?

options.text: Anemia of inflammation — treat with erythropoietin
Transfusional iron overload — start iron chelation therapy

questions.explanation: Chronic transfusion → iron overload (ferritin 2,800, cardiac iron); treat with chelation.

questions.stem: During massive transfusion with citrate-containing blood products, the patient's ionized calcium falls and the QT interval prolongs. What is the mechanism and the correct treatment?

options.text: Citrate chelates ionized calcium — give calcium supplementation
Citrate causes hyperkalemia — give insulin and glucose
Dilutional coagulopathy from volume replacement — give plasma
Hypothermia from cold blood products — actively warm the patient

questions.explanation: Citrate chelates ionized calcium; massive transfusion can overwhelm hepatic citrate metabolism, causing hypocalcemia with QT prolongation — treat with calcium.

questions.stem: Three weeks after receiving RBCs during summer in New England, a 70-year-old develops fever, fatigue, and hemolytic anemia. The blood smear shows intraerythrocytic ring forms and Maltese-cross tetrads. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Maltese-cross forms weeks after RBC transfusion = transfusion-transmitted Babesia.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman is scheduled for elective total hip replacement in 6 weeks. Preoperative labs show Hb 9.8 g/dL with iron deficiency. From a patient blood management perspective, what is the best plan?

options.text: Proceed with surgery and transfuse 2 units preoperatively
Delay elective surgery, treat the iron deficiency, and plan cell salvage/antifibrinolytic use
Transfuse to Hb 13 g/dL the day before surgery

questions.explanation: PBM: treat preoperative iron-deficiency anemia before elective surgery; minimize loss intraoperatively.

questions.stem: A healthy 24-year-old woman volunteers to donate whole blood. Her hemoglobin is 12.2 g/dL, blood pressure 118/76, pulse 72, temperature 98.4°F, weight 135 lb. What is the correct donor action?

options.text: Accept her; hemoglobin is adequate for donation
Temporarily defer her for low hemoglobin
Accept her but collect a reduced volume

questions.explanation: Female donor Hb 12.2 g/dL is below the ≥12.5 g/dL minimum: temporary deferral for low Hb.

notes.note: US rule (21 CFR 630.10): female allogeneic ≥ 12.5 g/dL (12.0–12.5 only under an FDA-acceptable procedure); male allogeneic ≥ 13.0 g/dL.

questions.stem: A repeat donor gave whole blood 5 weeks ago and returns to donate again. He meets all other criteria. What should the collection staff tell him?

options.text: He may donate today since he feels well
He may donate a half unit today
He may donate by apheresis instead with no waiting period
He must wait until at least 8 weeks after his last whole-blood donation

questions.explanation: Minimum whole-blood donation interval is 8 weeks (56 days).

questions.stem: During a whole-blood collection, flow is sluggish and 450 mL is finally collected 16 minutes after venipuncture. The unit looks normal. What is the correct disposition?

options.text: Discard the unit; collections exceeding 10 minutes are not acceptable
Transfuse it as whole blood only, not as components
Use it but label it "slow draw" for the transfusion service
Incubate it 30 minutes to dissolve microclots, then process normally

questions.explanation: Collection must finish within 10 minutes of venipuncture; a 16-minute draw is discarded.

questions.stem: Midway through a whole-blood donation, the donor becomes pale and diaphoretic, complains of nausea, and her pulse drops to 48. What is the reaction and the correct immediate management?

options.text: Citrate toxicity — give IV calcium gluconate
Vasovagal syncope — stop the collection, place her supine with legs elevated, apply a cold compress

questions.explanation: Vasovagal syncope: stop collection, supine with legs elevated, cold compress, monitor.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man scheduled for elective hip replacement in 3 weeks wants to donate autologous blood. His hemoglobin is 11.5 g/dL and he is otherwise healthy. What is the correct decision?

options.text: Defer — he does not meet the 12.5 g/dL allogeneic hemoglobin minimum
Accept — autologous donors may donate with Hb ≥11.0 g/dL
Accept only if he also finds a directed donor as backup
Defer — autologous donation is not allowed within 4 weeks of surgery

questions.explanation: Autologous donation allows Hb ≥11.0 g/dL (lower than the allogeneic minimum).

questions.stem: A family insists on directed donation from the patient's brother for an upcoming surgery, believing it is safer than community blood. What is the most accurate counseling?

options.text: Directed donors must meet all standard donor criteria with full infectious-disease testing, and there is no evidence directed donation is safer than volunteer blood
Directed donation eliminates the risk of transfusion-transmitted infections
Directed donors are exempt from infectious-disease testing
Directed donation is prohibited for elective surgery

questions.explanation: Directed donors meet full criteria/testing; no evidence of superior safety.

questions.stem: A patient with a recent high-risk exposure has a reactive 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab screen but a negative HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay. What is the next step?

options.text: Perform HIV-1 nucleic acid testing to evaluate for acute infection
Report the patient as HIV-negative; the screen was a false positive
Repeat the 4th-generation screen in one year
Start antiretroviral therapy immediately without further testing

questions.explanation: Reactive Ag/Ab + negative differentiation → HIV-1 NAT for acute (p24-positive, antibody-negative) infection.

questions.stem: Which HIV marker becomes detectable first after infection?
questions.explanation: p24 antigen is the earliest detectable HIV marker.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks' gestation has negative rubella IgG. She asks about vaccination. What is the correct advice?

options.text: Give MMR now — pregnancy is not a contraindication
She is susceptible: avoid exposure during pregnancy and vaccinate with MMR postpartum
She is immune — negative IgG means past infection
Give rubella immune globulin monthly until delivery

questions.explanation: Rubella IgG-negative pregnant woman is susceptible; MMR is given postpartum, not during pregnancy.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman has positive CMV IgM with low-avidity CMV IgG. What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: Recent primary CMV infection — the highest risk pattern for congenital transmission
Old CMV infection with no fetal risk
Laboratory error — IgM and IgG cannot both be positive

questions.explanation: CMV IgM + low-avidity IgG = recent primary infection; highest congenital risk.

questions.stem: A specimen arrives in the laboratory with an unlabeled tube containing urine. The patient is standing at the counter asking about wait times. What is the correct action?

options.text: Process it immediately to save time
Reject the specimen and request a recollection
Label it based on the requisition information
Hold it until the phlebotomist returns

questions.explanation: Never process or relabel an unlabeled specimen; reject and recollect.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects current guidance on specimen processing areas?

options.text: All clinical specimens must always be processed inside a Class II biosafety cabinet
Routine chemistry specimens require a Class II BSC
Specimens likely to generate aerosols or containing suspected high-risk (e.g., BSL-3) agents require appropriate BSC handling; routine closed-specimen chemistry work follows standard precautions
Urine cultures are processed on the open bench even when aerosol risk exists

questions.explanation: Aerosol-generating/high-risk-agent processing requires BSC containment; routine closed-specimen work follows standard precautions.

questions.stem: A hospital wants to reduce needlestick injuries from blood collection. Which OSHA-required intervention is most effective?

options.text: Using needleless systems and engineering controls (e.g., safety needles)

questions.explanation: OSHA requires engineering controls (safety needles, needleless systems); recapping is prohibited.

questions.stem: A coagulase-negative staphylococcus isolated from blood cultures causes aggressive endocarditis clinically resembling S. aureus infection. Which organism and breakpoint rule apply?

options.text: S. lugdunensis — use S. aureus breakpoints
S. haemolyticus — use S. aureus breakpoints

questions.explanation: S. lugdunensis is coagulase-negative but uses S. aureus breakpoints because it behaves clinically like S. aureus.

questions.stem: Which two organisms are both catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci?
questions.explanation: Strep and enterococci are catalase-negative; staph and Micrococcus are catalase-positive.

questions.stem: Which reaction pattern is seen with Streptococcus pneumoniae?
questions.explanation: S. pneumoniae: optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble; viridans strep are the opposite.

questions.stem: A Gram-negative rod isolated from a wound grows on blood agar, is oxidase-positive, and produces a fruity (grape-like) odor. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Fruity-odor, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod = Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.stem: A stool culture from a patient with bloody diarrhea grows colorless colonies on MacConkey agar. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Colorless (non-lactose-fermenting) MacConkey colonies + bloody diarrhea = Shigella.

questions.stem: Which organism is associated with puncture wounds through the soles of sneakers?
questions.explanation: Sneaker-sole puncture wound → Pseudomonas aeruginosa osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: A laboratory worker is stuck by a needle contaminated with blood from a patient with unknown HBV status. The worker completed the HBV vaccine series 5 years ago. What is the recommended post-exposure action?

options.text: No action needed — vaccinated workers are always protected
Test the worker's anti-HBs; if inadequate, give HBIG plus a vaccine booster
Give HBIG to all exposed workers regardless of vaccine history
Wait 6 months and test for HBsAg

questions.explanation: Verify anti-HBs after exposure; inadequate responders get HBIG + booster.

questions.stem: An oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod is isolated from a blood culture. Which organism group is ruled OUT?
questions.explanation: E. coli (Enterobacterales) is oxidase-negative; Pseudomonas, Vibrio, and Aeromonas are oxidase-positive.

questions.stem: A sheep blood agar plate shows beta-hemolytic, catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains. Bacitracin disk: no zone of inhibition. PYR test: positive. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Bacitracin-resistant + PYR-positive beta-hemolytic streptococcus = Enterococcus (group B is PYR-negative).

notes.note: Enterococcus is its own genus, and most isolates are not β-hemolytic (about 20% were in one 2026 study). The answer stands, but confirm Enterococcus by growth in 6.5% NaCl and a positive bile esculin test.

questions.stem: A sputum culture grows chalky white colonies with an earthy odor. Gram stain shows beaded Gram-positive rods in chains; the modified Kinyoun stain is positive. Which organism is most likely, and what is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation: Partially acid-fast Nocardia: TMP-SMX is the drug of choice.

questions.stem: An HIV-positive patient with CD4 45/μL has a positive serum cryptococcal antigen. India ink of CSF shows encapsulated budding yeasts. Which antifungal regimen is indicated for induction?
questions.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis induction: amphotericin B + flucytosine.

questions.stem: A patient with a CD4 count of 30/μL develops painless white plaques on the tongue that cannot be scraped off. Biopsy shows parakeratosis with EBV-positive cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Non-scrapable EBV-positive white plaques = oral hairy leukoplakia; thrush scrapes off.

questions.stem: A sputum sample grows a mold with septate hyphae, uniseriate phialides covering the entire vesicle, and smooth round conidia. Which Aspergillus species is most likely?
questions.explanation: A. niger: uniseriate phialides over the entire vesicle, smooth round conidia.

questions.stem: A mold isolated from a sinus aspirate shows broad, aseptate hyphae with 90-degree branching and rhizoids. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Broad aseptate hyphae + 90° branching + rhizoids = Rhizopus (mucormycosis).

questions.stem: Which hepatitis B serologic pattern indicates immunity from vaccination rather than past infection?
questions.explanation: Anti-HBs positive + anti-HBc negative = vaccine immunity; anti-HBc positivity marks natural infection.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive RPR (1:16) and a positive FTA-ABS. After treatment, the RPR falls to 1:4. What does the RPR decline demonstrate?

options.text: The treponemal test has become negative
Adequate treatment response by a fourfold (two-dilution) titer decline

questions.explanation: A fourfold (two-dilution) RPR decline = adequate syphilis treatment; treponemal tests stay positive for life.

questions.stem: A new lot of group A strep rapid antigen kits arrives. The laboratory runs the kit's positive and negative external controls. Why are these required even though the kit has an internal control line?

options.text: Internal controls only verify sample flow, not that the kit detects antigen
External controls are optional for waived kits
The FDA requires daily calibration of lateral-flow kits

questions.explanation: Internal control lines check flow only; external controls verify antigen detection with each new lot.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a positive NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis from a vaginal swab. She is asymptomatic. What is the recommended management?

options.text: No treatment — asymptomatic infections clear spontaneously
Treat with an appropriate antichlamydial regimen and ensure partner evaluation/treatment
Repeat the NAAT in 6 months before deciding
Treat only if a culture confirms the result

questions.explanation: Asymptomatic NAAT-positive chlamydia is treated without culture confirmation, with partner evaluation/treatment.

questions.stem: Which specimen is unacceptable for anaerobic culture?

options.text: Tissue aspirate in an anaerobic transport vial
A superficial wound swab of a decubitus ulcer
Blood in anaerobic blood culture bottles

questions.explanation: Superficial swabs are unacceptable for anaerobic culture; submit deep aspirates or tissue.

questions.stem: A stool specimen from a patient with watery diarrhea after clindamycin therapy is submitted for C. difficile testing. Which test approach is recommended?

options.text: Culture for C. difficile on selective agar as the sole test
Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) plus toxin A/B EIA, or a NAAT for the toxin gene
Gram stain of stool for Gram-positive rods
Repeat testing of three consecutive stools by toxin EIA alone

questions.explanation: C. difficile: GDH + toxin EIA algorithm or toxin-gene NAAT; neither toxin EIA alone nor culture alone suffices.

questions.stem: A burn patient develops bacteremia; blood cultures grow a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod that is indole-negative and produces a positive string test. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Indole-negative lactose fermenter with positive string test = Klebsiella pneumoniae.

questions.stem: A blood culture from a neutropenic patient grows Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains that are PYR-positive and grow in 6.5% NaCl. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: PYR-positive + 6.5% NaCl growth = Enterococcus.

questions.stem: A technologist performs an AFB smear on a sputum specimen from a patient with suspected tuberculosis. Where must this work be performed, and what is the minimum containment for propagating M. tuberculosis cultures?

options.text: Open bench for smears; BSL-2 for cultures
Class II BSC for smear preparation; BSL-3 practices for propagating cultures
BSL-4 laboratory for all TB work
Fume hood for smears; BSL-1 for cultures

questions.explanation: AFB smears: Class II BSC; M. tuberculosis culture propagation: BSL-3 practices.

questions.stem: A CSF specimen from a meningitis patient is inoculated to chocolate agar and incubated at 35°C in 5–10% CO₂. Which organism is the intended target of these conditions?
questions.explanation: Chocolate agar + 5–10% CO₂ targets fastidious N. meningitidis.

questions.stem: A patient with bacterial meningitis has CSF with markedly decreased glucose, elevated protein, and a neutrophilic pleocytosis. Which pattern does this represent?
questions.explanation: Low CSF glucose + high protein + neutrophilic pleocytosis = bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: A child with otitis media is treated with amoxicillin. Which organism is the most common bacterial cause of acute otitis media?
questions.explanation: S. pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of acute otitis media.

questions.stem: A sputum Gram stain from a patient with community-acquired pneumonia shows many neutrophils but no predominant organism, and the culture grows normal respiratory flora. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The patient does not have pneumonia
An atypical pathogen (e.g., Mycoplasma) not recovered on routine culture
The Gram stain was performed incorrectly
Normal flora is the cause of the pneumonia

questions.explanation: Purulent sputum + no dominant routine-culture organism = atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma/Chlamydophila/Legionella).

questions.stem: A sputum culture from a cystic fibrosis patient grows a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod that is oxidase-positive and smells like grapes. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Fruity-odor oxidase-positive nonfermenter in CF = Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.stem: A catheterized patient's urine grows 50,000 CFU/mL of E. coli with pyuria, and she has dysuria and fever. How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Significant bacteriuria: in symptomatic or catheterized patients lower counts are clinically significant

questions.explanation: In symptomatic/catheterized patients with pyuria, counts well below 100,000 CFU/mL are significant bacteriuria.

questions.stem: A urine culture grows >100,000 CFU/mL of three different organisms in an asymptomatic patient. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: ≥3 organisms at high counts in an asymptomatic patient = contamination; recollect.

questions.stem: A wound culture grows Staphylococcus aureus susceptible to oxacillin. The laboratory also reports a positive beta-lactamase test. What does the beta-lactamase result mean for therapy?

options.text: The isolate is MRSA — avoid all beta-lactams
Penicillin G will be ineffective but antistaphylococcal penicillins (nafcillin/oxacillin) remain effective

questions.explanation: Beta-lactamase-positive but oxacillin-susceptible S. aureus = MSSA; penicillin G fails but nafcillin/oxacillin work.

questions.stem: A blood culture set (two bottles) grows coagulase-negative staphylococci in one bottle only; the patient has no indwelling device and is clinically stable. What is the most likely interpretation?
questions.explanation: Single-bottle CoNS, stable patient, no device = contamination.

questions.stem: A laboratory identifies a pure bacterial colony by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry within minutes. What is a recognized limitation of this method?

options.text: It cannot identify bacteria to the species level
It requires a pure isolate — it cannot reliably identify organisms directly from polymicrobial specimens
It requires 48 hours of incubation before testing
It only works on Gram-positive organisms

questions.explanation: MALDI-TOF requires a pure isolate; it cannot reliably identify organisms directly from polymicrobial specimens.

questions.stem: A patient with fever and a new heart murmur has three sets of blood cultures drawn before antibiotics; all grow viridans streptococci. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Multiple pre-antibiotic blood culture sets + new murmur growing viridans strep = infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with Clostridioides difficile infection. Which antibiotic is a recommended first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) is first-line for C. difficile; clindamycin is a precipitant, not a treatment.

questions.stem: A stool ova-and-parasite examination shows cysts with four nuclei and no ingested red blood cells. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Multinucleated (up to 8) cysts without ingested RBCs = commensal Entamoeba coli.

questions.stem: A traveler with watery diarrhea has stool ova-and-parasite testing positive for Giardia lamblia. Which treatment is indicated?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is first-line for Giardia lamblia.

questions.stem: A patient's serum is positive for HBsAg and HBeAg, with elevated ALT. Which phase of chronic hepatitis B does this represent?
questions.explanation: HBeAg-positive chronic HBV with elevated ALT = immune-active phase.

questions.stem: A rapid influenza molecular assay is positive in a hospitalized patient during flu season. What is the recommended action?

options.text: No action — rapid tests are unreliable
Initiate appropriate antiviral therapy and infection-control precautions
Repeat the test in one week

questions.explanation: Positive molecular flu assay in a hospitalized patient → antivirals + infection-control precautions.

questions.stem: A sputum smear from a patient with suspected tuberculosis is being stained. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Crystal violet → Gram's iodine → acetone-alcohol → safranin
Carbolfuchsin (driven in with heat or phenol) → acid-alcohol decolorizer → methylene blue counterstain

questions.explanation: Acid-fast order: carbolfuchsin (heat/phenol) → acid-alcohol → methylene blue; mycolic acid resists decolorization.

questions.stem: A bronchoalveolar lavage specimen is screened for fungi with calcofluor white and fluoresces brightly under UV light. The correct interpretation is:

options.text: Fungal elements are present — calcofluor white binds chitin/cellulose in fungal walls; culture is still needed for speciation
The specimen needs no further workup

questions.explanation: Calcofluor white binds chitin/cellulose, fluoresces under UV; screen only — culture still needed to speciate.

questions.stem: A CSF specimen with a very low organism burden is stained with acridine orange. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The stain identifies the bacterial species
It replaces the Gram stain for all specimen types
Bacteria appear blue against a bright background
Bacteria fluoresce bright orange against a dark background — more sensitive than Gram stain for detection, but Gram stain and culture must follow

questions.explanation: Acridine orange: bacteria fluoresce orange, more sensitive than Gram stain for scant organisms; detects, does not identify.

questions.stem: During a Salmonella outbreak investigation, isolates are serotyped by the Kauffmann-White scheme. Serotype assignment is based on:
questions.explanation: Kauffmann-White Salmonella serotyping = O (somatic) + H (flagellar) antigens; drives outbreak tracking.

questions.stem: A gastroenterologist wants to confirm H. pylori infection from a gastric biopsy taken at endoscopy. Which test exploits the organism's defining enzyme?

options.text: Rapid urease test on the biopsy — H. pylori urease neutralizes gastric acid (urea breath test and stool antigen are the noninvasive alternatives)

questions.explanation: H. pylori detected via urease: rapid urease on biopsy, urea breath test, or stool antigen.

questions.stem: A laboratory is evaluating an automated identification system (Vitek 2 / MicroScan / BD Phoenix). Which statement is correct?

options.text: It eliminates the need for conventional confirmation of unusual profiles
It performs susceptibility testing by disk diffusion
It identifies organisms from biochemical profiles in hours; unusual or low-discrimination profiles still require conventional confirmation
It sequences 16S rRNA on every isolate

questions.explanation: Automated ID (Vitek 2/MicroScan/Phoenix) from biochemical profiles in hours; confirm unusual profiles conventionally.

questions.stem: A blood-culture isolate cannot be identified by any biochemical panel. The definitive next step is:

options.text: Repeating the same panel until it resolves
16S rRNA sequencing — universal primers amplify conserved and variable regions for a definitive bacterial identification

questions.explanation: Unidentifiable isolate → 16S rRNA sequencing (universal primers, conserved + variable regions).

questions.stem: A patient receiving gentamicin and clindamycin asks how the two antibiotics differ. The best answer is:

options.text: Gentamicin targets the 30S ribosome and is bactericidal; clindamycin targets the 50S ribosome and is generally bacteriostatic — "30S kills, 50S stills"
Both block the folate pathway at sequential steps

questions.explanation: "30S kills, 50S stills": aminoglycosides bactericidal at 30S; macrolides/clindamycin generally bacteriostatic at 50S.

questions.stem: A technologist notes large boxcar Gram-positive rods that are non-hemolytic and non-motile, with Medusa-head colonies. The correct immediate action is:

options.text: Stop open-bench work, perform rule-out testing in the biological safety cabinet only, and refer the isolate to the state public health laboratory (LRN reference lab)
Continue full identification on the open bench
Dismiss it as a Bacillus subtilis contaminant
Autoclave the plate without notifying anyone

questions.explanation: Boxcar rods + Medusa-head = presumptive B. anthracis: BSC rule-out only, refer to LRN reference lab.

questions.stem: A MGIT broth culture flags positive and the smear shows acid-fast bacilli. The fastest reliable identification is:

options.text: A nucleic acid probe (MTBC, MAC, M. kansasii, M. gordonae) or 16S rRNA/hsp65/rpoB sequencing; Xpert MTB/RIF detects MTBC and rifampin resistance directly

questions.explanation: Rapid mycobacterial ID: nucleic acid probes or 16S/hsp65/rpoB sequencing; Xpert MTB/RIF = MTBC + rifampin resistance.

questions.stem: Which set of elements must be documented for every microbiology result in the LIS?

options.text: Positive results only; negatives need no documentation
Organism and susceptibility; collection details are optional
Organism, quantity/colony count, susceptibility interpretation, collection date/time, specimen source, and collector

questions.explanation: Document organism, quantity, susceptibility, collection date/time, source, collector; chain of custody for forensic specimens.

questions.stem: A CSF Gram stain is positive in a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis. The required action is:

options.text: Release the result to the chart; the provider will see it
Directly notify the provider with read-back, and document who was notified and when
Hold the result until culture confirms the organism

questions.explanation: Positive CSF Gram stain = critical value: direct provider notification with read-back, documented.

questions.stem: A laboratory proposes autoverifying negative urine cultures after complete incubation and positive blood cultures. Which is correct?

options.text: Defined negatives after complete incubation may auto-release; positive and critical results always require technologist review and never autoverify
Positive blood cultures may autoverify; negatives require review
Autoverification applies to all microbiology results equally

questions.explanation: Only defined negatives after complete incubation may auto-release; micro positives never autoverify.

questions.stem: A released blood-culture report is discovered to name the wrong organism. The correct procedure is:

options.text: Silently overwrite the result in the LIS
Delete the original report and re-enter it
Issue a corrected report, directly notify the ordering provider, and document the correction and notification
Add a bench-only comment invisible to the provider

questions.explanation: Corrected report + direct provider notification + documentation; never silently overwrite.

questions.stem: The microbiology laboratory identifies a cluster of CRE bloodstream infections across two nursing units. The required response is:

options.text: Document the cluster in the LIS and take no further action
Alert infection control immediately and report to public health authorities as required by law — the micro lab is the hospital's early-warning system for MDROs and outbreaks
Wait to see whether the cluster resolves on its own
Notify only the ordering providers of the individual patients

questions.explanation: MDRO/outbreak clusters → infection control immediately; notifiable diseases → public health by law.

questions.stem: A patient's CBC shows WBC 8.0 × 10⁹/L with a manual differential of 62% segmented neutrophils and 5% band neutrophils. What is the absolute neutrophil count (ANC)?
questions.explanation: ANC = WBC × (segmented % + band %) = 8.0 × 0.67 = 5.36 × 10⁹/L; both segs and bands count toward the ANC.
